questions.title: European mid-size and enterprise accounts created in 2024
questions.primary: SELECT with column aliases and WHERE
questions.secondary: IN, half-open date range, ORDER BY, CAST to DATE

sections.context: Sales operations wants a quick list of the larger European accounts that signed up during calendar year 2024 so they can be offered a regional onboarding workshop.
sections.problem:
Return every organization whose `segment` is `'Mid-Market'` or `'Enterprise'`, whose `country_code` is Germany (`DE`), the United Kingdom (`GB`) or the Netherlands (`NL`), and that was created in calendar year 2024 (UTC).
Show the creation date only (no time part) in a column called `created_date`.
sections.expected:
One row per organization with columns `org_id, org_name, segment, country_code, created_date`.
Sort by `created_date`, then `org_id`.
sections.edge_cases:
- "Created in 2024" must include 2024-12-31 23:59:59 and exclude 2025-01-01 00:00:00.
- Several organizations can be created on the same date, so `org_id` is needed as a tie-breaker.
- Soft-deleted organizations are still customers for this list (no filter on `is_deleted`).
sections.hint1: You need three independent filters combined with AND: one on segment, one on country, one on the creation time.
sections.hint2: `IN (...)` is the readable way to test membership in a short list. For the time filter, prefer a half-open range `>= start AND < next_start` over functions on the column.
sections.hint3: `WHERE segment IN (...) AND country_code IN (...) AND created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01'`, then `CAST(created_at AS DATE) AS created_date` in the SELECT list.
sections.solution:
SELECT org_id,
       org_name,
       segment,
       country_code,
       CAST(created_at AS DATE) AS created_date
FROM organizations
WHERE segment IN ('Mid-Market', 'Enterprise')
  AND country_code IN ('DE', 'GB', 'NL')
  AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
ORDER BY created_date, org_id;
sections.explanation:
1. `IN` keeps the segment and country filters short and readable; each list is an OR in disguise.
2. The year filter uses a **half-open interval**: `>= 2024-01-01 00:00:00` and `< 2025-01-01 00:00:00`. It includes every instant of 2024 regardless of the time part and does not wrap the column in a function, so an index on `created_at` stays usable.
3. `CAST(created_at AS DATE)` drops the time for display only. Ordering by the alias `created_date` is allowed in both engines because ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT.
4. `org_id` makes the ordering deterministic when two organizations share a date.

`TIMESTAMP '...'` is the standard typed literal and works in PostgreSQL and MySQL. A plain string `'2024-01-01'` would also be converted implicitly.
sections.mistakes:
- `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) = 2024` returns the right rows but prevents index use on large tables.
- `created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'` silently drops everything after midnight on 31 December.
- Writing `segment = 'Mid-Market' OR segment = 'Enterprise' AND country_code IN (...)` without parentheses changes the meaning (AND binds tighter than OR).
sections.performance: On a large table, a B-tree index on `(country_code, created_at)` or `(created_at)` serves this query. A function on the column, such as `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at)`, would need an expression index instead.
sections.interview: Interviewers look for half-open date ranges and deterministic ordering. They also check that the candidate knows about the BETWEEN-with-timestamps trap without being prompted.

questions.title: Distinct acquisition channels including unknowns
questions.secondary: COALESCE, NULL as a value in DISTINCT, ORDER BY

sections.context: Marketing is cleaning up its channel taxonomy and needs the list of channel values that actually occur in the user table, including users whose channel was never captured.
sections.problem: List every distinct acquisition channel found in `users`. Show missing channels (NULL) as the text `'unknown'`. Return one row per channel, sorted alphabetically.
sections.expected: Column `channel`; one row per distinct value; sorted ascending. Expect six rows (five real channels plus `unknown`).
sections.edge_cases:
- DISTINCT treats all NULLs as one group, so without COALESCE NULL would appear once as an empty value.
- If a real channel were literally called 'unknown' it would merge with NULLs. Here it is not, but a reviewer would ask.
sections.hint1: DISTINCT works on the expressions in the SELECT list, not only on raw columns.
sections.hint2: Replace NULL with a label before de-duplicating, using COALESCE.
sections.hint3: `SELECT DISTINCT COALESCE(acquisition_channel, 'unknown') AS channel FROM users ORDER BY channel;`
sections.explanation:
`SELECT DISTINCT` removes duplicate result rows after the SELECT expressions have been computed. Applying `COALESCE` first turns the NULL group into the visible label `'unknown'`. NULLs are "not distinct from each other" for DISTINCT and GROUP BY, even though `NULL = NULL` is not true in a WHERE clause.

Ordering by the alias is portable. Sorting the raw column would place NULL differently in the two engines: PostgreSQL puts NULLs last in ascending order, MySQL puts them first. Labelling NULL avoids that difference.
sections.mistakes:
- `WHERE acquisition_channel IS NOT NULL` hides the data-quality signal the team asked for.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT acquisition_channel)` returns 5, because aggregate DISTINCT ignores NULLs, while `SELECT DISTINCT` returns 6 groups. Mixing up the two is a classic off-by-one.
sections.performance: DISTINCT needs a sort or a hash over the expression. On 1,800 rows that is trivial. On very large tables, a GROUP BY on an indexed column can sometimes use the index.
sections.interview: Shows whether the candidate knows how DISTINCT treats NULLs, as opposed to `=` and COUNT(DISTINCT).

questions.title: Marketing consent and three-valued logic
questions.secondary: conditional aggregation, IS NULL, boolean comparison

sections.context: A campaign must only target users who opted in, and the compliance team wants to know how many users must NOT be e-mailed. `marketing_opt_in` is TRUE, FALSE or NULL (never asked).
sections.problem:
Return a single row with:
- `opted_in`: users with TRUE
- `opted_out`: users with FALSE
- `unknown`: users with NULL
- `naive_not_opted_in`: the count produced by `WHERE marketing_opt_in <> TRUE`
- `correct_not_opted_in`: users who must not be e-mailed (FALSE **or** NULL)
sections.expected: Exactly one row, five integer columns. `opted_in + opted_out + unknown` equals the number of users. `correct_not_opted_in = opted_out + unknown`.
sections.edge_cases:
- `NULL <> TRUE` evaluates to NULL (unknown), and WHERE keeps only TRUE, so NULL rows vanish from the naive count.
- In MySQL a BOOLEAN is TINYINT(1), so TRUE is 1. The comparison logic is the same.
sections.hint1: Count each category with a CASE expression inside SUM, so everything comes back in one row.
sections.hint2: `CASE WHEN marketing_opt_in IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END` counts NULLs. Comparisons with `=` never match NULL.
sections.hint3: For the naive count, use `SUM(CASE WHEN marketing_opt_in <> TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`. A NULL condition makes CASE fall through to ELSE, which is exactly what WHERE does.
sections.solution:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN marketing_opt_in = TRUE  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS opted_in,
       SUM(CASE WHEN marketing_opt_in = FALSE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS opted_out,
       SUM(CASE WHEN marketing_opt_in IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS unknown,
       SUM(CASE WHEN marketing_opt_in <> TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS naive_not_opted_in,
       SUM(CASE WHEN marketing_opt_in IS NULL OR marketing_opt_in = FALSE
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                AS correct_not_opted_in
FROM users;
sections.explanation:
SQL uses three-valued logic: a comparison involving NULL yields UNKNOWN. A WHERE clause, and a `CASE WHEN`, only take the TRUE branch, so rows whose condition is UNKNOWN behave like FALSE. That is why `naive_not_opted_in` equals `opted_out`: the NULL users are silently lost.

The correct condition names the NULL case explicitly. PostgreSQL offers `marketing_opt_in IS NOT TRUE`, which is TRUE for FALSE and NULL. MySQL also supports `IS NOT TRUE`, but the explicit `IS NULL OR = FALSE` form reads clearly in any engine.

Conditional aggregation (`SUM(CASE ...)`) returns all counts in one pass over the table.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `NOT marketing_opt_in` has the same NULL problem as `<> TRUE`.
- `COUNT(marketing_opt_in)` counts only non-NULL values, which is another way the unknown group goes missing.
- Writing `marketing_opt_in = NULL` matches nothing. Use `IS NULL`.
sections.performance: A single scan with conditional aggregation is better than five separate COUNT queries.
sections.interview: A very common screening question. Strong candidates explain *why* the naive count is wrong (UNKNOWN is filtered out) rather than just fixing it.

questions.title: Operator precedence in a revenue filter
questions.secondary: parentheses, IN, half-open date range

sections.context: An analyst wrote `WHERE status = 'completed' OR status = 'refunded' AND sales_channel = 'web' AND order_ts >= '2025-01-01' AND order_ts < '2025-04-01'` to count Q1-2025 web orders that generated revenue at some point. The number looks far too high.
sections.problem: Return one row with two counts: `buggy_count` evaluates the analyst's filter exactly as written, and `correct_count` counts orders that are (completed or refunded) **and** web **and** placed in Q1 2025.
sections.expected: One row, columns `buggy_count, correct_count`. The buggy count is much larger.
sections.edge_cases:
- AND binds tighter than OR, so the buggy filter counts every completed order ever placed, through any channel.
- Q1 2025 is `[2025-01-01, 2025-04-01)`.
sections.hint1: Rewrite the buggy condition with explicit parentheses to see what the database actually evaluates.
sections.hint2: `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`.
sections.hint3: Put each filter inside a `SUM(CASE WHEN <condition> THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` and wrap the status test in parentheses (or use IN) for the correct version.
sections.solution:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' OR status = 'refunded'
                     AND sales_channel = 'web'
                     AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
                     AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS buggy_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status IN ('completed', 'refunded')
                     AND sales_channel = 'web'
                     AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
                     AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS correct_count
FROM orders;
sections.explanation:
Precedence is NOT, then AND, then OR. The buggy filter is evaluated as
`status = 'completed' OR (status = 'refunded' AND sales_channel = 'web' AND <Q1>)`,
so every completed order in the whole history passes. Using `IN ('completed','refunded')`, or wrapping the OR in parentheses, gives the intended logic.

Putting both conditions inside conditional aggregation shows the two numbers side by side, which is a good habit when you debug a filter.
sections.mistakes:
- Fixing only the date part, or adding parentheses in the wrong place, such as `(status = 'completed' OR status = 'refunded' AND sales_channel = 'web')`.
- Assuming the database evaluates conditions left to right.
sections.performance: No difference: both conditions are evaluated in one scan.
sections.interview: Tests careful reading of boolean logic. Mentioning that `IN` avoids the trap altogether is a plus.

questions.title: BETWEEN and timestamp boundaries
questions.secondary: half-open intervals, timestamp literals

sections.context: The monthly revenue report for March 2025 uses `order_ts BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31'`. Finance noticed that orders placed on 31 March are missing.
sections.problem:
Return one row with three counts of orders placed in March 2025:
1. `naive_between`: `order_ts BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31'`
2. `between_end_of_day`: `order_ts BETWEEN '2025-03-01 00:00:00' AND '2025-03-31 23:59:59'`
3. `half_open`: `order_ts >= '2025-03-01' AND order_ts < '2025-04-01'`
sections.expected: One row with three integers. Only `half_open` is robust.
sections.edge_cases:
- `'2025-03-31'` compared to a timestamp means `2025-03-31 00:00:00`.
- The end-of-day variant works for whole-second data but breaks once the column stores fractional seconds (e.g. 23:59:59.5).
sections.hint1: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends. Think about what the upper bound means for a timestamp column.
sections.hint2: Count each variant with `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
sections.hint3: The half-open interval `>= first day AND < first day of next month` is correct for any precision.
sections.solution:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN order_ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '2025-03-01 00:00:00'
                                  AND TIMESTAMP '2025-03-31 00:00:00' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS naive_between,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '2025-03-01 00:00:00'
                                  AND TIMESTAMP '2025-03-31 23:59:59' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS between_end_of_day,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-03-01 00:00:00'
                 AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS half_open
FROM orders;
sections.explanation: `BETWEEN a AND b` means `>= a AND <= b`. When `b` is a date literal compared with a timestamp, it becomes midnight at the *start* of 31 March, so the last day is lost. The "23:59:59" patch works for this dataset because it stores whole seconds. It fails with fractional seconds, and it is easy to get wrong for months of different lengths. The half-open form needs only the first day of the next period and is precise for any column type.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `CAST(order_ts AS DATE) BETWEEN ...`. It is correct, but it disables a plain index on `order_ts`.
- Assuming BETWEEN is exclusive on the upper bound.
sections.performance: All three predicates are sargable (index friendly) because the column is not wrapped in a function.
sections.interview: Expect follow-up questions on fractional seconds and on time zones, for example whether March means March in UTC or in local time.

questions.title: SLA targets with CASE and a custom sort order
questions.secondary: CASE in ORDER BY, date filter

sections.context: The support dashboard shows the response-time target for every new ticket. Targets: urgent = 1 hour, high = 4, medium = 24, low = 72. Tickets in status `open` or `pending` are "active"; `resolved` and `closed` are "done".
sections.problem: For tickets created in the last 3 days of data (from 2025-06-28 00:00 up to, but excluding, 2025-07-01), return `ticket_id`, `priority`, the target as `sla_hours`, and `status_group` (`'active'` or `'done'`). Sort by priority severity (urgent first, then high, medium, low), then by `ticket_id`.
sections.expected: One row per ticket in the window; columns `ticket_id, priority, sla_hours, status_group`; custom priority order.
sections.edge_cases:
- Sorting by `priority` alphabetically would give high, low, medium, urgent, which is wrong.
- A CASE without ELSE returns NULL for an unexpected value; decide whether that is acceptable.
sections.hint1: Use one CASE to map priority to hours and another to map status to a group.
sections.hint2: ORDER BY accepts any expression, including a CASE that turns a label into a rank number.
sections.hint3: `ORDER BY CASE priority WHEN 'urgent' THEN 1 WHEN 'high' THEN 2 WHEN 'medium' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END, ticket_id`.
sections.solution:
SELECT ticket_id,
       priority,
       CASE priority
            WHEN 'urgent' THEN 1
            WHEN 'high'   THEN 4
            WHEN 'medium' THEN 24
            WHEN 'low'    THEN 72
       END AS sla_hours,
       CASE WHEN status IN ('open', 'pending') THEN 'active' ELSE 'done' END AS status_group
FROM support_tickets
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-28 00:00:00'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
ORDER BY CASE priority WHEN 'urgent' THEN 1 WHEN 'high' THEN 2 WHEN 'medium' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END,
         ticket_id;
sections.explanation:
The *simple* CASE form (`CASE priority WHEN 'urgent' THEN ...`) compares one expression against several values. The *searched* form (`CASE WHEN status IN (...) THEN ...`) evaluates arbitrary conditions in order and returns the first match.

The custom sort works because ORDER BY can use an expression that is not in the SELECT list. In production, store a priority rank in a lookup table so that the same mapping is not copy-pasted across reports.
sections.mistakes:
- `ORDER BY priority` sorts alphabetically.
- Forgetting ELSE in the status CASE would return NULL for a future status like `'on_hold'`.
sections.performance: Negligible here. CASE expressions are evaluated per row after filtering.
sections.interview: Simple, but interviewers watch for deterministic tie-breaking and a sensible default (ELSE) branch.

questions.title: Effective annual price per plan with COALESCE
questions.secondary: arithmetic, CASE for display labels, ROUND

sections.context: The pricing page shows each active plan's monthly price, the effective monthly price when billed annually, and its seat limit. Plans that do not offer annual billing have a NULL discount, and unlimited plans have a NULL seat limit.
sections.problem: For active plans only, return `plan_name`, `price_per_seat_month`, `annual_price_per_seat_month` (monthly price after the annual discount, rounded to 2 decimals; equal to the monthly price when no discount exists), and `seat_limit_label` (`'unlimited'` when NULL, otherwise e.g. `'50 seats'`). Sort by `price_per_seat_month`.
sections.expected: 5 rows (the legacy plan is inactive), columns as listed, cheapest first.
sections.edge_cases:
- `price * (1 - NULL/100)` is NULL. Arithmetic with NULL yields NULL.
- String concatenation with NULL differs by engine: `CONCAT` ignores NULL in PostgreSQL but returns NULL in MySQL.
sections.hint1: Replace the missing discount by 0 before doing arithmetic.
sections.hint2: `COALESCE(annual_discount_pct, 0)` turns NULL into 0. Divide by `100.0` to stay in decimal arithmetic.
sections.hint3: Build the label with `CASE WHEN seat_limit IS NULL THEN 'unlimited' ELSE CONCAT(seat_limit, ' seats') END`, which is safe in both engines because CONCAT never sees a NULL.
sections.solution:
SELECT plan_name,
       price_per_seat_month,
       ROUND(price_per_seat_month * (1 - COALESCE(annual_discount_pct, 0) / 100.0), 2)
           AS annual_price_per_seat_month,
       CASE WHEN seat_limit IS NULL THEN 'unlimited'
            ELSE CONCAT(seat_limit, ' seats')
       END AS seat_limit_label
FROM plans
WHERE is_active = TRUE
ORDER BY price_per_seat_month, plan_name;
sections.explanation:
`COALESCE(x, 0)` returns the first non-NULL argument, so plans without annual billing get no discount instead of a NULL price. Dividing by `100.0` (not `100`) keeps the arithmetic in DECIMAL. PostgreSQL would do integer division if both operands were integers; here the column is DECIMAL, so it is safe either way, but the habit matters.

The label is built inside a CASE so that CONCAT never receives a NULL. That matters because **CONCAT treats NULL differently**: PostgreSQL skips NULL arguments, while MySQL returns NULL. `CONCAT_WS` and PostgreSQL's `||` operator have their own rules too. MySQL's `||` is logical OR unless `PIPES_AS_CONCAT` is enabled.

NULLIF is the mirror image of COALESCE: `NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when `a = b`. Its classic use, `x / NULLIF(y, 0)`, appears in many later questions.
sections.mistakes:
- `price * (1 - annual_discount_pct / 100)` returns NULL for the Free plan.
- Using `||` for concatenation in MySQL.
sections.performance: Not relevant for a 6-row lookup table.
sections.interview: Tests NULL propagation in arithmetic and awareness of engine-specific string concatenation.

questions.title: Line-level revenue and discount percentage
questions.secondary: NULLIF to avoid division by zero, decimal precision, ROUND
questions.tables: order_items(order_id, line_number, product_id, quantity, unit_price, discount_amount); orders(order_id, order_ts)
questions.columns: order_id, line_number, product_id, gross_amount, discount_amount, net_amount, discount_pct

sections.context: Finance wants to audit discounting on Black Friday 2024 (2024-11-29, UTC). For every order line placed that day, they need the gross and net amounts and the discount as a percentage of gross.
sections.problem: For order lines whose order was placed on 2024-11-29, return `order_id`, `line_number`, `product_id`, `gross_amount` (= quantity x unit_price), `discount_amount`, `net_amount` (gross - discount) and `discount_pct` (discount / gross x 100, rounded to 1 decimal; NULL if gross is 0). Sort by `order_id`, `line_number`.
sections.expected: One row per order line on that date. Monetary columns with 2 decimals, `discount_pct` with 1 decimal.
sections.edge_cases:
- A zero gross amount would cause a division-by-zero error in PostgreSQL. MySQL returns NULL (with a warning) in its default mode.
- Integer x decimal is decimal in both engines. No rounding happens until ROUND.
sections.hint1: Join the lines to their order header only to filter by the order date.
sections.hint2: Protect the division with `NULLIF(gross, 0)`: dividing by NULL returns NULL instead of an error.
sections.hint3: `ROUND(100.0 * discount_amount / NULLIF(quantity * unit_price, 0), 1)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT oi.order_id,
       oi.line_number,
       oi.product_id,
       oi.quantity * oi.unit_price                              AS gross_amount,
       oi.discount_amount,
       oi.quantity * oi.unit_price - oi.discount_amount         AS net_amount,
       ROUND(100.0 * oi.discount_amount
             / NULLIF(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price, 0), 1)       AS discount_pct
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2024-11-29 00:00:00'
  AND o.order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2024-11-30 00:00:00'
ORDER BY oi.order_id, oi.line_number;
sections.explanation:
- `quantity * unit_price` multiplies an INT by a DECIMAL(10,2) and keeps 2 decimals in both engines.
- `NULLIF(x, 0)` returns NULL when x is 0, and any division by NULL yields NULL, so the query cannot fail on a free line.
- Multiplying by `100.0` before dividing keeps precision. Dividing first and multiplying later also works for decimals, but it can lose digits with integer columns.

The join to `orders` is one-to-many from orders to lines, but we only use it to filter, so no duplication occurs: each line has exactly one parent order.
sections.mistakes:
- Computing `discount_amount / quantity * unit_price`. Without parentheses this divides by the quantity only.
- Filtering on `DATE(order_ts) = '2024-11-29'`. The result is correct, but the column is wrapped in a function, and `DATE()` does not exist in PostgreSQL.
sections.performance: The index on `orders(order_ts)` supports the date filter; `order_items` is reached through its primary key `(order_id, line_number)`.
sections.interview: Tests safe division and precision handling, both of which come up in every metric question.

questions.title: Spot e-mails that are not normalized
questions.secondary: LOWER, TRIM, SUBSTRING, POSITION, case-sensitive comparison, collations

sections.context: Duplicate accounts are suspected. Before deduplicating, the data team wants to see every user whose stored e-mail differs from its normalized form (lower case, no surrounding spaces), together with the extracted domain.
sections.problem: Return `user_id`, `raw_email` (as stored), `normalized_email` (`LOWER(TRIM(email))`) and `email_domain` (the part after `@` of the normalized e-mail) for users whose stored e-mail is not already normalized. Sort by `user_id`.
sections.expected: One row per affected user (about two dozen rows). Columns as listed.
sections.edge_cases:
- **MySQL's default collation `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` is case-insensitive**, so `'Anna@x.com' <> 'anna@x.com'` is FALSE in MySQL and those rows disappear. The comparison must be made case-sensitive explicitly.
- Trailing spaces: the default `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` and `utf8mb4_0900_bin` collations are NO PAD (trailing spaces count), but the legacy `utf8mb4_bin` collation is PAD SPACE and ignores trailing spaces in comparisons.
sections.hint1: Compute the normalized form, then keep rows where it differs from the stored value.
sections.hint2: Domain = substring starting one character after the position of '@'. `POSITION('@' IN s)` and `SUBSTRING(s FROM n)` work in both engines.
sections.hint3: In MySQL, compare with a case-sensitive NO PAD collation: `email COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_bin <> LOWER(TRIM(email)) COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_bin` (or compare `CAST(... AS BINARY)`). PostgreSQL compares case-sensitively by default.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT user_id,
       email                                    AS raw_email,
       LOWER(TRIM(email))                       AS normalized_email,
       SUBSTRING(LOWER(TRIM(email)) FROM POSITION('@' IN LOWER(TRIM(email))) + 1) AS email_domain
FROM users
WHERE email <> LOWER(TRIM(email))
ORDER BY user_id;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT user_id,
       email                                    AS raw_email,
       LOWER(TRIM(email))                       AS normalized_email,
       SUBSTRING(LOWER(TRIM(email)) FROM POSITION('@' IN LOWER(TRIM(email))) + 1) AS email_domain
FROM users
WHERE email COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_bin <> LOWER(TRIM(email)) COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_bin
ORDER BY user_id;
sections.dialect_note:
The SELECT list is identical; only the comparison differs. PostgreSQL compares strings case-sensitively (deterministic collations). MySQL's default `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` collation is accent- and case-insensitive, so equality, `<>`, GROUP BY, DISTINCT and UNIQUE indexes all ignore case.

On this dataset the same `<>` test finds 26 rows in PostgreSQL, but in MySQL:
| comparison | rows | why |
|---|---:|---|
| default `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` | 11 | case differences are ignored; only space problems are found |
| `COLLATE utf8mb4_bin` | 22 | case-sensitive, but PAD SPACE ignores *trailing* spaces |
| `COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_bin` or `CAST(x AS BINARY)` | 26 | case-sensitive and NO PAD, so it matches PostgreSQL |
sections.explanation:
1. `TRIM` removes leading/trailing spaces and `LOWER` folds case. Together they produce a canonical key for matching people across accounts.
2. `POSITION('@' IN s)` returns the 1-based index of '@'; `SUBSTRING(s FROM p + 1)` returns everything after it. PostgreSQL also has `SPLIT_PART(s, '@', 2)` and MySQL has `SUBSTRING_INDEX(s, '@', -1)`, but the POSITION/SUBSTRING form is portable.
3. The WHERE clause keeps rows whose canonical form differs from the stored form. In MySQL that comparison must be case-sensitive or the upper-case variants are missed. Running the PostgreSQL query unchanged on MySQL silently returns only the whitespace cases.
sections.mistakes:
- Running the same `<>` comparison on MySQL and trusting the smaller result.
- Using `LENGTH` to detect spaces: MySQL `LENGTH` counts bytes, so multi-byte characters like 'ü' break it. Use `CHAR_LENGTH`.
- Forgetting to normalize before extracting the domain, which gives 'SILVERFINANCE.COM' and 'silverfinance.com' as different domains.
sections.performance: Functions on the column make this a full scan. For repeated lookups, store a normalized column (or a generated column, see SQL-163) with its own index.
sections.interview: A favourite "gotcha" when a company runs MySQL: candidates who know about collations stand out. It is also the first step of entity resolution in ML feature pipelines.

questions.title: Daily sign-ups in the last week of data
questions.secondary: interval arithmetic, CAST to DATE, GROUP BY date

sections.context: Growth reviews the most recent week of sign-ups every Monday. "Today" in this workbook is 2025-07-01, so the last 7 full days are 2025-06-24 through 2025-06-30.
sections.problem: Count new users per calendar day (UTC) for the 7 days before 2025-07-01. Express the window start as an interval subtraction from the anchor date. Show only days that have at least one sign-up, sorted by date.
sections.expected: Columns `signup_date, signups`; at most 7 rows; ascending date.
sections.edge_cases:
- Days without sign-ups do not appear (filling gaps needs a date spine, see SQL-053).
- `INTERVAL '7' DAY` is standard SQL syntax that both engines accept; `INTERVAL '7 days'` is PostgreSQL-only.
sections.hint1: Filter a half-open window, then group by the date part of the timestamp.
sections.hint2: `TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00' - INTERVAL '7' DAY` is portable.
sections.hint3: `GROUP BY CAST(signup_at AS DATE)` and select the same expression.
sections.solution:
SELECT CAST(signup_at AS DATE) AS signup_date,
       COUNT(*)                AS signups
FROM users
WHERE signup_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00' - INTERVAL '7' DAY
  AND signup_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CAST(signup_at AS DATE)
ORDER BY signup_date;
sections.explanation:
- `TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00' - INTERVAL '7' DAY` evaluates to 2025-06-24 00:00:00 in both engines. The SQL-standard interval literal (quantity in quotes, unit outside) is the portable spelling.
- Grouping by `CAST(signup_at AS DATE)` buckets timestamps into UTC calendar days.
- In real reports you would use `CURRENT_DATE` instead of a fixed anchor. The workbook uses a fixed date so that results are reproducible.
sections.mistakes:
- `signup_at > NOW() - INTERVAL ...` makes the report change every time it runs and includes partial days.
- PostgreSQL-only `signup_at::date` or MySQL-only `DATE(signup_at)` in a query advertised as portable.
sections.performance: The range predicate can use the `users(signup_at)` index. Grouping on an expression requires computing it per row, which is cheap here.
sections.interview: Expect to be asked how the answer changes for a user in another time zone (see SQL-164).

questions.title: First-response time in hours for urgent tickets
questions.secondary: EXTRACT(EPOCH) vs TIMESTAMPDIFF, NULL handling, CASE

sections.context: Urgent tickets must receive a first response within 1 hour. The support lead wants to review all urgent tickets created in May 2025.
sections.problem: For urgent tickets created in May 2025 return `ticket_id`, `created_at`, `response_hours` (hours between creation and first response, rounded to 2 decimals; NULL when there is no response) and `sla_status`: `'met'` (responded within 1 hour), `'breached'` (responded later), or `'no_response'`. Sort by `ticket_id`.
sections.expected: One row per urgent ticket created in May 2025.
sections.edge_cases:
- `first_response_at` is NULL for tickets never answered. The difference is then NULL, and CASE must test it explicitly.
- Exactly 60 minutes counts as met (`<= 1`).
sections.hint1: Compute the difference in seconds, then divide by 3600.
sections.hint2: PostgreSQL: `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (b - a))` returns seconds. MySQL: `TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, a, b)`.
sections.hint3: Test `first_response_at IS NULL` as the first WHEN branch, then compare the hours with 1.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT ticket_id,
       created_at,
       ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (first_response_at - created_at)) / 3600, 2) AS response_hours,
       CASE WHEN first_response_at IS NULL THEN 'no_response'
            WHEN first_response_at <= created_at + INTERVAL '1' HOUR THEN 'met'
            ELSE 'breached'
       END AS sla_status
FROM support_tickets
WHERE priority = 'urgent'
  AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-05-01 00:00:00'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
ORDER BY ticket_id;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT ticket_id,
       created_at,
       ROUND(TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, created_at, first_response_at) / 3600, 2) AS response_hours,
       CASE WHEN first_response_at IS NULL THEN 'no_response'
            WHEN first_response_at <= created_at + INTERVAL '1' HOUR THEN 'met'
            ELSE 'breached'
       END AS sla_status
FROM support_tickets
WHERE priority = 'urgent'
  AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-05-01 00:00:00'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
ORDER BY ticket_id;
sections.dialect_note: Subtracting two timestamps returns an INTERVAL in PostgreSQL. `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM interval)` converts it to seconds (a NUMERIC since PostgreSQL 14). MySQL has no interval data type: `TIMESTAMPDIFF(unit, start, end)` returns an integer number of units. Note the reversed argument order compared with the subtraction. Adding a fixed interval (`ts + INTERVAL '1' HOUR`) is portable.
sections.explanation:
1. The difference in seconds divided by 3600 gives fractional hours, and ROUND keeps 2 decimals. In MySQL, `/` on integers returns a DECIMAL, so no precision is lost.
2. The SLA test compares timestamps directly (`first_response_at <= created_at + 1 hour`). This avoids rounding problems that could misclassify a response at 59.999 minutes.
3. CASE evaluates branches in order, so the NULL case is handled first. Without it, `NULL <= ...` is UNKNOWN and the row would fall into ELSE ('breached'), which is wrong.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, ...)` truncates to whole hours, so 1h59m counts as 1 hour.
- Treating no response as breached without checking. The team may want to see these separately.
sections.performance: Fine at this size. The `support_tickets(org_id, created_at)` index does not start with `created_at`, so the filter scans the table.
sections.interview: Shows command of date arithmetic in both dialects and correct handling of missing timestamps.

questions.title: Paginate the document catalogue deterministically
questions.secondary: deterministic ordering, keyset pagination concept

sections.context: An admin UI lists knowledge-base document versions, most recently updated first, 10 per page. Users reported that some versions appear on two pages and others never appear.
sections.problem: Return page 3 (rows 21-30) of the list ordered by `updated_at` descending. Make the order deterministic so that every row appears on exactly one page.
sections.expected: Exactly 10 rows; columns `document_id, doc_key, version_number, updated_at`.
sections.edge_cases:
- Many versions share the same `updated_at`. Without a unique tie-breaker the database may return them in any order, and the order can differ between executions.
- OFFSET still reads and discards the skipped rows; deep pages get slower.
sections.hint1: Why can rows "move" between pages? Think about ties in the sort key.
sections.hint2: Add a unique column as the last ORDER BY key.
sections.hint3: `ORDER BY updated_at DESC, document_id DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20`.
sections.solution:
SELECT document_id,
       doc_key,
       version_number,
       updated_at
FROM documents
ORDER BY updated_at DESC, document_id DESC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;
sections.explanation:
SQL tables are unordered sets. A sort on a non-unique key leaves the order of tied rows unspecified, so LIMIT/OFFSET pages may overlap or skip rows. Adding the primary key as a final sort key makes the order total and the paging stable.

**Keyset pagination** ("seek method") is the scalable alternative: remember the last `(updated_at, document_id)` of the previous page and request `WHERE (updated_at, document_id) < (:last_ts, :last_id) ORDER BY updated_at DESC, document_id DESC LIMIT 10`. It does not read skipped rows, so every page costs the same, and concurrent inserts don't shift rows between pages. Both engines support row-value comparison, but PostgreSQL uses a composite index for it more reliably.

`LIMIT n OFFSET m` works in both engines. MySQL also accepts `LIMIT m, n`, and PostgreSQL also accepts the standard `OFFSET m ROWS FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY`, which MySQL does not.
sections.mistakes:
- Ordering only by `updated_at`.
- Using OFFSET = page x 10 for page numbers starting at 1, which skips the first page.
sections.performance: OFFSET cost grows linearly with depth. An index on `(updated_at, document_id)` makes keyset pagination use an index range scan.
sections.interview: Senior candidates mention keyset pagination and explain why OFFSET is fragile under concurrent writes.

questions.title: The NOT IN trap with NULLs
questions.secondary: three-valued logic, NOT EXISTS, subquery in WHERE

sections.context: The referral team asks: "How many users have never referred anyone?" The first attempt, `WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT referred_by_user_id FROM users)`, returned zero, which cannot be right.
sections.problem:
Return one row with three counts of users who never referred anyone:
`naive_not_in` (the query above), `filtered_not_in` (NOT IN with NULLs removed from the subquery), and `not_exists_count` (using NOT EXISTS).
sections.expected: One row; `naive_not_in` is 0, the other two are equal and large.
sections.edge_cases: - Most users have `referred_by_user_id IS NULL`. A single NULL in a NOT IN list makes the predicate UNKNOWN for every row that is not explicitly in the list.
sections.hint1: Write out `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` as a chain of `<>` comparisons joined with AND.
sections.hint2: `x <> NULL` is UNKNOWN, and `TRUE AND UNKNOWN` is UNKNOWN. WHERE drops UNKNOWN.
sections.hint3: Use scalar subqueries in the SELECT list, one per approach: `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users u WHERE ...)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users u
         WHERE u.user_id NOT IN (SELECT r.referred_by_user_id FROM users r))          AS naive_not_in,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users u
         WHERE u.user_id NOT IN (SELECT r.referred_by_user_id FROM users r
                                  WHERE r.referred_by_user_id IS NOT NULL))           AS filtered_not_in,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users u
         WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM users r
                            WHERE r.referred_by_user_id = u.user_id))                AS not_exists_count;
sections.explanation:
`u.user_id NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` is evaluated as `u.user_id <> a AND u.user_id <> b AND u.user_id <> NULL`. The last comparison is UNKNOWN, so the whole conjunction can never be TRUE. Every row is filtered out, and the count is 0.

Two fixes:
1. Remove NULLs inside the subquery (`WHERE referred_by_user_id IS NOT NULL`).
2. Use `NOT EXISTS`. It asks "is there no matching row?" and is unaffected by NULLs in unrelated rows. NOT EXISTS is the idiomatic anti-join and is usually planned as one (see SQL-033).

A SELECT without FROM (only scalar subqueries) is valid in both PostgreSQL and MySQL.
sections.mistakes:
- Assuming NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are interchangeable. They are only equivalent when the subquery column cannot be NULL.
- "Fixing" it with `COALESCE(referred_by_user_id, 0)`. This works only while 0 is never a real id; it is a fragile magic value.
sections.performance: Both engines turn NOT EXISTS into an anti-join. The naive NOT IN is often slower because of its NULL-aware semantics.
sections.interview: One of the most frequently asked SQL gotchas. Explaining the three-valued logic is more important than the fix itself.

questions.title: Format feature values with CAST and ROUND
questions.secondary: ROUND on DOUBLE PRECISION in PostgreSQL, DECIMAL casting

sections.context: A model-debugging dashboard prints feature snapshots in a compact format. The feature store keeps `avg_session_minutes` and `seats_used_pct` as DOUBLE PRECISION.
sections.problem: For entity 10, list every snapshot with `as_of_date` (date only), `avg_session_minutes` rounded to 1 decimal, and `seats_used_pct` converted to a percentage (x 100) rounded to 1 decimal. Sort by `as_of_date`.
sections.expected: One row per snapshot of entity 10; NULL feature values stay NULL.
sections.edge_cases:
- **PostgreSQL has no `ROUND(double precision, integer)`**. `ROUND(avg_session_minutes, 1)` raises "function round(double precision, integer) does not exist". MySQL accepts it.
- NULL feature values must remain NULL (CAST of NULL is NULL).
sections.hint1: Convert the floating-point value to an exact DECIMAL before rounding to a number of decimals.
sections.hint2: `CAST(x AS DECIMAL(10,1))` rounds to one decimal in both engines.
sections.hint3: `CAST(seats_used_pct * 100 AS DECIMAL(10,1))`.
sections.solution:
SELECT entity_id,
       CAST(as_of_ts AS DATE)                         AS as_of_date,
       CAST(avg_session_minutes AS DECIMAL(10,1))     AS avg_session_minutes,
       CAST(seats_used_pct * 100 AS DECIMAL(10,1))    AS seats_used_pct
FROM entity_features
WHERE entity_id = 10
ORDER BY as_of_date;
sections.alternative:
SELECT entity_id,
       CAST(as_of_ts AS DATE)                                       AS as_of_date,
       ROUND(CAST(avg_session_minutes AS DECIMAL(12,4)), 1)         AS avg_session_minutes,
       ROUND(CAST(seats_used_pct * 100 AS DECIMAL(12,4)), 1)        AS seats_used_pct
FROM entity_features
WHERE entity_id = 10
ORDER BY as_of_date;
sections.alternative_note: Casting to a wide DECIMAL first and then calling ROUND is equivalent and makes the intent ("round to 1 decimal") explicit.
sections.explanation:
Floating-point types (DOUBLE PRECISION) store binary approximations. PostgreSQL deliberately offers `ROUND(numeric, int)` only. For doubles there is just `ROUND(double)` to the nearest integer. Casting to `DECIMAL(p, s)` converts to an exact type and rounds to `s` decimals in both engines.

`CAST(as_of_ts AS DATE)` is the portable way to drop the time part. PostgreSQL's `::` operator and MySQL's `DATE()` function are engine-specific shortcuts.
sections.mistakes:
- `ROUND(avg_session_minutes, 1)` works in MySQL but fails in PostgreSQL.
- Casting to `DECIMAL(3,1)` overflows for values >= 100. Choose a precision that fits the range.
sections.performance: Casting is per-row CPU work on the filtered rows only.
sections.interview: A practical portability check. Candidates who have moved queries between engines know this one.

questions.title: Find knowledge-base articles by pattern
questions.secondary: case-insensitive matching, wildcards, AND/OR

sections.context: The support bot keeps answering refund questions with outdated content. The content team wants every **published** help-center article under the billing area (`doc_key` starting with `help/billing/`) whose title mentions "refund" or "payment" in any letter case.
sections.problem: Return `document_id`, `doc_key` and `title` of matching published documents, sorted by `doc_key`.
sections.expected: One row per matching published document version; columns as listed.
sections.edge_cases:
- PostgreSQL `LIKE` is case-sensitive, while MySQL's default collation makes `LIKE` case-insensitive. Normalize case to get the same answer everywhere.
- `_` and `%` are wildcards. A literal underscore in a pattern must be escaped (`\_`, or with an ESCAPE clause).
sections.hint1: Combine a prefix match on `doc_key` with a "contains" match on the title.
sections.hint2: `LOWER(title) LIKE '%refund%'` is case-insensitive in both engines.
sections.hint3: Parenthesize the OR of the two title conditions before AND-ing it with the other filters.
sections.solution:
SELECT document_id,
       doc_key,
       title
FROM documents
WHERE status = 'published'
  AND doc_key LIKE 'help/billing/%'
  AND (LOWER(title) LIKE '%refund%' OR LOWER(title) LIKE '%payment%')
ORDER BY doc_key;
sections.explanation:
- `LIKE 'help/billing/%'` is a prefix match; `%` matches any sequence of characters, `_` exactly one character.
- Lower-casing the title makes the search case-insensitive in both engines. PostgreSQL's `ILIKE` does the same but is PostgreSQL-only.
- The OR is parenthesized so that the `status` and prefix filters apply to both alternatives.

Prefix patterns can use a B-tree index (in PostgreSQL only with the C collation or a `text_pattern_ops` index). Leading-wildcard patterns like `'%refund%'` cannot. For real text search use full-text indexes (SQL-166/SQL-167).
sections.mistakes:
- `title LIKE '%Refund%'` misses lower-case titles in PostgreSQL but "works" in MySQL, which makes the bug engine-dependent.
- Missing parentheses around the OR.
sections.performance: `LOWER(title) LIKE '%...%'` forces a scan. That is acceptable for a few hundred documents, but not for millions.
sections.interview: Tests wildcard semantics and awareness of case sensitivity differences between engines.

questions.title: Order statistics by status
questions.primary: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX with GROUP BY
questions.secondary: ROUND, ORDER BY aggregate
questions.columns: status, orders, total_amount, avg_amount, first_order_ts, last_order_ts

sections.context: Before building revenue dashboards, an analyst profiles the `orders` table to understand how the order statuses are distributed.
sections.problem: For each order `status`, return the number of orders, the sum and the average of `order_total` (average rounded to 2 decimals), and the earliest and latest `order_ts`. Sort by number of orders descending.
sections.expected: One row per status (4 rows); columns `status, orders, total_amount, avg_amount, first_order_ts, last_order_ts`.
sections.edge_cases:
- Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY (MySQL enforces this with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, which is on by default).
- Ties in the order count would need a tie-breaker; add `status`.
sections.hint1: GROUP BY the column that defines a row of the output.
sections.hint2: All five aggregates can be computed in one pass.
sections.hint3: `SELECT status, COUNT(*), SUM(order_total), ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2), MIN(order_ts), MAX(order_ts) FROM orders GROUP BY status`.
sections.solution:
SELECT status,
       COUNT(*)                   AS orders,
       SUM(order_total)           AS total_amount,
       ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_amount,
       MIN(order_ts)              AS first_order_ts,
       MAX(order_ts)              AS last_order_ts
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY orders DESC, status;
sections.explanation:
GROUP BY collapses the table to one row per distinct `status`. Each aggregate is then computed over the rows of its group. `AVG` on a DECIMAL column returns DECIMAL in both engines, so ROUND works directly. (Contrast with DOUBLE in SQL-014.)

The ORDER BY uses the output alias `orders`. Both engines allow aliases in ORDER BY, but not in WHERE (see SQL-019 for HAVING).
sections.mistakes:
- Selecting `order_id` without aggregating it: PostgreSQL raises an error, MySQL raises an error under ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY (older MySQL versions silently returned an arbitrary value).
- Calling `total_amount` "revenue". Pending and canceled orders never generated revenue.
sections.performance: One sequential scan plus a hash aggregate. Fine for any size that fits the workbook.
sections.interview: A warm-up question. Interviewers check that the candidate knows what GROUP BY does to the row count and why ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY exists.

questions.title: COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column) versus COUNT(DISTINCT)
questions.secondary: COUNT DISTINCT, AVG ignores NULLs
questions.columns: tickets, tickets_with_user, distinct_users, tickets_with_csat, avg_csat_rated, avg_csat_null_as_zero, unanswered

sections.context: The support manager's report says the average CSAT is 3.9. A colleague computed 1.7 from the same table. Both are "right" for different definitions.
sections.problem: Return one row with: total tickets, tickets that have a `user_id`, number of distinct users who opened tickets, tickets with a CSAT answer, average CSAT over rated tickets (2 decimals), average CSAT if unrated tickets were counted as 0 (2 decimals), and the number of tickets without a first response.
sections.expected: One row with seven columns. The two averages differ a lot.
sections.edge_cases:
- `COUNT(col)` skips NULLs; `COUNT(*)` counts rows.
- `AVG(col)` ignores NULLs in both numerator and denominator.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` also ignores NULL.
sections.hint1: Each of the requested numbers is one aggregate expression.
sections.hint2: Counting NULLs: `COUNT(*) - COUNT(col)` or `SUM(CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
sections.hint3: `AVG(COALESCE(csat_score, 0))` treats missing answers as zero, which is usually wrong but shows the effect.
sections.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                                   AS tickets,
       COUNT(user_id)                             AS tickets_with_user,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)                    AS distinct_users,
       COUNT(csat_score)                          AS tickets_with_csat,
       ROUND(AVG(csat_score), 2)                  AS avg_csat_rated,
       ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(csat_score, 0)), 2)     AS avg_csat_null_as_zero,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(first_response_at)        AS unanswered
FROM support_tickets;
sections.explanation:
- `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(expr)` counts rows where expr is not NULL, and `COUNT(DISTINCT expr)` counts distinct non-NULL values.
- `AVG(csat_score)` = SUM over non-NULL / COUNT of non-NULL. It answers "how satisfied are customers **who answered**?"
- `AVG(COALESCE(csat_score, 0))` puts every unrated ticket in the denominator with a score of 0. That is almost always the wrong business definition, but it shows how NULL handling moves a metric.
- `AVG` of a SMALLINT returns NUMERIC in PostgreSQL and DECIMAL in MySQL, so there is no integer-division problem here.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `COUNT(csat_score)` as "number of tickets".
- Reporting an average without stating the denominator, for example the response rate of the survey.
sections.performance: One scan. COUNT(DISTINCT) needs a sort or hash of the distinct values, which is more expensive than plain counts on big data (see SQL-094 for approximate alternatives).
sections.interview: Classic. Strong answers also mention *survey response bias*: the 45% of customers who answered are not a random sample.

questions.title: CSAT satisfaction rate without integer division
questions.secondary: integer division, conditional aggregation, HAVING

sections.context: "Satisfied" means a CSAT of 4 or 5. Leadership wants the satisfaction rate per ticket category, but only for categories with at least 30 rated tickets so the numbers are meaningful.
sections.problem: Per `category`, return `rated_tickets` (tickets with a CSAT), `satisfied` (CSAT >= 4) and `satisfaction_pct` (satisfied / rated x 100, 1 decimal). Keep categories with at least 30 rated tickets. Sort by `satisfaction_pct` descending, then category.
sections.expected: One row per qualifying category.
sections.edge_cases:
- In PostgreSQL, `COUNT(...) / COUNT(...)` is integer division: 45 / 60 = 0.
- MySQL's `/` always returns a decimal, so the same query "works" in MySQL and fails silently in PostgreSQL.
- Categories with zero rated tickets would cause division by zero; HAVING removes them, and NULLIF guards anyway.
sections.hint1: Compute numerator and denominator with conditional aggregation, then divide.
sections.hint2: Force decimal arithmetic by multiplying by `100.0` before dividing.
sections.hint3: Filter groups with `HAVING COUNT(csat_score) >= 30`.
sections.solution:
SELECT category,
       COUNT(csat_score)                                         AS rated_tickets,
       SUM(CASE WHEN csat_score >= 4 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)          AS satisfied,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN csat_score >= 4 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(COUNT(csat_score), 0), 1)                  AS satisfaction_pct
FROM support_tickets
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(csat_score) >= 30
ORDER BY satisfaction_pct DESC, category;
sections.explanation:
1. `SUM(CASE WHEN csat_score >= 4 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts satisfied answers. NULL scores fail the condition and add 0.
2. `100.0 * x / y` makes the numerator DECIMAL, so the division is exact in PostgreSQL. Without the `.0`, PostgreSQL would return an integer quotient (0 for most rows).
3. `HAVING` filters *groups* after aggregation. The predicate must be repeated as an expression, because aliases cannot be referenced in HAVING in PostgreSQL (MySQL allows it as an extension).
4. `NULLIF(..., 0)` is defensive: if the HAVING threshold were removed, empty categories would yield NULL instead of an error.
sections.mistakes:
- `SUM(...) / COUNT(*)`: COUNT(*) includes unrated tickets, which changes the definition.
- `HAVING satisfaction_pct > ...` works in MySQL and fails in PostgreSQL.
sections.performance: Single scan with hash aggregation.
sections.interview: Integer division is a top-5 SQL bug in analytics. Mentioning the engine difference earns extra credit.

questions.title: Large organizations by user count
questions.secondary: conditional counting, aggregate-level filtering

sections.context: Customer success assigns a dedicated manager to organizations with more than 25 user accounts that have at least 20 active ones.
sections.problem: Return `org_id`, `total_users` and `active_users` (status `'active'`) for organizations matching both thresholds. Sort by `total_users` descending, then `org_id`.
sections.expected: One row per qualifying organization.
sections.edge_cases: - The status filter must not be in WHERE, otherwise `total_users` would only count active users.
sections.hint1: You need two different counts per organization, one of them conditional.
sections.hint2: Row filters go in WHERE, group filters in HAVING.
sections.hint3: `HAVING COUNT(*) > 25 AND SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'active' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 20`.
sections.solution:
SELECT org_id,
       COUNT(*)                                          AS total_users,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'active' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS active_users
FROM users
GROUP BY org_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 25
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'active' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 20
ORDER BY total_users DESC, org_id;
sections.explanation: The query mixes a row-level concept (status) with a group-level threshold. Putting `status = 'active'` in WHERE would remove inactive users *before* grouping, so the total would be wrong. Conditional aggregation computes both counts from the same group, and HAVING then applies both thresholds.
sections.mistakes:
- `WHERE status = 'active'` plus `HAVING COUNT(*) > 25` answers a different question.
- Writing the HAVING with aliases (`HAVING total_users > 25`): this is a MySQL extension that fails in PostgreSQL.
sections.performance: An index on `users(org_id)` lets some plans aggregate in index order, but a hash aggregate over 1,800 rows is instant anyway.
sections.interview: Checks the WHERE-versus-HAVING distinction.

questions.title: Monthly revenue and average order value
questions.secondary: DATE_TRUNC vs DATE_FORMAT, AOV, completed orders only

sections.context: Finance tracks monthly revenue and average order value (AOV) of one-off product orders. Revenue counts completed orders only (refunds are handled separately in SQL-024).
sections.problem: For every month from January 2024 to June 2025, return `month_start` (the first day of the month, as a DATE), `completed_orders`, `revenue` (sum of `order_total`) and `avg_order_value` (revenue / completed orders, 2 decimals). Sort by month.
sections.expected: 18 rows (one per month with completed orders), ascending.
sections.edge_cases:
- Grouping by `EXTRACT(MONTH ...)` alone would merge January 2024 and January 2025.
- Orders before 2024 exist and must be excluded.
sections.hint1: Truncate each timestamp to its month and group by that value.
sections.hint2: PostgreSQL: `DATE_TRUNC('month', ts)`. MySQL has no DATE_TRUNC; `DATE_FORMAT(ts, '%Y-%m-01')` builds the first day as a string that you can CAST to DATE.
sections.hint3: AOV = `SUM(order_total) / COUNT(*)` over the completed orders of the month, which is the same as `AVG(order_total)`.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT CAST(DATE_TRUNC('month', order_ts) AS DATE) AS month_start,
       COUNT(*)                                    AS completed_orders,
       SUM(order_total)                            AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2)                  AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
  AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_ts)
ORDER BY month_start;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT CAST(DATE_FORMAT(order_ts, '%Y-%m-01') AS DATE) AS month_start,
       COUNT(*)                                        AS completed_orders,
       SUM(order_total)                                AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2)                      AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
  AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CAST(DATE_FORMAT(order_ts, '%Y-%m-01') AS DATE)
ORDER BY month_start;
sections.dialect_note:
PostgreSQL's `DATE_TRUNC('month', ts)` returns a TIMESTAMP at midnight on the first day, and casting it to DATE keeps the first day. MySQL lacks DATE_TRUNC. The common idioms are `DATE_FORMAT(ts, '%Y-%m-01')` (string → CAST to DATE) or `LAST_DAY(ts) + INTERVAL 1 DAY - INTERVAL 1 MONTH`.

A *fully portable* version is possible but not recommended. You can group by `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_ts), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_ts)` and return those two numbers instead of a date. Rebuilding a DATE from them portably runs into engine differences: PostgreSQL pads `CHAR(n)` values, and MySQL's ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY rejects expressions that are not literally in the GROUP BY. Use each engine's native truncation function.
sections.explanation:
1. Filter first: completed orders in the 18-month window (half-open).
2. Bucket each order into its month. Grouping by the truncated value (not by the month number) keeps different years apart.
3. `AVG(order_total)` equals revenue / number of completed orders, because every row is one order. If the query joined order lines, AVG would be per line, not per order (see SQL-031).
4. The DATE column sorts chronologically. A string like '2024-1' would sort incorrectly.
sections.mistakes:
- `GROUP BY EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_ts)` merges years.
- Computing AOV from `order_items`, which averages lines, not orders.
- Including refunded orders in revenue without subtracting refunds.
sections.performance: The range filter can use `orders(order_ts)`. Grouping on an expression is computed per row. For very large fact tables, store a pre-computed `order_month` column or use a calendar dimension.
sections.interview: Expect to discuss what "revenue" means (gross vs net of refunds, recognized vs booked) before writing SQL.

questions.title: LLM request outcomes pivoted by feature
questions.secondary: failure rate, ratios
questions.columns: feature, requests, success, error, timeout, rate_limited, content_filtered, failure_rate_pct

sections.context: The AI platform team monitors which product features suffer most from LLM failures. A row per feature with outcome counts side by side is easier to read than a long table.
sections.problem: For each `feature`, return the total number of requests, one column per status (`success, error, timeout, rate_limited, content_filtered`), and `failure_rate_pct` = non-success requests / all requests x 100 (2 decimals). Sort by `failure_rate_pct` descending.
sections.expected: 3 rows (one per feature), 8 columns.
sections.edge_cases:
- A status that never occurs for a feature must show 0, not NULL. That is why the solution uses `SUM(CASE ... ELSE 0)`.
- Definition choice: is `content_filtered` a failure? Here it is (the user got no answer). State such assumptions.
sections.hint1: One output column per status means one conditional aggregate per status.
sections.hint2: `SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'error' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts errors.
sections.hint3: `failure_rate_pct = 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status <> 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT feature,
       COUNT(*)                                                     AS requests,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'success'          THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS success,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'error'            THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS error,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'timeout'          THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS timeout,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'rate_limited'     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS rate_limited,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'content_filtered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS content_filtered,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status <> 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2)
                                                                    AS failure_rate_pct
FROM llm_requests
GROUP BY feature
ORDER BY failure_rate_pct DESC, feature;
sections.explanation:
Conditional aggregation is the portable pivot. PostgreSQL also offers `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'error')` (cleaner, PostgreSQL-only, see SQL-170), and MySQL can use `SUM(status = 'error')` because booleans are integers there. The CASE form works in both.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** failure rates by feature tell you where to add retries, fallbacks to another model, or user-facing degradation. Rate limits and timeouts call for different fixes: quota and backoff for the first, model choice and prompt size for the second.
sections.mistakes:
- Hard-coding the status list and forgetting a new status. Add a "sum of columns = requests" sanity check.
- `COUNT(CASE WHEN status='error' THEN 1 END)` also works, because COUNT skips NULLs, but mixing styles confuses reviewers.
sections.performance: One scan; cost grows with the number of CASE branches only marginally.
sections.interview: Common pivot question. Mentioning FILTER and the boolean-sum shortcut, with their portability limits, shows depth.

questions.title: Revenue by product category across three tables
questions.secondary: COUNT DISTINCT orders, line-level net revenue, multi-table join
questions.tables: order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, discount_amount); orders(order_id, status, order_ts); products(product_id, category_id); product_categories(category_id, category_name)

sections.context: Product management asks which product categories drive revenue from completed orders placed in 2025.
sections.problem: For each leaf category, return the number of distinct orders containing it, total units, and net revenue (`quantity * unit_price - discount_amount`) from completed orders placed in 2025. Sort by `net_revenue` descending.
sections.expected: One row per category with sales; `orders` counts each order once per category.
sections.edge_cases:
- One order can contain several lines of the same category, so `COUNT(*)` would count lines, not orders.
- Order header `order_total` must not be summed here: it repeats once per line after the join (fan-out).
sections.hint1: Start from the line table, which is the grain of the measures you sum.
sections.hint2: Join upward to `orders` for the filter and to `products` → `product_categories` for the name.
sections.hint3: Use `COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)` for the order count.
sections.solution:
SELECT pc.category_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)                                AS orders,
       SUM(oi.quantity)                                           AS units,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price - oi.discount_amount)      AS net_revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o              ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p            ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
JOIN product_categories pc ON pc.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  AND o.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND o.order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY pc.category_name
ORDER BY net_revenue DESC, pc.category_name;
sections.explanation:
Reason about **grain** first: the measures (quantity, price, discount) live on `order_items`, one row per order line. Joining to `orders`, `products` and `product_categories` moves along many-to-one relationships, so the line count stays the same and summing line amounts is safe.

`COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)` answers "in how many orders did this category appear?". `COUNT(*)` would answer "how many lines".
sections.mistakes:
- `SUM(o.order_total)` after joining lines: every order's total is repeated once per line, which inflates revenue (see SQL-031).
- Filtering on `products.is_active`, which would drop revenue from discontinued products that was really earned.
sections.performance: The join to `orders` is through the primary key, and `order_items(product_id)` supports the product join. The date filter on `orders(order_ts)` drives the plan.
sections.interview: Interviewers want to hear the word "grain" and see the candidate pick the right table to aggregate.

questions.title: First and last order of repeat buyers
questions.secondary: HAVING on a count, status filter

sections.context: The CRM team wants a list of loyal buyers (at least 5 completed orders) with their first and last purchase times and lifetime value.
sections.problem: Return `user_id`, `completed_orders`, `first_order_ts`, `last_order_ts` and `lifetime_value` (sum of `order_total`) for users with at least 5 completed orders. Sort by `lifetime_value` descending, then `user_id`.
sections.expected: One row per qualifying user.
sections.edge_cases: - Only completed orders count, both for the threshold and for the amounts.
sections.hint1: Filter rows to completed orders first, then group by user.
sections.hint2: The threshold is a group property, so it goes in HAVING.
sections.hint3: `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5`.
sections.solution:
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*)         AS completed_orders,
       MIN(order_ts)    AS first_order_ts,
       MAX(order_ts)    AS last_order_ts,
       SUM(order_total) AS lifetime_value
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC, user_id;
sections.explanation: WHERE removes non-completed orders before grouping, so all aggregates and the HAVING threshold refer to completed orders only. MIN/MAX on timestamps return the earliest and latest values. They work on any orderable type: numbers, strings, dates.
sections.mistakes: - Putting `status = 'completed'` in HAVING: it is not an aggregate. PostgreSQL rejects it, and MySQL would require it in GROUP BY.
sections.performance: The index `orders(user_id, order_ts)` makes MIN/MAX per user cheap for single-user lookups. For the whole table a hash aggregate is used.
sections.interview: Basic, but often extended: "now also return the product of their first order", which needs window functions (SQL-061).

questions.title: Refund rate by sales channel
questions.secondary: joining payments to orders, COALESCE in SUM, two different denominators
questions.tables: orders(order_id, status, sales_channel); payments(order_id, status, amount, refunded_amount)
questions.columns: sales_channel, paid_orders, refunded_orders, refund_rate_pct, collected_amount, refunded_amount, refunded_amount_pct

sections.context: Finance wants to know whether some sales channels generate disproportionate refunds, both by count and by money.
sections.problem: Using **payments that succeeded or were later refunded** (status `'succeeded'` or `'refunded'`), compute per `sales_channel` of the order: `paid_orders` (distinct orders), `refunded_orders` (distinct orders with a refunded payment), `refund_rate_pct` (2 decimals), `collected_amount` (sum of payment `amount`), `refunded_amount` (sum of `refunded_amount`, 0 if none) and `refunded_amount_pct` (2 decimals). Sort by `sales_channel`.
sections.expected: 3 rows (web, sales, marketplace).
sections.edge_cases:
- `refunded_amount` is NULL for non-refunded payments. SUM ignores NULLs, but SUM over an all-NULL group returns NULL, not 0.
- Partial refunds make the count-based and amount-based rates differ.
- Failed attempts must not count as paid.
sections.hint1: Join payments to orders to get the channel, after filtering payments to the two relevant statuses.
sections.hint2: Count refunded orders with `COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN p.status = 'refunded' THEN p.order_id END)`.
sections.hint3: Wrap money sums in `COALESCE(SUM(...), 0)` and divide with `NULLIF(..., 0)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.sales_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.order_id)                                              AS paid_orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN p.status = 'refunded' THEN p.order_id END)      AS refunded_orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN p.status = 'refunded' THEN p.order_id END)
             / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT p.order_id), 0), 2)                        AS refund_rate_pct,
       SUM(p.amount)                                                           AS collected_amount,
       COALESCE(SUM(p.refunded_amount), 0)                                     AS refunded_amount,
       ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(SUM(p.refunded_amount), 0) / NULLIF(SUM(p.amount), 0), 2)
                                                                               AS refunded_amount_pct
FROM payments p
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = p.order_id
WHERE p.status IN ('succeeded', 'refunded')
GROUP BY o.sales_channel
ORDER BY o.sales_channel;
sections.explanation:
1. Filtering payments to succeeded/refunded leaves one successful payment per paid order (failed retries are excluded). `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` still protects against double counting if an order ever had two successful payments.
2. `COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ... THEN order_id END)` counts refunded orders: the CASE yields NULL otherwise, and COUNT ignores NULLs.
3. `SUM(refunded_amount)` ignores NULLs; COALESCE converts an all-NULL group to 0.
4. Two rates with two denominators: share of orders refunded and share of money refunded. Partial refunds make the second smaller.
sections.mistakes:
- Counting refunds from `orders.status = 'refunded'` while summing money from payments. Both are valid sources, but mixing them hides inconsistencies.
- Including failed payments in `collected_amount`.
sections.performance: `payments(order_id)` index plus the orders primary key make the join cheap.
sections.interview: Shows careful thinking about NULLs in sums and about which denominator a rate uses.

questions.title: Daily active users and engagement depth in June 2025
questions.secondary: events per active user, date bucketing

sections.context: Product analytics defines a daily active user (DAU) as a user with at least one event that day (UTC). Engagement depth is events per active user.
sections.problem: For each day of June 2025, return `event_date`, `active_users`, `events` and `events_per_active_user` (2 decimals). Sort by date.
sections.expected: Up to 30 rows, one per day with activity.
sections.edge_cases:
- Duplicate events (client retries) inflate `events` but not `active_users`. That is accepted here (SQL-064 removes them).
- Server-side `purchase` events count as activity by this definition.
sections.hint1: Group events by calendar day.
sections.hint2: `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` gives DAU; `COUNT(*)` gives events.
sections.hint3: Divide with `1.0 *` (or `100.0`-style) to avoid integer division in PostgreSQL.
sections.solution:
SELECT CAST(event_ts AS DATE)                                   AS event_date,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)                                  AS active_users,
       COUNT(*)                                                 AS events,
       ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), 2)       AS events_per_active_user
FROM events
WHERE event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
  AND event_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CAST(event_ts AS DATE)
ORDER BY event_date;
sections.explanation: DAU is a distinct count per day. It cannot be summed across days to get monthly actives, because a user active on 10 days would count 10 times. Monthly active users need their own distinct count (SQL-078). The ratio uses `1.0 *` so PostgreSQL does not truncate.
sections.mistakes:
- `SUM(DAU)` as MAU.
- Integer division producing whole-number ratios in PostgreSQL.
sections.performance: `events(event_name, event_ts)` does not start with `event_ts` alone. PostgreSQL can still use it for the range only through a skip-scan (PostgreSQL 18) or by scanning. A dedicated `(event_ts)` index or partitioning by date helps large event tables.
sections.interview: Expect the follow-up "why can't you add up DAUs into MAU?"; this is non-additivity of distinct counts.

questions.title: Token usage with subtotals (ROLLUP)
questions.secondary: GROUPING(), subtotal labelling, dialect syntax

sections.context: The monthly AI usage report shows requests and tokens per model and feature, with a subtotal per model and a grand total, for June 2025.
sections.problem: Return requests and total tokens (`input_tokens + COALESCE(output_tokens, 0)`) for June 2025 grouped by `model_name` and `feature`, plus a subtotal row per model (feature = `'ALL'`) and a grand-total row (model = `'ALL'`, feature = `'ALL'`). Order: models alphabetically with each model's subtotal after its features, grand total last.
sections.expected: Detail rows + one subtotal per model + one grand total.
sections.edge_cases:
- Rollup rows carry NULL in the rolled-up columns. Use `GROUPING()` rather than `IS NULL` to recognise them, because real NULL keys would be ambiguous.
- `output_tokens` is NULL for failed requests.
sections.hint1: Both engines support ROLLUP but spell it differently.
sections.hint2: PostgreSQL: `GROUP BY ROLLUP (model_name, feature)`. MySQL: `GROUP BY model_name, feature WITH ROLLUP`.
sections.hint3: Label with `CASE WHEN GROUPING(feature) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE feature END` and order by `GROUPING(model_name), model_name, GROUPING(feature), feature`.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(model_name) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE model_name END AS model_name,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(feature) = 1    THEN 'ALL' ELSE feature END    AS feature,
       COUNT(*)                                           AS requests,
       SUM(input_tokens + COALESCE(output_tokens, 0))     AS total_tokens
FROM llm_requests
WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
  AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY ROLLUP (model_name, feature)
ORDER BY GROUPING(llm_requests.model_name), llm_requests.model_name,
         GROUPING(llm_requests.feature), llm_requests.feature;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(model_name) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE model_name END AS model_name,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(feature) = 1    THEN 'ALL' ELSE feature END    AS feature,
       COUNT(*)                                           AS requests,
       SUM(input_tokens + COALESCE(output_tokens, 0))     AS total_tokens
FROM llm_requests
WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
  AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY model_name, feature WITH ROLLUP
ORDER BY GROUPING(llm_requests.model_name), llm_requests.model_name,
         GROUPING(llm_requests.feature), llm_requests.feature;
sections.dialect_note: PostgreSQL implements the SQL-standard `ROLLUP`, `CUBE` and `GROUPING SETS`. MySQL supports only `WITH ROLLUP` (no CUBE or GROUPING SETS) plus the `GROUPING()` function (8.0+); ORDER BY together with WITH ROLLUP is allowed from 8.0.12. In both engines, ORDER BY qualifies the base columns with the table name so that `model_name` refers to the grouped column and not to the CASE alias of the same name.
sections.explanation:
ROLLUP(a, b) produces the grouping sets (a, b), (a), (). `GROUPING(col)` returns 1 when `col` was rolled up in that row. Labelling and sorting with GROUPING is robust even if the data had genuine NULL keys.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** token totals by model and feature are the basis for cost allocation (chargeback) and capacity planning; subtotals make the report readable without a BI tool.
sections.mistakes:
- `COALESCE(model_name, 'ALL')` mislabels a real NULL model as a subtotal.
- Summing `input_tokens + output_tokens` without COALESCE: failed requests contribute NULL and silently drop out of the sum.
sections.performance: Same scan as a normal GROUP BY plus a little extra aggregation work.
sections.interview: Shows reporting fluency. Mentioning GROUPING SETS/CUBE and MySQL's limitations is a plus.

questions.title: Average output tokens and the NULL denominator question
questions.secondary: AVG ignores NULL vs COALESCE to zero, COUNT(col)

sections.context: Capacity planning needs "average completion length per model". A failed request has `output_tokens = NULL`. Two engineers produced different numbers.
sections.problem: Per `model_name`, return all requests, requests with a non-NULL `output_tokens`, the average output tokens over answered requests, and the average over all requests treating NULL as 0 (both 1 decimal). Sort by model name.
sections.expected: 5 rows, one per model.
sections.edge_cases: - Both averages are "correct" for different questions: the size of an answer versus tokens generated per request sent.
sections.hint1: AVG silently drops NULLs from numerator and denominator.
sections.hint2: `AVG(COALESCE(output_tokens, 0))` keeps every request in the denominator.
sections.hint3: `COUNT(output_tokens)` is the denominator AVG actually used.
sections.solution:
SELECT model_name,
       COUNT(*)                                   AS requests,
       COUNT(output_tokens)                       AS requests_with_output,
       ROUND(AVG(output_tokens), 1)               AS avg_output_tokens_answered,
       ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(output_tokens, 0)), 1)  AS avg_output_tokens_all_requests
FROM llm_requests
GROUP BY model_name
ORDER BY model_name;
sections.explanation:
`AVG(output_tokens)` = SUM / COUNT(output_tokens), the size of a typical completion. `AVG(COALESCE(output_tokens, 0))` = SUM / COUNT(*), the expected output per request sent, which is what a cost forecast needs when failures are free. The gap between the two grows with the failure rate.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** output tokens are usually the most expensive tokens. Forecasting spend with the "answered only" average over-estimates cost when many requests fail before generating output.
sections.mistakes:
- Reporting one average without saying which denominator it uses.
- Treating NULL as 0 when computing "typical answer length" for UI design.
sections.performance: Trivial aggregation.
sections.interview: Tests whether the candidate asks "what should happen to NULLs?" before computing a metric.

questions.title: Average session length: overall versus average of user averages
questions.secondary: derived table, timestamp differences, per-dialect duration

sections.context: The mobile team claims mobile sessions are longer than desktop ones; the desktop team claims the opposite. Each team uses a different average.
sections.problem: For sessions started in Q2 2025 with a known `ended_at`, return per `device_type`: number of sessions, distinct users, the overall mean session length in minutes (every session weighs the same), and the mean of per-user mean session lengths (every user weighs the same). Both averages with 2 decimals. Sort by device type.
sections.expected: 3 rows (desktop, mobile, tablet).
sections.edge_cases:
- Sessions without `ended_at` have unknown length; exclude them and say so.
- Heavy users with many short sessions pull the session-weighted mean down but have only one vote in the user-weighted mean.
sections.hint1: The second metric needs two levels of aggregation: per (device, user), then per device.
sections.hint2: Compute session minutes first. PostgreSQL: `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM ended_at - started_at) / 60`. MySQL: `TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, started_at, ended_at) / 60`.
sections.hint3: Aggregate per user in a derived table, then aggregate again: `AVG(user_avg)` per device, `SUM(n)` for sessions, `COUNT(*)` for users, and a weighted mean `SUM(total_minutes) / SUM(n)`.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT device_type,
