       SUM(n_sessions)                                 AS sessions,
       COUNT(*)                                        AS users,
       ROUND(SUM(total_minutes) / SUM(n_sessions), 2)  AS avg_minutes_per_session,
       ROUND(AVG(user_avg_minutes), 2)                 AS avg_of_user_avg_minutes
FROM (
    SELECT device_type,
           user_id,
           COUNT(*)                                              AS n_sessions,
           SUM(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ended_at - started_at)) / 60) AS total_minutes,
           AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ended_at - started_at)) / 60) AS user_avg_minutes
    FROM sessions
    WHERE ended_at IS NOT NULL
      AND started_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
      AND started_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY device_type, user_id
) per_user
GROUP BY device_type
ORDER BY device_type;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT device_type,
       SUM(n_sessions)                                 AS sessions,
       COUNT(*)                                        AS users,
       ROUND(SUM(total_minutes) / SUM(n_sessions), 2)  AS avg_minutes_per_session,
       ROUND(AVG(user_avg_minutes), 2)                 AS avg_of_user_avg_minutes
FROM (
    SELECT device_type,
           user_id,
           COUNT(*)                                                 AS n_sessions,
           SUM(TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, started_at, ended_at) / 60)    AS total_minutes,
           AVG(TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, started_at, ended_at) / 60)    AS user_avg_minutes
    FROM sessions
    WHERE ended_at IS NOT NULL
      AND started_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
      AND started_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY device_type, user_id
) per_user
GROUP BY device_type
ORDER BY device_type;
sections.explanation:
1. The inner query (a *derived table*) has grain (device, user). It keeps both the per-user mean and the ingredients of the overall mean (session count and total minutes).
2. The outer query rolls up to device. The session-weighted mean must be recomputed as `SUM(total) / SUM(n)`. **Averaging the inner averages would give the user-weighted number instead.**
3. The two numbers answer different questions: "how long is a typical session?" versus "how long are a typical user's sessions?". Neither is wrong; the report must say which one it shows.

This is the aggregation version of Simpson's-paradox-style confusion: the weighting changes the conclusion.
sections.mistakes:
- `AVG(avg_minutes)` presented as the overall average.
- Including sessions with NULL `ended_at` (their duration is NULL, so they drop out of AVG anyway, but they still count in `COUNT(*)`).
sections.performance: Two-level aggregation over ~3,000 sessions is cheap. For large data, the same pattern runs in one scan plus a small second aggregation.
sections.interview: Senior DS interviews love "average of averages". Expect to justify which weighting the business question needs.

questions.title: Latency summary statistics per model
questions.secondary: STDDEV_SAMP, coefficient of variation, CAST before ROUND, filtering cache hits
questions.columns: model_name, requests, mean_ms, stddev_ms, min_ms, max_ms, cv

sections.context: Before setting latency alerts, the AI platform team wants basic distribution statistics per model for successful, non-cached requests in Q2 2025.
sections.problem: Per `model_name`: number of requests, mean latency, sample standard deviation, min, max (mean and stddev rounded to 1 decimal) and the coefficient of variation `cv` = stddev / mean (3 decimals). Sort by mean latency ascending.
sections.expected: One row per model with qualifying requests.
sections.edge_cases:
- Cache hits (~50-150 ms) would distort provider latency; exclude them.
- `STDDEV_SAMP` returns DOUBLE PRECISION in PostgreSQL; ROUND needs a DECIMAL cast there.
- A model with a single request has a NULL sample standard deviation.
sections.hint1: Filter to `status = 'success' AND cache_hit = FALSE` for Q2 2025.
sections.hint2: Both engines provide `STDDEV_SAMP` (and `STDDEV_POP`).
sections.hint3: `ROUND(CAST(STDDEV_SAMP(latency_ms) AS DECIMAL(12,4)), 1)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT model_name,
       COUNT(*)                                                         AS requests,
       ROUND(AVG(latency_ms), 1)                                        AS mean_ms,
       ROUND(CAST(STDDEV_SAMP(latency_ms) AS DECIMAL(14,4)), 1)         AS stddev_ms,
       MIN(latency_ms)                                                  AS min_ms,
       MAX(latency_ms)                                                  AS max_ms,
       ROUND(CAST(STDDEV_SAMP(latency_ms) / AVG(latency_ms) AS DECIMAL(14,6)), 3) AS cv
FROM llm_requests
WHERE status = 'success'
  AND cache_hit = FALSE
  AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
  AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY model_name
ORDER BY mean_ms, model_name;
sections.explanation:
- Mean and standard deviation summarize the distribution, but latency is right-skewed (long tail). The max is often 5-10x the mean, which is why SLOs use percentiles (SQL-117).
- The coefficient of variation makes the spread comparable across models with different speeds.
- `AVG(int)` returns NUMERIC/DECIMAL, which ROUND accepts. `STDDEV_SAMP` returns a double in PostgreSQL, so it is cast first.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** a high CV means unpredictable response times. Users perceive variance as slowness even when the mean is good.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `STDDEV` without knowing it is population (MySQL) or sample (PostgreSQL) depending on the engine. `STDDEV_SAMP`/`STDDEV_POP` are explicit and portable.
- Mixing cache hits into provider latency.
sections.performance: `llm_requests(model_name, requested_at)` supports this query well: equality on the first column, range on the second, per group.
sections.interview: Shows statistical literacy: mean vs median, skew, and choosing the right spread measure.

questions.title: Admins of enterprise customers
questions.secondary: table aliases, filtering on both sides of a join
questions.tables: users(user_id, org_id, full_name, email, role, status); organizations(org_id, org_name, segment)

sections.context: Account managers want to e-mail the active administrators of every Enterprise organization about an upcoming security feature.
sections.problem: List `org_id`, `org_name`, `user_id`, `full_name` and `email` of users with role `'admin'` and status `'active'` who belong to an organization in the `'Enterprise'` segment. Sort by `org_id`, then `user_id`.
sections.expected: One row per qualifying user.
sections.edge_cases: - `org_name` is not unique, so sort and group by `org_id`, not by name.
sections.hint1: The role and status live on `users`, the segment on `organizations`.
sections.hint2: Join on the foreign key `users.org_id = organizations.org_id`.
sections.hint3: `FROM users u JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id WHERE o.segment = 'Enterprise' AND u.role = 'admin' AND u.status = 'active'`.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.org_id,
       o.org_name,
       u.user_id,
       u.full_name,
       u.email
FROM users u
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id
WHERE o.segment = 'Enterprise'
  AND u.role = 'admin'
  AND u.status = 'active'
ORDER BY o.org_id, u.user_id;
sections.explanation: An INNER JOIN keeps pairs of rows that satisfy the ON condition. Every user has exactly one organization (NOT NULL foreign key), so the join neither drops nor duplicates users. The WHERE clause then filters on columns from both tables. Table aliases (`u`, `o`) keep the query readable and remove any ambiguity about which table a column comes from.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining on `org_name`: names are not unique, so users would be attached to the wrong companies.
- Selecting `org_id` without a table prefix. It exists in both tables, and both engines raise an "ambiguous column" error.
sections.performance: `users(org_id)` is indexed. The planner typically filters the small `organizations` table first and then looks up users per org.
sections.interview: Warm-up join. Interviewers check for join keys on IDs, not on names.

questions.title: Revenue by segment and the join fan-out trap
questions.secondary: aggregate before joining, grain reasoning
questions.tables: orders(order_id, org_id, status, order_total, order_ts); order_items(order_id); organizations(org_id, segment)

sections.context: A dashboard computes 2025 revenue by customer segment. Someone joined `order_items` to count products in the same query, and revenue jumped by more than 50%.
sections.problem: For completed orders placed in H1 2025, return per `segment`: `naive_revenue` (SUM of `order_total` after joining orders to organizations **and order_items**), `correct_revenue` (SUM of `order_total` with each order counted once), and `inflation_pct` = (naive / correct - 1) x 100, 1 decimal. Sort by segment.
sections.expected: 3 rows. `naive_revenue >= correct_revenue`.
sections.edge_cases:
- An order with 3 lines appears 3 times after the join, so its header total is summed 3 times.
- `SUM(DISTINCT order_total)` is *not* a fix: two different orders with the same total would collapse.
sections.hint1: What is the grain of the result after joining `orders` to `order_items`?
sections.hint2: Measure columns must be summed at their own grain. Aggregate (or deduplicate) before joining a one-to-many child.
sections.hint3: Compute `correct_revenue` from orders joined to organizations only; compute `naive_revenue` from a second derived table that also joins order_items; join the two per segment.
sections.solution:
SELECT c.segment,
       n.naive_revenue,
       c.correct_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (n.naive_revenue / c.correct_revenue - 1), 1) AS inflation_pct
FROM (
    SELECT og.segment, SUM(o.order_total) AS correct_revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN organizations og ON og.org_id = o.org_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND o.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
      AND o.order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY og.segment
) c
JOIN (
    SELECT og.segment, SUM(o.order_total) AS naive_revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN organizations og ON og.org_id = o.org_id
    JOIN order_items oi  ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND o.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
      AND o.order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY og.segment
) n ON n.segment = c.segment
ORDER BY c.segment;
sections.assert:
all(num(r[1]) >= num(r[2]) for r in rows)
any(num(r[3]) > 10 for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
**Grain** is the key word. `orders` has one row per order. After joining `order_items` the grain becomes one row per order *line*, so every order-level measure (`order_total`) is repeated once per line. Summing it multiplies each order's total by its line count. That is the fan-out.

Rules of thumb:
1. Decide the grain of the output (here: segment).
2. Sum each measure at the grain where it lives (`order_total` per order, `quantity` per line).
3. If you need measures from several grains, **aggregate each to the common key first**, then join the aggregates (see SQL-043).

The many-to-one join to `organizations` is safe because each order matches exactly one organization.
sections.mistakes:
- `SUM(DISTINCT o.order_total)`: wrong whenever two orders have the same amount.
- Fixing it with `COUNT(DISTINCT)` and dividing: fragile and hard to read.
sections.performance: Pre-aggregating also reduces work: the join to the child table is avoided entirely when it is not needed for the measure.
sections.interview: The single most common analytical SQL bug. A good answer names the grain of each table before writing the join.

questions.title: Purchase conversion by acquisition channel
questions.secondary: pre-aggregation, COALESCE, conversion rate

sections.context: Marketing wants the share of users from each acquisition channel who ever completed a purchase, plus how many completed orders a buyer places on average.
sections.problem: For users who signed up in 2024 or later, return per channel (`'unknown'` for NULL): number of users, number of buyers (users with at least one completed order), `conversion_pct` (2 decimals) and `completed_orders_per_buyer` (2 decimals). Sort by `conversion_pct` descending.
sections.expected: 6 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- An INNER JOIN to orders would remove every non-buyer and make conversion 100%.
- Joining raw orders would duplicate users with several orders, so count users with DISTINCT or pre-aggregate orders per user.
sections.hint1: Aggregate orders to one row per user first (count of completed orders).
sections.hint2: LEFT JOIN users to that aggregate; non-buyers get NULL.
sections.hint3: `buyers = SUM(CASE WHEN o.completed_orders > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`; orders per buyer = `SUM(completed_orders) / buyers`.
sections.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(u.acquisition_channel, 'unknown')                       AS channel,
       COUNT(*)                                                          AS users,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.completed_orders > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)           AS buyers,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN o.completed_orders > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2)
                                                                         AS conversion_pct,
       ROUND(1.0 * COALESCE(SUM(o.completed_orders), 0)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN o.completed_orders > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 2)
                                                                         AS completed_orders_per_buyer
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS completed_orders
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
) o ON o.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE u.signup_at >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY COALESCE(u.acquisition_channel, 'unknown')
ORDER BY conversion_pct DESC, channel;
sections.explanation:
1. The derived table `o` has one row per buyer, so joining it cannot duplicate users.
2. LEFT JOIN keeps every user; users without completed orders get `o.completed_orders = NULL`, and `NULL > 0` is UNKNOWN, so they add 0 to `buyers`.
3. `COUNT(*)` after the LEFT JOIN counts users (one row each).
4. Orders per buyer divides the total completed orders by buyers, with NULLIF protecting channels without buyers.

The status filter sits *inside* the derived table. Putting `o.status = 'completed'` in the outer WHERE of a plain LEFT JOIN to `orders` would remove the non-buyers again (see SQL-034).
sections.mistakes:
- INNER JOIN, which gives 100% conversion.
- `COUNT(o.user_id)` on a raw LEFT JOIN to orders counts orders, not buyers.
sections.performance: Pre-aggregation reduces the join input to one row per buyer and supports the `orders(user_id, ...)` index.
sections.interview: Conversion questions test LEFT JOIN semantics and denominator choice: all users, or users exposed to a purchase opportunity?

questions.title: Completed orders without a payment record (anti-join)
questions.secondary: LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL alternative, data reconciliation
questions.tables: orders(order_id, order_ts, status, sales_channel, order_total); payments(order_id)

sections.context: Finance reconciles the order system with the payment provider. A completed order without any payment row means revenue was recognized without cash, a serious accounting issue.
sections.problem: List completed orders that have no row at all in `payments`. Return `order_id`, `order_ts`, `sales_channel`, `order_total`, sorted by `order_id`.
sections.expected: A short list (about 15 orders).
sections.edge_cases: - Orders with only failed payments are a different problem (they do have payment rows).
sections.hint1: You want rows of `orders` for which no matching row exists in `payments`.
sections.hint2: `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.order_id)`.
sections.hint3: Alternative: `LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id WHERE p.order_id IS NULL`. Test a column that is NOT NULL in payments.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.order_ts,
       o.sales_channel,
       o.order_total
FROM orders o
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM payments p
                  WHERE p.order_id = o.order_id)
ORDER BY o.order_id;
sections.alternative:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.order_ts,
       o.sales_channel,
       o.order_total
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  AND p.payment_id IS NULL
ORDER BY o.order_id;
sections.alternative_note: The LEFT JOIN / IS NULL form returns the same rows. Test a column that can never be NULL in a matched row (here the primary key `payment_id`). NOT EXISTS states the intent more directly and cannot produce duplicates.
sections.explanation: An **anti-join** returns rows of the left table that have *no* partner in the right table. `NOT EXISTS` with a correlated subquery is the clearest way to express it, and both PostgreSQL and MySQL 8 plan it as an anti-join (MySQL 8.0.17+). It is also NULL-safe, unlike `NOT IN` (SQL-013).
sections.mistakes:
- `WHERE o.order_id NOT IN (SELECT order_id FROM payments)` works here only because `payments.order_id` is NOT NULL. It is a habit that breaks elsewhere.
- In the LEFT JOIN form, testing a nullable column of `payments` (e.g. `refunded_at IS NULL`) matches real payments too.
sections.performance: The `payments(order_id)` index turns each existence probe into an index lookup.
sections.interview: Expect "show me two ways" and a question about NULL safety.

questions.title: LEFT JOIN filter placement (ON versus WHERE)
questions.primary: LEFT JOIN conditions versus WHERE conditions
questions.secondary: counting zero matches, COUNT(column)
questions.tables: organizations(org_id, org_name, segment); support_tickets(ticket_id, org_id, priority, created_at)

sections.context: For a quarterly business review, every Enterprise customer should appear with its number of urgent tickets in H1 2025, including customers with zero urgent tickets.
sections.problem: Return every Enterprise organization with `urgent_tickets_h1_2025` (0 when none). Sort by the count descending, then `org_id`.
sections.expected: One row per Enterprise organization, including zeros.
sections.edge_cases:
- A filter on the right table placed in WHERE removes the NULL-extended rows and turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
- `COUNT(*)` would count 1 for an organization without tickets (the NULL-extended row).
sections.hint1: Which filters describe *which tickets to attach*, and which describe *which organizations to show*?
sections.hint2: Ticket filters belong in the ON clause of the LEFT JOIN.
sections.hint3: `LEFT JOIN support_tickets t ON t.org_id = o.org_id AND t.priority = 'urgent' AND t.created_at >= ... AND t.created_at < ...`, then `COUNT(t.ticket_id)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.org_id,
       o.org_name,
       COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS urgent_tickets_h1_2025
FROM organizations o
LEFT JOIN support_tickets t
       ON t.org_id = o.org_id
      AND t.priority = 'urgent'
      AND t.created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
      AND t.created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
WHERE o.segment = 'Enterprise'
GROUP BY o.org_id, o.org_name
ORDER BY urgent_tickets_h1_2025 DESC, o.org_id;
sections.explanation:
With a LEFT JOIN, the ON condition decides which right-hand rows are attached. Left rows without a partner are still kept, padded with NULLs. The WHERE clause runs **after** the join. `WHERE t.priority = 'urgent'` evaluates to UNKNOWN for the NULL-padded rows and removes them, so organizations without urgent tickets disappear.

Rule: filters on the **preserved** (left) table go in WHERE; filters on the **optional** (right) table go in ON.

`COUNT(t.ticket_id)` counts only real matches; `COUNT(*)` would return 1 for an organization with no tickets.
sections.mistakes:
- Moving the priority/date filters to WHERE.
- Using `COUNT(*)`.
- Grouping by `org_name` only: two organizations share a name.
sections.performance: `support_tickets(org_id, created_at)` serves the join plus the date range.
sections.interview: Probably the most important LEFT JOIN question. Expect the interviewer to ask for the query with the bug and to explain the difference.

questions.title: AI feature adoption by segment (semi-join)
questions.secondary: conditional aggregation, adoption rate
questions.tables: organizations(org_id, segment, is_deleted); llm_requests(org_id, requested_at, status)

sections.context: Product leadership asks what share of current (non-deleted) customers in each segment used any AI feature successfully in Q2 2025.
sections.problem: Per `segment`, return the number of non-deleted organizations, the number that made at least one **successful** LLM request in Q2 2025 (`adopting_orgs`), and `adoption_pct` (1 decimal). Sort by segment.
sections.expected: 3 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- Joining to `llm_requests` directly would multiply organizations by their request count.
- Organizations created after Q2 2025 do not exist in this dataset, but in a live system the denominator should be "customers at the time".
sections.hint1: You only need to know *whether* a matching request exists, not how many.
sections.hint2: `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM llm_requests r WHERE r.org_id = o.org_id AND ...)` inside a CASE.
sections.hint3: `SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (...) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.segment,
       COUNT(*) AS organizations,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1
                             FROM llm_requests r
                             WHERE r.org_id = o.org_id
                               AND r.status = 'success'
                               AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                               AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS adopting_orgs,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1
                                           FROM llm_requests r
                                           WHERE r.org_id = o.org_id
                                             AND r.status = 'success'
                                             AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                                             AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
                              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS adoption_pct
FROM organizations o
WHERE o.is_deleted = FALSE
GROUP BY o.segment
ORDER BY o.segment;
sections.alternative:
SELECT o.segment,
       COUNT(*)                                                   AS organizations,
       COUNT(a.org_id)                                            AS adopting_orgs,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(a.org_id) / COUNT(*), 1)               AS adoption_pct
FROM organizations o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT org_id
           FROM llm_requests
           WHERE status = 'success'
             AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
             AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00') a
       ON a.org_id = o.org_id
WHERE o.is_deleted = FALSE
GROUP BY o.segment
ORDER BY o.segment;
sections.alternative_note: The DISTINCT derived table reduces requests to one row per adopting organization, so the LEFT JOIN cannot fan out. It avoids repeating the EXISTS expression and is often easier to extend (e.g. to count requests too).
sections.explanation:
A **semi-join** keeps a left row when at least one match exists, and never duplicates it. `EXISTS` stops at the first match. In the main solution it appears inside a CASE so that every organization stays in the denominator. The repeated EXISTS is verbose; the alternative computes the set of adopting organizations once and LEFT JOINs it.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** adoption by segment shows where AI features land. Low Enterprise adoption often points to access-control or data-residency blockers rather than to the quality of the feature.
sections.mistakes:
- `JOIN llm_requests` then `COUNT(*)` counts requests, not organizations.
- Counting all statuses: an organization whose every request was rate-limited did not really adopt the feature.
sections.performance: `llm_requests(org_id)` makes each EXISTS probe an index lookup; the DISTINCT version scans the date range once.
sections.interview: Shows the semi-join pattern and the "count entities, not events" discipline.

questions.title: Top referrers and whether referrals stay in the same company
questions.secondary: aggregate on the self-join, conditional count

sections.context: The referral program pays a bonus to users who bring in at least two new users. Finance also wants to know whether referrals are colleagues (same organization) or external.
sections.problem: For users who referred at least 2 users, return `referrer_id`, `referrer_name`, `referrals` and `same_org_referrals`. Sort by `referrals` descending, then `referrer_id`.
sections.expected: One row per qualifying referrer (about two dozen).
sections.edge_cases: - `users` references itself; give the two roles distinct aliases.
sections.hint1: Join `users` to itself: one copy plays the referred user, the other the referrer.
sections.hint2: `FROM users r JOIN users ref ON ref.user_id = r.referred_by_user_id`.
sections.hint3: Group by the referrer columns and filter with `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2`.
sections.solution:
SELECT ref.user_id                                              AS referrer_id,
       ref.full_name                                            AS referrer_name,
       COUNT(*)                                                 AS referrals,
       SUM(CASE WHEN r.org_id = ref.org_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)   AS same_org_referrals
FROM users r
JOIN users ref ON ref.user_id = r.referred_by_user_id
GROUP BY ref.user_id, ref.full_name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY referrals DESC, referrer_id;
sections.explanation: A self join treats one table as two logical tables. Here `r` is the referred user and `ref` the referrer, linked by `r.referred_by_user_id = ref.user_id`. The inner join automatically drops users without a referrer. Grouping by the referrer counts referred users, and comparing the two `org_id` columns classifies each referral.
sections.mistakes:
- Reversing the join direction (`ref.referred_by_user_id = r.user_id`) answers "who referred me" instead of "whom did I refer".
- Grouping by `full_name` alone: names repeat.
sections.performance: Each referred user looks up its referrer by primary key.
sections.interview: Self joins appear in hierarchy, referral, and "pairs of events" questions. Clear aliases are what interviewers look for.

questions.title: Most-retrieved knowledge-base documents (many-to-many)
questions.primary: Many-to-many joins through a bridge table
questions.secondary: COUNT DISTINCT at the right grain, multi-table join
questions.tables: llm_requests(request_id, feature, requested_at); llm_request_chunks(request_id, chunk_id); document_chunks(chunk_id, document_id); documents(document_id, doc_key, status)

sections.context: The content team wants to know which knowledge-base documents the support bot relies on most, so they can prioritise reviews.
sections.problem: For support-bot requests in June 2025, return the 10 `doc_key`s that appear in the most distinct requests. Show `requests` (distinct requests that retrieved at least one chunk of the document), `chunk_retrievals` (total retrieved chunks), and `distinct_versions` (different document versions retrieved). Ties: `doc_key` ascending.
sections.expected: 10 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- A request can retrieve several chunks of the same document, so `COUNT(*)` counts chunk retrievals, not requests.
- Different versions of the same document share a `doc_key`.
sections.hint1: `llm_request_chunks` is the bridge between requests and chunks; chunks belong to document versions.
sections.hint2: Join requests → request_chunks → document_chunks → documents and group by `doc_key`.
sections.hint3: `COUNT(DISTINCT rc.request_id)` for requests, `COUNT(*)` for retrievals, `COUNT(DISTINCT d.document_id)` for versions.
sections.solution:
SELECT d.doc_key,
       COUNT(DISTINCT rc.request_id)  AS requests,
       COUNT(*)                       AS chunk_retrievals,
       COUNT(DISTINCT d.document_id)  AS distinct_versions
FROM llm_requests r
JOIN llm_request_chunks rc ON rc.request_id = r.request_id
JOIN document_chunks c     ON c.chunk_id = rc.chunk_id
JOIN documents d           ON d.document_id = c.document_id
WHERE r.feature = 'support_bot'
  AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
  AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY d.doc_key
ORDER BY requests DESC, d.doc_key
LIMIT 10;
sections.explanation:
Requests and chunks have a **many-to-many** relationship: a request retrieves many chunks, and a chunk is retrieved by many requests. The bridge table `llm_request_chunks` stores one row per (request, rank). After the joins, the grain is one row per retrieved chunk. Each count therefore needs to say what it counts: DISTINCT requests, all retrievals, or DISTINCT versions.

`distinct_versions > 1` is a warning sign: answers were grounded in more than one version of the same document, possibly an outdated one (see SQL-127).

**Why it matters for AI apps:** retrieval frequency is a proxy for content importance and a starting point for content QA.
sections.mistakes:
- Ranking by `COUNT(*)`, which favours long documents with many chunks.
- Forgetting ties, so LIMIT returns an arbitrary 10th row.
sections.performance: `llm_request_chunks(chunk_id)` and the primary keys support every join; the date filter on `llm_requests(requested_at)` keeps the input small.
sections.interview: Many-to-many joins are where duplicate counting hides. Saying "after this join the grain is per retrieved chunk" earns trust.

questions.title: Attribute orders to the active subscription (range join)
questions.primary: Range join on a validity interval
questions.secondary: detecting zero and multiple matches, LEFT JOIN with range condition
questions.tables: orders(order_id, org_id, status, order_ts); subscriptions(subscription_id, org_id, started_at, ended_at)

sections.context: Revenue analysts want to attribute each completed order to the plan the organization was on when it ordered. Subscriptions are periods `[started_at, ended_at)` with `ended_at IS NULL` for open periods. Before trusting the attribution, check how many subscriptions each order matches.
sections.problem: For every completed order, count the subscriptions of the same organization whose period contains `order_ts`. Return how many orders have 0, 1, 2, ... matches (`matching_subscriptions`, `completed_orders`), sorted by the match count.
sections.expected: A small distribution table. Most orders match exactly one subscription.
sections.edge_cases:
- Open periods: `ended_at IS NULL` means "still running"; the comparison `order_ts < ended_at` would be UNKNOWN.
- Overlapping subscriptions (a known billing bug) produce 2 matches, which means fan-out if you join naively.
- Orders placed while the organization had no subscription produce 0 matches; an INNER JOIN would drop them silently.
sections.hint1: Join on the organization **and** on a time condition, not on equality of a key.
sections.hint2: `s.started_at <= o.order_ts AND (s.ended_at IS NULL OR o.order_ts < s.ended_at)`.
sections.hint3: LEFT JOIN, count matches per order in a derived table, then group by that count.
sections.solution:
SELECT matching_subscriptions,
       COUNT(*) AS completed_orders
FROM (
    SELECT o.order_id,
           COUNT(s.subscription_id) AS matching_subscriptions
    FROM orders o
    LEFT JOIN subscriptions s
           ON s.org_id = o.org_id
          AND s.started_at <= o.order_ts
          AND (s.ended_at IS NULL OR o.order_ts < s.ended_at)
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY o.order_id
) m
GROUP BY matching_subscriptions
ORDER BY matching_subscriptions;
sections.assert:
len(rows) >= 2
any(r[0] == '0' for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
A **range join** (also called an interval or "as-of" join) matches a point in time to the period containing it. Unlike a key join, nothing in the schema guarantees exactly one match:
- **0 matches**: gaps in subscription history. With an INNER JOIN these orders vanish from the revenue report.
- **2+ matches**: overlapping periods. A naive join would duplicate the order and double its revenue.

Checking the match distribution before using a range join is a cheap, high-value habit. To resolve multiple matches deterministically, pick one candidate per order with an explicit tie-break rule, such as the latest `started_at` (SQL-056).

Using `COALESCE(s.ended_at, '9999-12-31')` instead of the `IS NULL OR` form is equivalent and common.
sections.mistakes:
- `o.order_ts BETWEEN s.started_at AND s.ended_at`: fails for open periods (NULL) and double counts an order placed exactly at a boundary.
- INNER JOIN, which hides the 0-match orders.
sections.performance: `subscriptions(org_id, started_at)` narrows candidates per organization; range joins over large tables benefit from that equality prefix.
sections.interview: "As-of" joins are central in analytics and in ML feature engineering. Interviewers check boundary handling and the zero/many match cases.

questions.title: Complete model-by-feature grid (CROSS JOIN)
questions.primary: CROSS JOIN to build a complete grid
questions.secondary: LEFT JOIN aggregated facts, zero-filling

sections.context: A heat-map in the AI usage report must show every model x feature combination, including combinations that had no traffic in June 2025 (they show as 0, not as missing cells).
sections.problem: Return every combination of the 5 models in `llm_models` and the 3 features (`support_bot`, `sql_copilot`, `doc_summary`) with the number of requests in June 2025. Sort by model, then feature.
sections.expected: Exactly 15 rows; many requests counts are 0.
sections.edge_cases:
- Features are not stored in a table of their own; build the list (derived table or VALUES).
- `COUNT(*)` on a LEFT JOIN returns 1 for empty combinations; count a column of the right side instead, or zero-fill an aggregate.
sections.hint1: First build all combinations, then attach the facts.
sections.hint2: `llm_models CROSS JOIN (SELECT 'support_bot' AS feature UNION ALL SELECT ...)`.
sections.hint3: Aggregate requests per (model, feature) in a derived table and LEFT JOIN it to the grid with `COALESCE(n, 0)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT m.model_name,
       f.feature,
       COALESCE(r.requests, 0) AS requests
FROM llm_models m
CROSS JOIN (SELECT 'support_bot' AS feature
            UNION ALL SELECT 'sql_copilot'
            UNION ALL SELECT 'doc_summary') f
LEFT JOIN (SELECT model_name, feature, COUNT(*) AS requests
           FROM llm_requests
           WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
             AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
           GROUP BY model_name, feature) r
       ON r.model_name = m.model_name
      AND r.feature = f.feature
ORDER BY m.model_name, f.feature;
sections.explanation:
`CROSS JOIN` returns the Cartesian product: 5 models x 3 features = 15 cells. Facts are aggregated separately and attached with a LEFT JOIN on both keys; COALESCE turns missing cells into 0. This "spine + facts" pattern is the standard way to get complete grids for charts and for ML datasets, where a missing row and a zero mean different things.

`SELECT 'x' AS feature UNION ALL SELECT ...` builds an inline list in both engines. PostgreSQL also accepts `(VALUES ('support_bot'), ...) AS f(feature)`. MySQL 8 supports `VALUES ROW(...)` with a different syntax.
sections.mistakes:
- An accidental CROSS JOIN (missing ON clause) is a classic performance disaster. Here it is intentional and small.
- Zero-filling with `COUNT(*)` over the LEFT JOIN of raw requests (returns 1 for empty cells).
sections.performance: The grid is tiny; the aggregation scans June's requests once.
sections.interview: Shows the difference between "no rows" and "zero", which matters for dashboards and time series.

questions.title: Compare two retrieval configurations on the composite key
questions.secondary: conditional aggregation, NULL-safe boolean comparison
questions.columns: queries, same_top1_chunk, top1_relevant_cfg2, top1_relevant_cfg3, improved, regressed

sections.context: The retrieval team replaced config 2 (`dense_large_384_ov64`) with config 3 (`hybrid_rerank_k10`). For a quick sanity check they compare the **top-1** result of both configurations on each evaluation query.
sections.problem: Pair the rank-1 row of config 2 with the rank-1 row of config 3 for the same `query_id`. Return one row with: number of queries compared, queries where both returned the same chunk, queries whose top-1 was relevant for config 2, for config 3, `improved` (relevant only for config 3) and `regressed` (relevant only for config 2). Treat unjudged (`NULL`) as not relevant.
sections.expected: One row, six integer columns.
sections.edge_cases:
- The key of an evaluation row is `(config_id, query_id, rank_position)`. Joining on `query_id` alone would pair every rank with every other rank (100 pairs per query for k = 10).
- `is_relevant` can be NULL; use `COALESCE(is_relevant, FALSE)`.
sections.hint1: Self-join the table: one alias for config 2, another for config 3.
sections.hint2: Join on `query_id` **and** `rank_position`, and fix rank 1 and the two config IDs.
sections.hint3: `improved = SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(b.is_relevant, FALSE) AND NOT COALESCE(a.is_relevant, FALSE) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                                                                       AS queries,
       SUM(CASE WHEN a.chunk_id = b.chunk_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                       AS same_top1_chunk,
       SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(a.is_relevant, FALSE) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)               AS top1_relevant_cfg2,
       SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(b.is_relevant, FALSE) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)               AS top1_relevant_cfg3,
       SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(b.is_relevant, FALSE) AND NOT COALESCE(a.is_relevant, FALSE)
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                                   AS improved,
       SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(a.is_relevant, FALSE) AND NOT COALESCE(b.is_relevant, FALSE)
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                                   AS regressed
FROM retrieval_evaluations a
JOIN retrieval_evaluations b
  ON b.query_id = a.query_id
 AND b.rank_position = a.rank_position
WHERE a.config_id = 2
  AND b.config_id = 3
  AND a.rank_position = 1;
sections.explanation:
When a table's identity is a **composite key**, every key column that should match must be in the join condition; otherwise rows multiply. Here the config IDs are fixed by the WHERE clause, and the join matches `(query_id, rank_position)`.

The `improved`/`regressed` split is more informative than two accuracy numbers: a net gain of +20 could hide 40 wins and 20 losses, which matters if the losses fall on important query types.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** offline retrieval evaluation compares configurations query by query before a rollout. Win/loss counts are also the input for a paired significance test such as McNemar's test.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining on `query_id` only.
- Ignoring NULL judgments: `a.is_relevant AND NOT b.is_relevant` is UNKNOWN when either side is NULL, so those queries are silently dropped from both counts.
sections.performance: The primary key `(config_id, query_id, rank_position)` serves both sides of the join.
sections.interview: Tests composite-key discipline and how to compare two models on paired data.

questions.title: Reconcile event data with ingestion runs (FULL OUTER JOIN)
questions.primary: FULL OUTER JOIN and its MySQL emulation
questions.secondary: RIGHT/LEFT anti-join union, date-level reconciliation

sections.context: The ML platform team audits the `events_ingest` pipeline for Q2 2025. Every date that has events should have a successful ingestion run, and every successful run should correspond to a date with events.
sections.problem: Compare, per date in Q2 2025, the number of events (by `event_ts` date) with the number of successful `events_ingest` runs (by `run_date`). Return only dates where something is wrong: `activity_date`, `events` (0 if none), `successful_runs` (0 if none) and `issue` (`'no successful run'` or `'run without events'`). Sort by date.
sections.expected: A handful of problem dates.
sections.edge_cases:
- A date can be missing on either side, so you need a FULL OUTER JOIN of two daily aggregates.
- **MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN.** Emulate it with a LEFT JOIN plus the unmatched rows of the other side.
- A date can have failed runs only; it then has a row in `pipeline_runs`, but zero successful runs.
sections.hint1: Aggregate both sources to one row per date first (two derived tables).
sections.hint2: PostgreSQL: `FULL OUTER JOIN ... ON e.d = r.d` and `COALESCE(e.d, r.d)` for the date.
sections.hint3: MySQL: `(e LEFT JOIN r) UNION ALL (r rows with NOT EXISTS in e)`, then filter the problem rows.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT COALESCE(e.activity_date, r.run_date)                 AS activity_date,
       COALESCE(e.events, 0)                                 AS events,
       COALESCE(r.successful_runs, 0)                        AS successful_runs,
       CASE WHEN COALESCE(r.successful_runs, 0) = 0 THEN 'no successful run'
            ELSE 'run without events' END                    AS issue
FROM (SELECT CAST(event_ts AS DATE) AS activity_date, COUNT(*) AS events
      FROM events
      WHERE event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
        AND event_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
      GROUP BY CAST(event_ts AS DATE)) e
FULL OUTER JOIN
     (SELECT run_date,
             SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS successful_runs
      FROM pipeline_runs
      WHERE pipeline_name = 'events_ingest'
        AND run_date >= DATE '2025-04-01'
        AND run_date <  DATE '2025-07-01'
      GROUP BY run_date) r
  ON r.run_date = e.activity_date
WHERE COALESCE(e.events, 0) = 0
   OR COALESCE(r.successful_runs, 0) = 0
ORDER BY activity_date;
sections.solution_mysql:
WITH e AS (
    SELECT CAST(event_ts AS DATE) AS activity_date, COUNT(*) AS events
    FROM events
    WHERE event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
      AND event_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY CAST(event_ts AS DATE)
), r AS (
    SELECT run_date,
           SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS successful_runs
    FROM pipeline_runs
    WHERE pipeline_name = 'events_ingest'
      AND run_date >= DATE '2025-04-01'
      AND run_date <  DATE '2025-07-01'
    GROUP BY run_date
), full_outer AS (
    SELECT e.activity_date, e.events, r.successful_runs
    FROM e LEFT JOIN r ON r.run_date = e.activity_date
    UNION ALL
    SELECT r.run_date, NULL, r.successful_runs
    FROM r
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM e WHERE e.activity_date = r.run_date)
)
SELECT activity_date,
       COALESCE(events, 0)          AS events,
       COALESCE(successful_runs, 0) AS successful_runs,
       CASE WHEN COALESCE(successful_runs, 0) = 0 THEN 'no successful run'
            ELSE 'run without events' END AS issue
FROM full_outer
WHERE COALESCE(events, 0) = 0
   OR COALESCE(successful_runs, 0) = 0
ORDER BY activity_date;
sections.dialect_note: PostgreSQL supports `FULL [OUTER] JOIN`. MySQL does not. The standard emulation is `A LEFT JOIN B` **UNION ALL** the rows of B with no partner in A (anti-join). Do not use `A LEFT JOIN B UNION A RIGHT JOIN B`: plain UNION also removes legitimate duplicate rows, and it costs an extra sort. The MySQL version uses CTEs (MySQL 8.0+) so that each aggregate is written once.
sections.explanation:
1. Each side is aggregated to the same grain, one row per date, before joining. That makes the outer join one-to-one and avoids fan-out.
2. A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from **both** sides, which is what a reconciliation needs.
3. `COALESCE(e.activity_date, r.run_date)` produces a single date column whichever side exists.
4. The final filter keeps the problem dates only. In this dataset these are dates whose run is missing because of scheduler outages, and the last day, whose run only starts the following morning.

In MySQL, the anti-join branch adds the run-only dates that a LEFT JOIN from events would miss.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining raw tables (events x runs) before aggregating: every event row is multiplied by the number of runs on that day.
- Emulating FULL JOIN with UNION (not ALL) between a LEFT and a RIGHT JOIN, which silently deduplicates rows.
sections.performance: Both sides are reduced to ≤ 91 rows before the join; the expensive part is the events aggregation over the date range.
sections.interview: Reconciliation between two systems is a common data-engineering and MLE interview task; knowing the MySQL emulation is a practical plus.

questions.title: Open subscriptions per plan with RIGHT JOIN
questions.secondary: equivalence with LEFT JOIN, filter in ON
questions.tables: subscriptions(subscription_id, plan_id, mrr, ended_at); plans(plan_id, plan_name, tier_rank)

sections.context: The pricing team wants the current number of open subscriptions and their MRR for **every** plan, including plans nobody is on.
sections.problem: Using a RIGHT JOIN from `subscriptions` to `plans`, return `plan_name`, `open_subscriptions` (periods with `ended_at IS NULL`) and `open_mrr` (0 when none). Sort by `tier_rank`, then `plan_name`.
sections.expected: 6 rows; the legacy plan has 0 open subscriptions.
sections.edge_cases: - The "open" condition must be in the ON clause, otherwise plans without open subscriptions disappear.
sections.hint1: `A RIGHT JOIN B` keeps every row of B.
sections.hint2: Put `s.ended_at IS NULL` in the ON clause.
sections.hint3: `COUNT(s.subscription_id)` and `COALESCE(SUM(s.mrr), 0)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT p.plan_name,
       COUNT(s.subscription_id)   AS open_subscriptions,
       COALESCE(SUM(s.mrr), 0)    AS open_mrr
FROM subscriptions s
RIGHT JOIN plans p
        ON p.plan_id = s.plan_id
       AND s.ended_at IS NULL
GROUP BY p.plan_id, p.plan_name, p.tier_rank
ORDER BY p.tier_rank, p.plan_name;
sections.alternative:
SELECT p.plan_name,
       COUNT(s.subscription_id)   AS open_subscriptions,
       COALESCE(SUM(s.mrr), 0)    AS open_mrr
FROM plans p
LEFT JOIN subscriptions s
       ON s.plan_id = p.plan_id
      AND s.ended_at IS NULL
GROUP BY p.plan_id, p.plan_name, p.tier_rank
ORDER BY p.tier_rank, p.plan_name;
sections.alternative_note: Swapping the table order turns the RIGHT JOIN into the more common LEFT JOIN. Most style guides prefer LEFT JOIN so that the "preserved" table always comes first.
sections.explanation: `A RIGHT JOIN B` is exactly `B LEFT JOIN A`. It is rarely necessary, but you will meet it in legacy queries and interviews. As with LEFT JOIN, filters on the optional side (`subscriptions`) must live in the ON clause.
sections.mistakes:
- `WHERE s.ended_at IS NULL` (with only the key in ON) looks right, because the NULL-extended row of a plan *without any* subscriptions also has a NULL `ended_at`. But a plan whose subscriptions have **all ended**, like the legacy plan, keeps only its ended rows, they are all filtered out, and the plan disappears from the result.
- `SUM(s.mrr)` without COALESCE returns NULL for plans without subscriptions.
sections.performance: `subscriptions(plan_id)` index supports the join.
sections.interview: Expect "rewrite this as a LEFT JOIN". Mixing LEFT and RIGHT joins in one query is a readability smell.

questions.title: Two one-to-many children: lines and payment attempts per order
questions.primary: Fan-out from joining two child tables
questions.secondary: pre-aggregation per child, COUNT(DISTINCT) limits
questions.tables: orders(order_id, status, order_ts); order_items(order_id, quantity, unit_price, discount_amount); payments(order_id, payment_id, amount, status)
questions.columns: order_id, line_count, line_net_amount, payment_attempts, failed_attempts, naive_line_net_amount

sections.context: The checkout team investigates orders that needed several payment attempts in May 2025. For each such order they want the number of lines, the net amount of the lines, and the payment attempts. A first draft joined both child tables to `orders` and reported inflated amounts.
sections.problem: For completed orders placed in May 2025 with **at least 2 payment attempts**, return `order_id`, `line_count`, `line_net_amount`, `payment_attempts`, `failed_attempts`, and `naive_line_net_amount` (the line amount computed after joining both children directly). Sort by `order_id`.
sections.expected: One row per qualifying order. `naive_line_net_amount = line_net_amount x payment_attempts`.
sections.edge_cases:
- Joining lines (L rows) and payments (P rows) to the same order produces L x P rows.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` can rescue counts but **not** sums.
sections.hint1: Each child table must be reduced to one row per order before the two are combined.
sections.hint2: Two derived tables: lines per order and payments per order, both grouped by `order_id`.
sections.hint3: For the naive column, a third derived table joins `orders`, `order_items` and `payments` together and sums the line amounts.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.order_id,
       li.line_count,
       li.line_net_amount,
       pa.payment_attempts,
       pa.failed_attempts,
       nv.naive_line_net_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT order_id,
             COUNT(*)                                          AS line_count,
             SUM(quantity * unit_price - discount_amount)      AS line_net_amount
      FROM order_items
      GROUP BY order_id) li ON li.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN (SELECT order_id,
             COUNT(*)                                          AS payment_attempts,
             SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failed_attempts
      FROM payments
      GROUP BY order_id) pa ON pa.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN (SELECT o2.order_id,
             SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price - oi.discount_amount) AS naive_line_net_amount
      FROM orders o2
      JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o2.order_id
      JOIN payments p     ON p.order_id = o2.order_id
      GROUP BY o2.order_id) nv ON nv.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  AND o.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-05-01 00:00:00'
  AND o.order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
  AND pa.payment_attempts >= 2
ORDER BY o.order_id;
sections.assert: all(abs(num(r[5]) - num(r[2]) * num(r[3])) < 0.01 for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
`order_items` and `payments` are both one-to-many children of `orders` but are unrelated to each other. Joining both to the same order pairs every line with every payment, a mini Cartesian product per order. `COUNT(DISTINCT payment_id)` would repair the attempt count, but nothing repairs `SUM(line amount)`: it is multiplied by the number of payments.

The fix is to reduce each child to one row per order (derived tables `li` and `pa`) and join those. All joins are then one-to-one. The `nv` derived table reproduces the bug for comparison only.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `SUM(DISTINCT line_amount)`, which merges different lines with equal amounts.
- Filtering `payments.status = 'failed'` in WHERE, which removes the successful attempt and changes `payment_attempts`.
- Naming a column `lines`: it is a **reserved word in MySQL** (`LOAD DATA ... LINES TERMINATED BY`) and causes a syntax error there, while PostgreSQL accepts it. Prefer descriptive, non-reserved aliases such as `line_count`.
sections.performance: Pre-aggregation scans each child once; in production, push the date filter into the derived tables (via a join to filtered orders) to avoid aggregating the whole history.
sections.interview: "Two one-to-many joins" is the advanced version of fan-out. Explaining why DISTINCT is not a general fix is the key insight.

questions.title: Pair duplicate user accounts (self join on a normalized key)
questions.secondary: avoiding mirrored pairs, entity resolution
questions.columns: original_user_id, duplicate_user_id, normalized_email, same_org, original_signup_at, duplicate_signup_at

sections.context: Identity resolution: a person who registered twice should be merged. Two accounts are considered the same person when their e-mails match after `LOWER(TRIM(...))`.
sections.problem: Return one row per pair of matching accounts, with the earlier account as `original_user_id` and the later one as `duplicate_user_id`, the shared `normalized_email`, whether both belong to the same organization (`same_org` 1/0), and both sign-up times. Sort by `original_user_id`, `duplicate_user_id`.
sections.expected: About two dozen pairs.
sections.edge_cases:
- A self join without an ordering condition returns each pair twice (A,B) and (B,A), plus every row matched with itself.
- Three accounts of one person would produce three pairs. That is acceptable for a pair list; clustering needs more work (SQL-142).
sections.hint1: Join `users` to itself on the normalized e-mail.
sections.hint2: `a.user_id < b.user_id` keeps each pair once and removes self-matches.
sections.hint3: `CASE WHEN a.org_id = b.org_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS same_org`.
sections.solution:
SELECT a.user_id                                  AS original_user_id,
       b.user_id                                  AS duplicate_user_id,
       LOWER(TRIM(a.email))                       AS normalized_email,
       CASE WHEN a.org_id = b.org_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS same_org,
       a.signup_at                                AS original_signup_at,
       b.signup_at                                AS duplicate_signup_at
FROM users a
JOIN users b
  ON LOWER(TRIM(b.email)) = LOWER(TRIM(a.email))
 AND a.user_id < b.user_id
ORDER BY original_user_id, duplicate_user_id;
sections.explanation:
The join condition is an expression on both sides, so each account is compared with all accounts sharing its canonical e-mail. `a.user_id < b.user_id` (user IDs increase with sign-up time) orients each pair from the original to the duplicate and eliminates mirrored and self pairs.

Because both sides are normalized explicitly, the result is the same in PostgreSQL and MySQL. Contrast with SQL-009, where a raw comparison behaved differently because of MySQL's collation.

**ML angle:** duplicate entities leak information between training and test splits (the same person on both sides). Pairs like these feed entity-resolution tables used before splitting.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `<>` instead of `<`, which returns every pair twice.
- Comparing raw e-mails, which misses case and whitespace variants.
sections.performance: Joining on a function of the column cannot use the plain index; an expression index (PostgreSQL) or a generated column with an index (MySQL, SQL-163) fixes that for large tables.
sections.interview: Self-join pair generation with `<` is a pattern interviewers expect to see written without hesitation.

questions.title: Experiment overlap matrix (composite keys)
questions.primary: Joining assignments on composite primary keys
questions.secondary: cross-tab of two categorical variables, interaction risk

sections.context: `ai_assist_default_on` (Nov–Dec 2024) and `onboarding_checklist` (Dec 2024–Feb 2025) overlapped in time. If many users were in both, one experiment's treatment could contaminate the other's results.
sections.problem: For users assigned to **both** experiments, count users per combination of variants. Look the experiment IDs up by name instead of hard-coding them. Return `ai_assist_variant`, `onboarding_variant`, `users`, sorted by both variants.
sections.expected: Up to 4 rows (2x2).
sections.edge_cases: - The assignments table's key is `(experiment_id, user_id)`; each user appears at most once per experiment.
sections.hint1: Self-join `experiment_assignments` on `user_id`, with each side restricted to one experiment.
sections.hint2: Join each side to `experiments` to filter by `experiment_name`.
sections.hint3: Group by the two variant columns.
sections.solution:
SELECT a.variant  AS ai_assist_variant,
       b.variant  AS onboarding_variant,
       COUNT(*)   AS users
FROM experiment_assignments a
JOIN experiments ea ON ea.experiment_id = a.experiment_id
JOIN experiment_assignments b ON b.user_id = a.user_id
JOIN experiments eb ON eb.experiment_id = b.experiment_id
WHERE ea.experiment_name = 'ai_assist_default_on'
  AND eb.experiment_name = 'onboarding_checklist'
GROUP BY a.variant, b.variant
ORDER BY ai_assist_variant, onboarding_variant;
sections.explanation:
Joining the assignment table to itself on `user_id`, with each side pinned to one experiment, gives one row per user who is in both experiments. The 2x2 table shows whether assignment to one experiment is independent of the other. In a healthy setup the four cells are roughly proportional to the variant splits. A skew would suggest that one experiment's assignment logic depended on the other.

Looking IDs up by name makes the query robust if IDs differ between environments.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining on `experiment_id` as well, which makes the two sides refer to the same experiment and returns nothing.
- Hard-coding IDs copied from a staging database.
sections.performance: The primary key `(experiment_id, user_id)` serves side `a`; the `experiment_assignments(user_id)` index serves side `b`.
sections.interview: Shows practical A/B-testing hygiene (interaction effects) expressed with simple joins.

questions.title: Products priced above the catalogue average
questions.secondary: subquery in WHERE and SELECT

sections.context: The pricing team reviews active products whose list price is above the average active list price.
sections.problem: Return `product_name`, `list_price`, the average active list price (`avg_list_price`, 2 decimals) and the difference `above_avg_by` (2 decimals) for active products priced above that average. Sort by `list_price` descending, then name.
sections.expected: One row per expensive product. Every row shows the same average.
sections.edge_cases: - The average must be computed over active products only, the same population as the filter.
sections.hint1: You need a single number (the average) next to every row and in the filter.
sections.hint2: A scalar subquery `(SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM products WHERE is_active = TRUE)` returns exactly one value.
sections.hint3: Use it twice, once in SELECT and once in WHERE (or compute it once in a CTE and CROSS JOIN it).
sections.solution:
SELECT product_name,
       list_price,
       ROUND((SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM products WHERE is_active = TRUE), 2) AS avg_list_price,
       ROUND(list_price - (SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM products WHERE is_active = TRUE), 2) AS above_avg_by
FROM products
WHERE is_active = TRUE
  AND list_price > (SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM products WHERE is_active = TRUE)
ORDER BY list_price DESC, product_name;
sections.alternative:
WITH stats AS (
    SELECT AVG(list_price) AS avg_price
    FROM products
    WHERE is_active = TRUE
)
SELECT p.product_name,
       p.list_price,
       ROUND(s.avg_price, 2)                AS avg_list_price,
       ROUND(p.list_price - s.avg_price, 2) AS above_avg_by
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN stats s
WHERE p.is_active = TRUE
  AND p.list_price > s.avg_price
ORDER BY p.list_price DESC, p.product_name;
sections.alternative_note: A one-row CTE cross-joined to the table avoids repeating the subquery and makes the threshold reusable. Both engines evaluate an uncorrelated scalar subquery only once, so performance is the same.
sections.explanation: A **scalar subquery** returns one row and one column, and can be used wherever a single value is allowed. Because it does not reference the outer query (it is *uncorrelated*), the engine evaluates it once. If a scalar subquery ever returned more than one row, the query would fail at runtime: "more than one row returned by a subquery".
sections.mistakes:
- `WHERE list_price > AVG(list_price)`: aggregates are not allowed in WHERE.
- Averaging all products (including discontinued ones) while filtering active ones.
sections.performance: Uncorrelated scalar subqueries are computed once and cached.
sections.interview: Basic subquery fluency; the CTE rewrite shows code-organisation skills.

questions.title: Latest ticket per enterprise organization (correlated subquery)
questions.secondary: ties in "latest", MAX per group
questions.tables: support_tickets(ticket_id, org_id, created_at, priority, status); organizations(org_id, segment)

sections.context: Account managers open each Enterprise customer's most recent support ticket before a call.
sections.problem: For every Enterprise organization that has tickets, return its most recent ticket (`org_id`, `ticket_id`, `created_at`, `priority`, `status`). If two tickets share the latest timestamp, return the one with the higher `ticket_id`. Sort by `org_id`.
sections.expected: One row per Enterprise organization with at least one ticket.
sections.edge_cases: - `created_at = MAX(created_at)` alone returns several rows when timestamps tie.
sections.hint1: For each ticket, compare it to the maximum timestamp *of its own organization*.
sections.hint2: A correlated subquery refers to the outer row: `WHERE t2.org_id = t.org_id`.
sections.hint3: To break ties deterministically, look for the maximum `ticket_id` among tickets of the org ordered by `(created_at, ticket_id)`, e.g. `t.ticket_id = (SELECT t2.ticket_id FROM ... ORDER BY t2.created_at DESC, t2.ticket_id DESC LIMIT 1)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT t.org_id,
       t.ticket_id,
       t.created_at,
       t.priority,
       t.status
FROM support_tickets t
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = t.org_id
WHERE o.segment = 'Enterprise'
  AND t.ticket_id = (SELECT t2.ticket_id
                     FROM support_tickets t2
                     WHERE t2.org_id = t.org_id
                     ORDER BY t2.created_at DESC, t2.ticket_id DESC
                     LIMIT 1)
ORDER BY t.org_id;
sections.explanation:
The subquery runs logically once per outer row and returns the ID of that organization's newest ticket. Using ORDER BY + LIMIT 1 inside the scalar subquery gives a deterministic winner even with tied timestamps. The simpler `t.created_at = (SELECT MAX(created_at) ...)` returns all tied rows.

Window functions (`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY org_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, ticket_id DESC)`, SQL-061) solve the same problem in one pass and are usually preferred on large tables.
sections.mistakes:
- Using MAX(created_at) and assuming uniqueness.
- Correlating on the wrong column (e.g. `t2.ticket_id = t.ticket_id`), which makes every ticket "the latest".
sections.performance: With the `support_tickets(org_id, created_at)` index each probe is an index range scan (backwards). Without that index this would be O(n²).
sections.interview: Interviewers often ask for both the correlated-subquery and the window-function versions and when each is preferable.

questions.title: Active users left in fully churned organizations
questions.secondary: set membership, data-quality rule
questions.tables: users(user_id, org_id, status); subscriptions(org_id, status, ended_at)

sections.context: When an organization churns, its users should be deactivated. Data quality wants to find organizations that have **no open subscription**, have at least one canceled subscription, and still have users with status `'active'`.
sections.problem: Return `org_id` and the number of still-active users for such organizations, sorted by `active_users` descending, then `org_id`.
sections.expected: A list of organizations with stale user statuses.
sections.edge_cases:
- "No open subscription" = no subscription with `ended_at IS NULL`. `subscriptions.org_id` is NOT NULL, so `NOT IN` is safe here, but say so.
- An organization that canceled and later came back has an open subscription and must be excluded.
sections.hint1: Express each condition as a set of `org_id`s.
sections.hint2: `org_id IN (SELECT org_id FROM subscriptions WHERE status = 'canceled')` and `org_id NOT IN (SELECT org_id FROM subscriptions WHERE ended_at IS NULL)`.
sections.hint3: Filter users by status and both conditions, then group by org.
sections.solution:
SELECT u.org_id,
       COUNT(*) AS active_users
FROM users u
WHERE u.status = 'active'
  AND u.org_id IN (SELECT s.org_id FROM subscriptions s WHERE s.status = 'canceled')
  AND u.org_id NOT IN (SELECT s.org_id FROM subscriptions s WHERE s.ended_at IS NULL)
GROUP BY u.org_id
ORDER BY active_users DESC, u.org_id;
sections.explanation:
`IN (subquery)` keeps rows whose value appears in the subquery result (a semi-join). `NOT IN (subquery)` keeps rows whose value does not appear (an anti-join). NOT IN is only safe when the subquery cannot return NULL (SQL-013); `subscriptions.org_id` is declared NOT NULL. In code that will be maintained, prefer NOT EXISTS anyway.

The query encodes a business rule as a data-quality check: a churned customer should not have active seats.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `status = 'canceled'` alone and forgetting reactivated customers.
- Checking only the latest subscription row by ID instead of "any open period".
sections.performance: Both engines turn IN into a semi-join and NOT IN (non-nullable) into an anti-join; `subscriptions(org_id, ...)` supports both.
sections.interview: Shows set-based thinking. Expect follow-up questions on NULL safety and on how to turn this into an automated test.

questions.title: Organizations above average 2025 revenue (CTEs)
questions.secondary: multiple CTEs, CROSS JOIN of a one-row CTE
questions.tables: orders(org_id, status, order_total, order_ts); organizations(org_id, org_name, segment)
questions.columns: org_id, org_name, segment, revenue, avg_org_revenue, revenue_vs_avg

sections.context: Customer success wants to know which accounts bring in more than twice the average H1-2025 revenue of paying organizations.
sections.problem: Compute each organization's revenue from completed orders in H1 2025, the average across organizations with revenue, and list organizations with revenue > 2x average. Return `org_id`, `org_name`, `segment`, `revenue`, `avg_org_revenue` (2 decimals), `revenue_vs_avg` (ratio, 2 decimals). Sort by revenue descending.
sections.expected: A short list of top accounts.
sections.edge_cases: - The average is over *organizations that bought*, not over all organizations; state this assumption.
sections.hint1: Break the problem into named steps: revenue per org → average → filter.
sections.hint2: `WITH org_rev AS (...), stats AS (SELECT AVG(revenue) ... FROM org_rev)`.
sections.hint3: Join `org_rev` to `organizations` and `CROSS JOIN stats`.
sections.solution:
WITH org_rev AS (
    SELECT org_id, SUM(order_total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
      AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
      AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY org_id
),
stats AS (
    SELECT AVG(revenue) AS avg_revenue FROM org_rev
)
SELECT r.org_id,
       o.org_name,
       o.segment,
       r.revenue,
       ROUND(s.avg_revenue, 2)               AS avg_org_revenue,
       ROUND(r.revenue / s.avg_revenue, 2)   AS revenue_vs_avg
FROM org_rev r
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = r.org_id
CROSS JOIN stats s
WHERE r.revenue > 2 * s.avg_revenue
ORDER BY r.revenue DESC, r.org_id;
sections.explanation:
CTEs name intermediate results, so a multi-step calculation reads top to bottom like a pipeline. `org_rev` has one row per paying organization; `stats` aggregates it to a single row. Because `stats` has exactly one row, the CROSS JOIN attaches the average to every row without changing the row count.

PostgreSQL (12+) inlines CTEs that are referenced once and are side-effect free, and MySQL merges or materializes them. Either way, CTEs are a readability tool, not an optimization fence (PostgreSQL < 12 always materialized them).
sections.mistakes:
- Averaging over all 200 organizations (including zero-revenue ones) without saying so.
- Joining `organizations` before computing the average, which is fine here, but would be wrong if the join could duplicate rows.
sections.performance: The orders date filter is applied once; the CTE `org_rev` is referenced twice (directly and via `stats`) and may be materialized.
sections.interview: Clear, named steps are what senior reviewers look for in analytical SQL.

questions.title: Account health dataset from several grains
questions.primary: Multiple CTEs as an analytical pipeline
questions.secondary: pre-aggregation per source, LEFT JOIN zero-filling, as-of date
questions.tables: organizations(org_id, segment, is_deleted); users(user_id, org_id); sessions(user_id, started_at); support_tickets(org_id, created_at, resolved_at); orders(org_id, status, order_total, order_ts); subscriptions(org_id, mrr, started_at, ended_at)
questions.columns: org_id, segment, users, active_users_30d, sessions_30d, open_tickets, revenue_h1_2025, open_mrr

sections.context: A churn-risk model and a CS dashboard both need one row per account with signals from different tables, all measured **as of 2025-07-01**.
sections.problem:
For non-deleted Mid-Market and Enterprise organizations, return:
`users` (all user accounts), `active_users_30d` (users with a session in the 30 days before 2025-07-01), `sessions_30d`, `open_tickets` (created before 2025-07-01 and not resolved by then), `revenue_h1_2025` (completed orders), and `open_mrr` (MRR of subscriptions open on 2025-07-01). Missing activity must show as 0. Sort by `open_mrr` descending, then `org_id`.
sections.expected: One row per qualifying organization; no NULLs in the metric columns.
sections.edge_cases:
- Every source has a different grain (user, session, ticket, order, subscription period). Joining them raw to organizations would multiply rows.
- An organization with overlapping open subscriptions (billing bug) sums both, which is consistent with the stored data.
sections.hint1: Write one CTE per source, each aggregated to one row per `org_id`.
sections.hint2: Start from organizations and LEFT JOIN every CTE; wrap metrics in COALESCE(…, 0).
sections.hint3: `active_users_30d` needs sessions joined to users: `COUNT(DISTINCT s.user_id)` per org within `[2025-06-01, 2025-07-01)`.
sections.solution:
WITH u AS (
    SELECT org_id, COUNT(*) AS users
    FROM users
    GROUP BY org_id
),
act AS (
    SELECT us.org_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT s.user_id) AS active_users_30d,
           COUNT(*)                  AS sessions_30d
    FROM sessions s
    JOIN users us ON us.user_id = s.user_id
    WHERE s.started_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00' - INTERVAL '30' DAY
      AND s.started_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY us.org_id
),
tix AS (
    SELECT org_id, COUNT(*) AS open_tickets
    FROM support_tickets
    WHERE created_at < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
      AND (resolved_at IS NULL OR resolved_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
    GROUP BY org_id
),
rev AS (
    SELECT org_id, SUM(order_total) AS revenue_h1_2025
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
      AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
      AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY org_id
),
mrr AS (
    SELECT org_id, SUM(mrr) AS open_mrr
    FROM subscriptions
    WHERE started_at < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
      AND (ended_at IS NULL OR ended_at > TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
    GROUP BY org_id
)
SELECT o.org_id,
       o.segment,
       COALESCE(u.users, 0)               AS users,
       COALESCE(act.active_users_30d, 0)  AS active_users_30d,
       COALESCE(act.sessions_30d, 0)      AS sessions_30d,
       COALESCE(tix.open_tickets, 0)      AS open_tickets,
       COALESCE(rev.revenue_h1_2025, 0)   AS revenue_h1_2025,
       COALESCE(mrr.open_mrr, 0)          AS open_mrr
FROM organizations o
LEFT JOIN u   ON u.org_id = o.org_id
LEFT JOIN act ON act.org_id = o.org_id
LEFT JOIN tix ON tix.org_id = o.org_id
LEFT JOIN rev ON rev.org_id = o.org_id
LEFT JOIN mrr ON mrr.org_id = o.org_id
WHERE o.is_deleted = FALSE
  AND o.segment IN ('Mid-Market', 'Enterprise')
ORDER BY open_mrr DESC, o.org_id;
sections.explanation:
This is the canonical **wide analytical table** pattern:
1. One CTE per source, each reduced to the target grain (organization).
2. A *spine* (`organizations`) that defines which rows exist.
3. LEFT JOINs from the spine to each aggregate, with COALESCE to turn "no activity" into 0.

Everything is measured relative to one **as-of instant** (2025-07-01). Tickets are "open" if created before it and not resolved by then. That is a point-in-time definition, not the current `status` column, which can change later. ML feature tables use the same approach (SQL-099).
sections.mistakes:
- Joining `sessions`, `tickets` and `orders` directly to `organizations` and using COUNT/SUM: fan-out across sources.
- Using `status IN ('open','pending')` for open tickets. That gives today's status, not the status as of the snapshot date.
- Forgetting COALESCE, so organizations without tickets show NULL instead of 0.
sections.performance: Each CTE scans its source once. On large data, filter the session CTE by date first (indexed) and only then join to users.
sections.interview: A realistic take-home style task. Clean CTE structure, explicit grain and as-of logic are what reviewers grade.

questions.title: Corporate hierarchy below a parent company (recursive CTE)
questions.secondary: depth tracking, path strings, dialect type rules

sections.context: For an enterprise deal, sales needs every subsidiary (at any depth) of organization 12, *Summit Networks Co*, with its level in the hierarchy.
sections.problem: Return organization 12 and all its descendants with `depth` (0 for the root) and `path`, a string of org IDs from the root, like `'12 > 49 > 94'`. Sort by `path`.
sections.expected: 5 rows (the root plus 4 descendants), depth up to 3.
sections.edge_cases:
- **Type rules differ.** PostgreSQL requires the recursive column to have the same type in both branches; MySQL sizes the column from the anchor row, so a longer path would be truncated or raise "Data too long". Cast the path in the anchor member explicitly.
- A cycle in the data would recurse forever; real code adds a depth limit.
sections.hint1: Anchor member: the root row. Recursive member: children of rows already found.
sections.hint2: `WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (SELECT ... WHERE org_id = 12 UNION ALL SELECT ... FROM organizations c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_org_id = t.org_id)`.
sections.hint3: PostgreSQL: `CAST(org_id AS TEXT)` in the anchor. MySQL: `CAST(org_id AS CHAR(200))`. Extend with `CONCAT(t.path, ' > ', c.org_id)`.
sections.solution_pg:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT org_id, org_name, 0 AS depth, CAST(org_id AS TEXT) AS path
    FROM organizations
    WHERE org_id = 12
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.org_id, c.org_name, t.depth + 1, CONCAT(t.path, ' > ', c.org_id)
    FROM organizations c
    JOIN tree t ON c.parent_org_id = t.org_id
    WHERE t.depth < 10
)
SELECT org_id, org_name, depth, path
FROM tree
ORDER BY path;
sections.solution_mysql:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT org_id, org_name, 0 AS depth, CAST(org_id AS CHAR(200)) AS path
    FROM organizations
    WHERE org_id = 12
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.org_id, c.org_name, t.depth + 1, CONCAT(t.path, ' > ', c.org_id)
    FROM organizations c
    JOIN tree t ON c.parent_org_id = t.org_id
    WHERE t.depth < 10
)
SELECT org_id, org_name, depth, path
FROM tree
ORDER BY path;
sections.assert:
len(rows) == 5
max(int(r[2]) for r in rows) == 3
sections.dialect_note: Both engines need `WITH RECURSIVE`. The difference is the type of the accumulating string: PostgreSQL rejects `character varying` vs `text` mismatches between the anchor and the recursive member, and MySQL derives the column width from the anchor (`CAST(... AS CHAR(n))` reserves room). `CAST(x AS TEXT)` is not valid in MySQL, and `CAST(x AS CHAR(200))` in PostgreSQL produces a blank-padded `character(200)`, so each engine gets its own cast.
sections.explanation:
A recursive CTE has two members joined by UNION ALL:
1. The **anchor** runs once and seeds the result (the root).
2. The **recursive member** joins the table to the rows produced in the previous iteration and stops when it adds no new rows.

`depth` counts iterations; `path` accumulates the route, which also gives a natural depth-first sort order. The `t.depth < 10` guard protects against accidental cycles. PostgreSQL 14+ also has a `CYCLE` clause, and MySQL limits recursion with `cte_max_recursion_depth` (default 1000).

Sorting by `path` as a string works here because IDs are compared character by character. For numeric-correct ordering, zero-pad the IDs.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining in the wrong direction (`c.org_id = t.parent_org_id`), which walks *up* the tree.
- Using `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL`: it adds a de-duplication step that is unnecessary here and can hide modelling errors.
sections.performance: Each iteration probes `organizations(parent_org_id)`, which is indexed.
sections.interview: Hierarchies (org charts, categories, bill of materials) are the classic recursive-CTE interview topic.

questions.title: Category tree with product counts rolled up to every ancestor
questions.secondary: rolling counts up a hierarchy, LEFT JOIN with zero counts
questions.tables: product_categories(category_id, category_name, parent_category_id); products(product_id, category_id, is_active)

sections.context: The storefront shows each category with the number of active products underneath it, including all sub-categories. "Services" should count the products of "Training", "Implementation" and "Custom Integration".
sections.problem: Return every category with `active_products_incl_descendants`. Sort by `category_id`.
sections.expected: 11 rows; root categories have the largest counts.
sections.edge_cases:
- Products sit on leaf categories only, but the query should also work if a product were attached to an inner node.
- Categories without products must show 0.
sections.hint1: First build a table of all (ancestor, descendant) pairs, including each category paired with itself.
sections.hint2: Anchor: `SELECT category_id AS ancestor_id, category_id AS descendant_id`. Recursive: add the children of each descendant.
sections.hint3: Join the pairs to products on `descendant_id` and count per ancestor.
sections.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE closure AS (
    SELECT category_id AS ancestor_id, category_id AS descendant_id
    FROM product_categories
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.ancestor_id, pc.category_id
    FROM closure c
    JOIN product_categories pc ON pc.parent_category_id = c.descendant_id
)
SELECT pc.category_id,
       pc.category_name,
       COUNT(p.product_id) AS active_products_incl_descendants
FROM product_categories pc
JOIN closure c       ON c.ancestor_id = pc.category_id
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.category_id = c.descendant_id
                    AND p.is_active = TRUE
GROUP BY pc.category_id, pc.category_name
ORDER BY pc.category_id;
sections.explanation:
The recursive CTE computes the **transitive closure** of the tree: every (ancestor, descendant) pair, including the zero-length pair (category, itself). Once you have the closure, any "roll-up through the hierarchy" is a plain join and GROUP BY. Products attached to any descendant count toward every ancestor.

The LEFT JOIN with the `is_active` filter in ON keeps categories with zero active products. Many production systems store this closure table permanently because hierarchy roll-ups are so common.
sections.mistakes:
- Counting only direct children (one level).
- Putting `p.is_active = TRUE` in WHERE, which removes categories whose products are all inactive.
