- Treating all late rows as harmless "because the values are correct". Correct values that arrived late still leak, because production never had them at scoring time.
- Not counting examples whose PIT snapshot is NULL.
sections.performance: The join produces at most ~20 snapshot rows per example; the PK `(entity_id, as_of_ts)` makes it an index range scan.
sections.interview: Advanced MLE question: quantifying leakage, not just knowing the definition.

questions.title: How future features fake model quality
questions.secondary: comparing feature separation between classes under two join rules
questions.tables: training_labels(label_id, entity_id, label_name, observation_date, label_value, label_available_at); ml_entities(entity_id, is_test_account); entity_features(entity_id, as_of_ts, days_since_last_session, ingested_at)

sections.context: A junior engineer built features by joining each label to the entity's **most recent snapshot in the table** (2025-06-30), arguing that "newer features are more accurate". Show the effect on `days_since_last_session` for the 2025-04-01 labels.
sections.problem: For authoritative, non-test, non-NULL labels with D = 2025-04-01, compute the average `days_since_last_session` for churned (1) and retained (0) entities under two joins: `'point_in_time'` (latest snapshot available at D) and `'latest_in_table'` (latest snapshot overall). Return `feature_join`, both averages (1 decimal) and `separation_ratio` = churned / retained (2 decimals). Sort by `feature_join`.
sections.expected: 2 rows; the latest-in-table version shows a dramatically larger separation.
sections.edge_cases: - Churned users stop using the product, so snapshots taken *after* D encode the outcome itself.
sections.hint1: Compute both snapshot timestamps per example, then join the feature values for each.
sections.hint2: PIT: `MAX(as_of_ts)` with `as_of_ts <= D AND ingested_at <= D`; latest: `MAX(as_of_ts)` without conditions.
sections.hint3: UNION ALL the two variants with a label column, then aggregate by variant and label.
sections.solution:
WITH labels AS (
    SELECT entity_id, label_value
    FROM (
        SELECT l.entity_id, l.label_value,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.entity_id ORDER BY l.label_available_at DESC, l.label_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM training_labels l
        WHERE l.label_name = 'churned_30d' AND l.observation_date = DATE '2025-04-01'
    ) x
    JOIN ml_entities e USING (entity_id)
    WHERE x.rn = 1 AND x.label_value IS NOT NULL AND e.is_test_account = FALSE
),
snap AS (
    SELECT l.entity_id,
           l.label_value,
           MAX(CASE WHEN f.as_of_ts <= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                     AND f.ingested_at <= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00' THEN f.as_of_ts END) AS pit_ts,
           MAX(f.as_of_ts) AS latest_ts
    FROM labels l
    JOIN entity_features f ON f.entity_id = l.entity_id
    GROUP BY l.entity_id, l.label_value
),
both_joins AS (
    SELECT 'point_in_time' AS feature_join, s.label_value, f.days_since_last_session
    FROM snap s JOIN entity_features f ON f.entity_id = s.entity_id AND f.as_of_ts = s.pit_ts
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'latest_in_table', s.label_value, f.days_since_last_session
    FROM snap s JOIN entity_features f ON f.entity_id = s.entity_id AND f.as_of_ts = s.latest_ts
)
SELECT feature_join,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN label_value = 1 THEN days_since_last_session END), 1) AS churned_avg_days_since_session,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN label_value = 0 THEN days_since_last_session END), 1) AS retained_avg_days_since_session,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN label_value = 1 THEN days_since_last_session END)
             / AVG(CASE WHEN label_value = 0 THEN days_since_last_session END), 2) AS separation_ratio
FROM both_joins
GROUP BY feature_join
ORDER BY feature_join;
sections.assert: num([r for r in rows if r[0]=='latest_in_table'][0][3]) > num([r for r in rows if r[0]=='point_in_time'][0][3])
sections.explanation:
A user labelled "churned at D" has, by definition, no sessions after D. A snapshot taken weeks later therefore shows a huge `days_since_last_session` for churners. The feature *contains the label*. A model trained this way looks excellent offline and fails in production, where only past data exists.

The comparison makes the leak measurable: the class separation of a single feature jumps when future snapshots are used. A sudden jump in a feature's importance or in offline AUC after a pipeline change is a classic leakage alarm.

`USING (entity_id)` is a standard join shorthand supported by both engines.
sections.mistakes:
- Believing "fresher features are always better" without checking when they were produced relative to the label.
- Validating with a random split, which hides this leak; only a time-based split plus point-in-time joins expose it.
sections.performance: Two snapshot lookups per example via the primary key.
sections.interview: Explaining *why* future snapshots leak (the outcome changes the feature) is what interviewers grade.

questions.title: Time-based train / validation / test split
questions.secondary: CASE-based split assignment, entity overlap across splits
questions.tables: training_labels(label_id, entity_id, label_name, observation_date, label_value, label_available_at); ml_entities(entity_id, is_test_account)
questions.columns: split, first_obs, last_obs, examples, positives, positive_rate_pct, entities_also_in_train

sections.context: The team splits by time: train on observation dates up to 2025-02-01, validate on 2025-03-01 and 2025-04-01, test on 2025-05-01. Random splits would let the model see the future.
sections.problem: Assign each authoritative, non-NULL, non-test label to a split and return per split: `first_obs`, `last_obs`, `examples`, `positives`, `positive_rate_pct` (2 decimals) and `entities_also_in_train` (distinct entities of this split that also appear in train; NULL for train itself). Sort by `first_obs`.
sections.expected: 3 rows (train, validation, test).
sections.edge_cases:
- The same entity appears in several months; a time split prevents temporal leakage but not entity overlap.
- 2025-06-01 labels are NULL and belong to no split.
sections.hint1: Assign splits with a CASE on `observation_date`.
sections.hint2: Deduplicate labels first (authoritative row).
sections.hint3: Entity overlap: `COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN entity_id IN (SELECT entity_id FROM ... WHERE split = 'train') THEN entity_id END)`.
sections.solution:
WITH labels AS (
    SELECT x.entity_id, x.observation_date, x.label_value
    FROM (
        SELECT l.entity_id, l.observation_date, l.label_value,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.entity_id, l.observation_date
                                  ORDER BY l.label_available_at DESC, l.label_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM training_labels l
        WHERE l.label_name = 'churned_30d'
    ) x
    JOIN ml_entities e ON e.entity_id = x.entity_id
    WHERE x.rn = 1 AND x.label_value IS NOT NULL AND e.is_test_account = FALSE
),
split AS (
    SELECT entity_id, observation_date, label_value,
           CASE WHEN observation_date <= DATE '2025-02-01' THEN 'train'
                WHEN observation_date <= DATE '2025-04-01' THEN 'validation'
                ELSE 'test' END AS split
    FROM labels
)
SELECT s.split,
       MIN(s.observation_date)                     AS first_obs,
       MAX(s.observation_date)                     AS last_obs,
       COUNT(*)                                    AS examples,
       SUM(s.label_value)                          AS positives,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(s.label_value) / COUNT(*), 2) AS positive_rate_pct,
       CASE WHEN s.split = 'train' THEN NULL
            ELSE COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM split t
                                                  WHERE t.split = 'train' AND t.entity_id = s.entity_id)
                                     THEN s.entity_id END)
       END                                         AS entities_also_in_train
FROM split s
GROUP BY s.split
ORDER BY first_obs;
sections.explanation:
A **time-based split** trains on the past and evaluates on the future, mirroring how the model is used. The CASE thresholds make the split rule explicit and reproducible, unlike random sampling.

The overlap column quantifies a remaining risk: many validation/test entities were also seen in training (at earlier dates). For churn models that is usually acceptable, since the model scores the same customers again later, but for problems where memorizing entities helps, add a **group split** by entity (e.g. `MOD(entity_id, 10) < 8` for train) in addition to the time cut.
sections.mistakes:
- Random row-level splits on temporal data.
- Forgetting that the label window (30 days) means train labels near the cut-off overlap the validation period. Leave a gap ("embargo") of at least the label horizon between splits for strict evaluation.
sections.performance: Small; the correlated EXISTS runs per distinct (split, entity) value and hits the CTE.
sections.interview: Expect "what is an embargo/purge gap and why?" as a follow-up.

questions.title: Feature missingness by snapshot date and source
questions.secondary: NULL-rate per column, structural vs failure NULLs
questions.tables: entity_features(as_of_ts, feature_source, sessions_7d, events_28d, avg_session_minutes, seats_used_pct, days_since_last_session)
questions.columns: as_of_date, feature_source, rows_count, null_sessions_7d_pct, null_events_28d_pct, null_avg_minutes_pct, null_seats_used_pct, null_days_since_pct

sections.context: Feature-quality dashboards show the NULL rate per feature per snapshot. Some NULLs are structural (no session yet means no `days_since_last_session`), others are pipeline failures.
sections.problem: For snapshots in 2025 Q1, return per `as_of_date` and `feature_source`: `rows_count` and the NULL percentage (2 decimals) of five features. Sort by date, source.
sections.expected: One row per (snapshot date, source) in Q1 2025.
sections.edge_cases:
- `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL; NULL rate = 1 − COUNT(col)/COUNT(*).
- `avg_session_minutes` and `days_since_last_session` have structural NULLs; `sessions_7d` and `events_28d` should never be NULL except on failures.
sections.hint1: Group by snapshot date and source.
sections.hint2: `100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(sessions_7d)) / COUNT(*)`.
sections.hint3: Repeat the expression for each feature.
sections.solution:
SELECT CAST(as_of_ts AS DATE)                                              AS as_of_date,
       feature_source,
       COUNT(*)                                                            AS rows_count,
       ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(sessions_7d)) / COUNT(*), 2)        AS null_sessions_7d_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(events_28d)) / COUNT(*), 2)         AS null_events_28d_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(avg_session_minutes)) / COUNT(*), 2) AS null_avg_minutes_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(seats_used_pct)) / COUNT(*), 2)     AS null_seats_used_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(days_since_last_session)) / COUNT(*), 2) AS null_days_since_pct
FROM entity_features
WHERE as_of_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND as_of_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CAST(as_of_ts AS DATE), feature_source
ORDER BY as_of_date, feature_source;
sections.explanation:
`COUNT(*) - COUNT(col)` is the NULL count for that column. Monitoring it per snapshot catches pipeline breakages (a sudden spike), and grouping by source separates normal batch rows from backfilled ones.

Interpretation needs domain knowledge: a high NULL rate for `avg_session_minutes` (no complete session in 28 days) is expected, so it is a *signal*. A NULL `sessions_7d` is a failure. Models should receive structural NULLs with a meaningful encoding, and failure NULLs should block training or trigger re-computation.

**Grain:** one row per snapshot date and source.
sections.mistakes:
- Imputing all NULLs with 0. "No complete session" is not "0 minutes".
- Monitoring the overall NULL rate only, which averages away a one-day spike.
sections.performance: Single scan over Q1 snapshots.
sections.interview: Feature-quality monitoring is a common MLE system-design talking point; this is its SQL core.

questions.title: Entities with incomplete features in the latest snapshot
questions.primary: Finding incomplete or missing feature records
questions.secondary: anti-join for missing rows, UNION ALL of reasons
questions.tables: ml_entities(entity_id, registered_at, is_test_account); entity_features(entity_id, as_of_ts, sessions_7d, sessions_28d, events_28d, open_tickets, seats_used_pct)

sections.context: The batch scorer requires a complete feature row for the most recent snapshot (2025-06-30). The on-call engineer wants to know how many non-test entities would fall back to older features and why.
sections.problem: For non-test entities registered before 2025-06-30, count entities by reason: `'missing_row'` (no row for the 2025-06-30 snapshot) and `'null_required_feature'` (row exists but any of `sessions_7d`, `sessions_28d`, `events_28d`, `open_tickets`, `seats_used_pct` is NULL). Return `reason`, `entities`, sorted by reason.
sections.expected: Two rows (both reasons occur).
sections.edge_cases:
- An entity is either missing or present for one snapshot, so the reasons do not overlap.
- `seats_used_pct` is also NULL when an org has no subscription at the snapshot. That is structural, but the scorer still cannot use the row.
sections.hint1: Missing rows: anti-join the entity list against the snapshot.
sections.hint2: NULL features: filter the snapshot rows with an OR of `IS NULL` tests.
sections.hint3: UNION ALL the two counts with a reason label.
sections.solution:
SELECT 'missing_row' AS reason, COUNT(*) AS entities
FROM ml_entities e
WHERE e.is_test_account = FALSE
  AND e.registered_at < TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 00:00:00'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM entity_features f
                  WHERE f.entity_id = e.entity_id
                    AND f.as_of_ts = TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 00:00:00')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'null_required_feature', COUNT(*)
FROM ml_entities e
JOIN entity_features f ON f.entity_id = e.entity_id
                      AND f.as_of_ts = TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 00:00:00'
WHERE e.is_test_account = FALSE
  AND e.registered_at < TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 00:00:00'
  AND (f.sessions_7d IS NULL OR f.sessions_28d IS NULL OR f.events_28d IS NULL
       OR f.open_tickets IS NULL OR f.seats_used_pct IS NULL)
ORDER BY reason;
sections.assert: len(rows) == 2 and all(num(r[1]) > 0 for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
Completeness has two failure modes, and they need different queries:
1. **Missing rows**: an anti-join from the expected population (`ml_entities`) to the snapshot. Only a population table can reveal what is absent.
2. **Partial rows**: present but with NULLs in required columns.

UNION ALL stacks both counts into one small report. The ORDER BY at the end applies to the combined result.

**ML angle:** knowing *why* features are missing determines the fix: re-run the pipeline for missing rows, or fix the upstream source for NULLs, and decide what the scorer does meanwhile (fallback snapshot, default values, or skip).
sections.mistakes:
- Checking NULLs only and never noticing missing rows.
- Using `UNION`, which would merge two reasons that happen to have the same count.
sections.performance: The anti-join probes the primary key `(entity_id, as_of_ts)`.
sections.interview: Shows that the candidate thinks about "absent" data, not only NULL data.

questions.title: Validate stored features by recomputing them from raw sessions
questions.primary: Historical feature generation from event timestamps
questions.secondary: point-in-time windows, reconciliation, NULL-aware equality
questions.tables: entity_features(entity_id, as_of_ts, sessions_7d, sessions_28d); ml_entities(entity_id, user_id, is_test_account); sessions(user_id, started_at)

sections.context: `sessions_7d` and `sessions_28d` are documented as counts of sessions in `[as_of_ts − 7 days, as_of_ts)` and `[as_of_ts − 28 days, as_of_ts)`. Recompute them from `sessions` for the 2025-06-16 snapshot and compare with the stored values.
sections.problem: Return per `is_test_account`: `rows_checked`, `both_match` (both stored features equal to the recomputed ones), `mismatch` (at least one differs, ignoring NULL stored values) and `stored_null` (at least one stored value NULL). Sort by `is_test_account`.
sections.expected: 2 rows. Real accounts match except for NULL failures; test accounts mismatch (their features are synthetic).
sections.edge_cases:
- Entities with no sessions in the window must recompute to 0 (LEFT JOIN + COALESCE).
- Comparison with NULL stored values is UNKNOWN; classify them separately.
sections.hint1: Recompute both counts per entity with conditional aggregation over a LEFT JOIN from the snapshot rows to sessions.
sections.hint2: Restrict joined sessions to `[as_of_ts − 28 days, as_of_ts)` in the ON clause.
sections.hint3: Classify each row with CASE: stored NULL first, then equality of both features.
sections.solution:
WITH recomputed AS (
    SELECT f.entity_id,
           e.is_test_account,
           f.sessions_7d,
           f.sessions_28d,
           SUM(CASE WHEN s.started_at >= f.as_of_ts - INTERVAL '7' DAY THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS calc_7d,
           COUNT(s.user_id)                                                           AS calc_28d
    FROM entity_features f
    JOIN ml_entities e ON e.entity_id = f.entity_id
    LEFT JOIN sessions s
           ON s.user_id = e.user_id
          AND s.started_at >= f.as_of_ts - INTERVAL '28' DAY
          AND s.started_at <  f.as_of_ts
    WHERE f.as_of_ts = TIMESTAMP '2025-06-16 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY f.entity_id, e.is_test_account, f.sessions_7d, f.sessions_28d
)
SELECT is_test_account,
       COUNT(*) AS rows_checked,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sessions_7d = calc_7d AND sessions_28d = calc_28d THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS both_match,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sessions_7d IS NOT NULL AND sessions_28d IS NOT NULL
                 AND (sessions_7d <> calc_7d OR sessions_28d <> calc_28d) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS mismatch,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sessions_7d IS NULL OR sessions_28d IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)      AS stored_null
FROM recomputed
GROUP BY is_test_account
ORDER BY is_test_account;
sections.assert: [r for r in rows if r[0] in ('0','f','false')][0][3] == '0'
sections.explanation:
The LEFT JOIN attaches each snapshot row's sessions within the 28-day window, measured relative to that row's own `as_of_ts`. That is the definition of a historical, point-in-time feature. Conditional aggregation then derives the 7-day count from the same joined rows, and `COUNT(s.user_id)` returns 0 when no session matched.

Real accounts: every non-NULL stored value equals the recomputation, so the feature pipeline implements its definition. Test accounts were seeded with synthetic activity in the feature store only, which is one more reason to exclude them.

This "recompute and diff" test is how feature pipelines are validated after code changes, and how offline/online feature parity is checked.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `<=` at the upper bound (a session exactly at `as_of_ts` belongs to the next snapshot).
- Comparing with `=` and treating UNKNOWN as mismatch.
sections.performance: `sessions(user_id, started_at)` turns each window into an index range scan.
sections.interview: A concrete answer to "how do you test a feature pipeline?".

questions.title: Latest valid prediction per entity
questions.primary: Selecting the latest valid record per entity
questions.secondary: deterministic tie-breaking, filtering failed scores, model registry join
questions.tables: model_predictions(prediction_id, model_version_id, entity_id, predicted_at, score, predicted_label); model_versions(model_version_id, model_name, stage)

sections.context: The CRM integration shows each account's current churn risk: the most recent **valid** (non-NULL) score from the churn model currently in production.
sections.problem: For the churn model whose `stage` is `'production'`, return for every entity its latest prediction with a non-NULL score (`predicted_at` descending, then `prediction_id` descending): `entity_id`, `prediction_id`, `predicted_at`, `score` (4 decimals), `predicted_label`. Sort by `entity_id`.
sections.expected: One row per entity scored by the production version.
sections.edge_cases:
- Re-runs create two predictions on the same day; the later one wins.
- A failed (NULL) latest score must fall back to the previous valid score, so filter NULLs **before** ranking.
sections.hint1: Identify the production version through `model_versions`.
sections.hint2: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY predicted_at DESC, prediction_id DESC)` over valid rows.
sections.hint3: Keep `rn = 1`.
sections.solution:
SELECT entity_id, prediction_id, predicted_at, CAST(score AS DECIMAL(6,4)) AS score, predicted_label
FROM (
    SELECT p.entity_id, p.prediction_id, p.predicted_at, p.score, p.predicted_label,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.entity_id
                              ORDER BY p.predicted_at DESC, p.prediction_id DESC) AS rn
    FROM model_predictions p
    JOIN model_versions v ON v.model_version_id = p.model_version_id
    WHERE v.model_name = 'churn_classifier'
      AND v.stage = 'production'
      AND p.score IS NOT NULL
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY entity_id;
sections.explanation:
Filtering `score IS NOT NULL` before the window makes "latest **valid**" a single ranking step. Filtering afterwards would drop an entity whose latest run failed instead of falling back to its previous score. `prediction_id` as the final key keeps the choice deterministic even when two rows have the same timestamp.

Looking up the production version by `stage` rather than hard-coding `model_version_id = 3` keeps the query correct after the next promotion.
sections.mistakes:
- `MAX(predicted_at)` joined back to the table: duplicates on ties and more code.
- Ranking first and filtering NULL scores afterwards.
sections.performance: `model_predictions(entity_id, predicted_at)` supports the per-entity ordering.
sections.interview: "Latest record per key" with validity rules and deterministic ties is a core production-SQL skill.

questions.title: Precision, recall, accuracy and F1 per model version
questions.primary: Classification metrics from prediction and label tables
questions.secondary: confusion matrix with conditional aggregation, zero-denominator guards, dedup on both sides
questions.tables: model_predictions(prediction_id, model_version_id, entity_id, predicted_at, score, predicted_label); model_versions(model_version_id, version_label, model_name); training_labels(label_id, entity_id, label_name, observation_date, label_value, label_available_at); ml_entities(entity_id, is_test_account)
questions.columns: version_label, examples, tp, fp, fn, tn, precision_pct, recall_pct, accuracy_pct, f1

sections.context: Each monthly run of the churn models scores entities on an observation date. Labels arrive 30+ days later. `predicted_label` is 1 when `score >= threshold`. Evaluate every churn model version on the predictions it actually made.
sections.problem: Per churn-classifier version, match each entity's **latest valid prediction per day** to the **authoritative** label of that observation date (`CAST(predicted_at AS DATE) = observation_date`), excluding test accounts and NULL labels. Return the confusion matrix and `precision_pct`, `recall_pct`, `accuracy_pct` (1 decimal) and `f1` (3 decimals). Sort by `version_label`.
sections.expected: 4 rows (v1-v4; v4 only has its shadow predictions for 2025-05-01 evaluated).
sections.edge_cases:
- Precision is undefined when there are no predicted positives; recall when there are no actual positives. Return NULL, not an error.
- Both tables contain duplicates (re-runs, label re-runs); deduplicate each before joining, or the confusion matrix double counts.
sections.hint1: CTE 1: authoritative labels. CTE 2: latest valid prediction per (version, entity, day).
sections.hint2: TP = `SUM(CASE WHEN predicted_label = 1 AND label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, and similarly FP, FN, TN.
sections.hint3: Precision = TP / NULLIF(TP + FP, 0); F1 = 2TP / NULLIF(2TP + FP + FN, 0).
sections.solution:
WITH labels AS (
    SELECT x.entity_id, x.observation_date, x.label_value
    FROM (
        SELECT l.entity_id, l.observation_date, l.label_value,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.entity_id, l.observation_date
                                  ORDER BY l.label_available_at DESC, l.label_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM training_labels l
        WHERE l.label_name = 'churned_30d'
    ) x
    JOIN ml_entities e ON e.entity_id = x.entity_id
    WHERE x.rn = 1 AND x.label_value IS NOT NULL AND e.is_test_account = FALSE
),
preds AS (
    SELECT model_version_id, entity_id, pred_date, predicted_label
    FROM (
        SELECT p.model_version_id, p.entity_id, CAST(p.predicted_at AS DATE) AS pred_date, p.predicted_label,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.model_version_id, p.entity_id, CAST(p.predicted_at AS DATE)
                                  ORDER BY p.predicted_at DESC, p.prediction_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM model_predictions p
        WHERE p.score IS NOT NULL
    ) y
    WHERE rn = 1
),
cm AS (
    SELECT v.version_label,
           COUNT(*)                                                                    AS examples,
           SUM(CASE WHEN p.predicted_label = 1 AND l.label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS tp,
           SUM(CASE WHEN p.predicted_label = 1 AND l.label_value = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fp,
           SUM(CASE WHEN p.predicted_label = 0 AND l.label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fn,
           SUM(CASE WHEN p.predicted_label = 0 AND l.label_value = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS tn
    FROM preds p
    JOIN labels l         ON l.entity_id = p.entity_id AND l.observation_date = p.pred_date
    JOIN model_versions v ON v.model_version_id = p.model_version_id
    WHERE v.model_name = 'churn_classifier'
    GROUP BY v.version_label
)
SELECT version_label, examples, tp, fp, fn, tn,
       ROUND(100.0 * tp / NULLIF(tp + fp, 0), 1)                AS precision_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * tp / NULLIF(tp + fn, 0), 1)                AS recall_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * (tp + tn) / NULLIF(examples, 0), 1)         AS accuracy_pct,
       ROUND(2.0 * tp / NULLIF(2 * tp + fp + fn, 0), 3)          AS f1
FROM cm
ORDER BY version_label;
sections.assert: all(num(r[1]) == num(r[2]) + num(r[3]) + num(r[4]) + num(r[5]) for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
**Column definitions:** `predicted_label` is the model's 0/1 decision at the run's `threshold`; `label_value` is the observed outcome (1 = churned). Each example is one (entity, observation date).

1. Deduplicate both sides to the example grain first: authoritative labels and the latest valid prediction per model, entity and day. Without this, re-runs would add duplicate confusion-matrix entries.
2. The confusion matrix is four conditional counts.
3. Metrics with explicit zero guards: precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN), accuracy = (TP + TN) / N, F1 = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN). This last form is algebraically equal to the harmonic mean of precision and recall, and avoids a division when both are 0.

With ~18% positives, accuracy is dominated by negatives. Precision and recall (or PR-AUC) are the meaningful metrics. Versions use different thresholds (0.50 → 0.35), so part of the recall change is threshold choice, not model quality (compare at a common threshold in SQL-109).
sections.mistakes:
- Joining raw predictions to raw labels (duplicates on both sides).
- Using a model's threshold from `model_versions.default_threshold` when the run used a different one; `predicted_label` already reflects the run's actual threshold.
sections.performance: Window sorts over a few thousand rows each; joins on the deduplicated keys.
sections.interview: Computing metrics from raw tables, including dedup and zero-denominator handling, is a frequent MLE take-home task.

questions.title: Paired comparison: production v3 versus shadow v4
questions.primary: Comparing model versions on identical examples
questions.secondary: intersection of scored sets, metrics at each model's threshold, agreement rate
questions.tables: model_predictions(prediction_id, model_version_id, entity_id, predicted_at, score, predicted_label); model_versions(model_version_id, version_label); training_labels(label_id, entity_id, label_name, observation_date, label_value, label_available_at); ml_entities(entity_id, is_test_account)
questions.columns: version_label, threshold, examples, precision_pct, recall_pct, f1, agreement_pct

sections.context: v4 ran in shadow mode next to v3 on 2025-05-01. A fair comparison must evaluate both versions on **exactly the same** labelled examples.
sections.problem: Take the entities scored validly by both v3 and v4 on 2025-05-01 (latest valid prediction per version and entity that day) that have an authoritative, non-NULL, non-test label. Per version, return the threshold used, `examples`, `precision_pct`, `recall_pct` (1 decimal), `f1` (3 decimals) and `agreement_pct`, the share of examples where both versions made the same decision (1 decimal; same value on both rows). Sort by version.
sections.expected: 2 rows with identical `examples` and `agreement_pct`.
sections.edge_cases: - Evaluating each model on its own scored set would compare different populations if one model failed to score some entities.
sections.hint1: Build one row per entity with both versions' decisions side by side (join v3 to v4 on entity).
sections.hint2: Join that to the labels; then unpivot to one row per (version, example) with UNION ALL.
sections.hint3: Agreement = `AVG(CASE WHEN label_v3 = label_v4 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)` over the paired rows.
sections.solution:
WITH labels AS (
    SELECT entity_id, label_value
    FROM (
        SELECT l.entity_id, l.label_value,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.entity_id ORDER BY l.label_available_at DESC, l.label_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM training_labels l
        WHERE l.label_name = 'churned_30d' AND l.observation_date = DATE '2025-05-01'
    ) x
    JOIN ml_entities e USING (entity_id)
    WHERE x.rn = 1 AND x.label_value IS NOT NULL AND e.is_test_account = FALSE
),
latest AS (
    SELECT model_version_id, entity_id, predicted_label, threshold
    FROM (
        SELECT p.model_version_id, p.entity_id, p.predicted_label, p.threshold,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.model_version_id, p.entity_id
                                  ORDER BY p.predicted_at DESC, p.prediction_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM model_predictions p
        WHERE p.model_version_id IN (3, 4)
          AND p.score IS NOT NULL
          AND p.predicted_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-05-01 00:00:00'
          AND p.predicted_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-05-02 00:00:00'
    ) y
    WHERE rn = 1
),
paired AS (
    SELECT l.entity_id, l.label_value,
           a.predicted_label AS pred_v3, a.threshold AS thr_v3,
           b.predicted_label AS pred_v4, b.threshold AS thr_v4
    FROM labels l
    JOIN latest a ON a.entity_id = l.entity_id AND a.model_version_id = 3
    JOIN latest b ON b.entity_id = l.entity_id AND b.model_version_id = 4
),
long_form AS (
    SELECT 'v3' AS version_label, thr_v3 AS threshold, pred_v3 AS pred, label_value,
           CASE WHEN pred_v3 = pred_v4 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS agree
    FROM paired
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'v4', thr_v4, pred_v4, label_value,
           CASE WHEN pred_v3 = pred_v4 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
    FROM paired
)
SELECT version_label,
       MAX(threshold)                                                                       AS threshold,
       COUNT(*)                                                                             AS examples,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN pred = 1 AND label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN pred = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 1)                     AS precision_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN pred = 1 AND label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(label_value), 0), 1)                                              AS recall_pct,
       ROUND(2.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN pred = 1 AND label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN pred = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) + SUM(label_value), 0), 3)  AS f1,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(agree) / COUNT(*), 1)                                              AS agreement_pct
FROM long_form
GROUP BY version_label
ORDER BY version_label;
sections.explanation:
The **paired** design (same examples for both models) removes population differences from the comparison. With few examples, a paired test (McNemar on the disagreement cells) is far more powerful than comparing two independent accuracies.

F1 uses the identity 2TP / (predicted positives + actual positives).

Note the threshold column: v4 runs at 0.35 versus v3 at 0.40. Differences in precision and recall mix model quality with threshold choice. For a clean comparison, evaluate both at the same threshold or compare threshold-free metrics (AUC, SQL-114).
sections.mistakes:
- Comparing v4's metrics on its scored set with v3's on a different set.
- Forgetting that shadow scoring can fail for some entities, which changes the population.
sections.performance: All CTEs are small; the window over one day of predictions uses `model_predictions(model_version_id, predicted_at)`.
sections.interview: Shadow deployments and paired evaluation are senior MLE topics.

questions.title: Precision and recall across a threshold sweep
questions.secondary: CROSS JOIN with a list of thresholds, metrics per threshold
questions.tables: model_predictions(prediction_id, model_version_id, entity_id, predicted_at, score); training_labels(label_id, entity_id, label_name, observation_date, label_value, label_available_at); ml_entities(entity_id, is_test_account)

sections.context: Customer success can call about 25% of accounts per month. Choose v3's threshold from its labelled predictions (April and May 2025 runs).
sections.problem: For thresholds 0.20, 0.30, …, 0.70, recompute decisions from `score` for v3's latest valid prediction per entity and day, joined to authoritative non-test labels. Return `threshold`, `flagged_pct` (share predicted positive), `precision_pct`, `recall_pct` (1 decimal) and `f1` (3 decimals). Sort by threshold.
sections.expected: 6 rows; lower thresholds flag more accounts with higher recall and lower precision.
sections.edge_cases: - Recompute decisions from the score; the stored `predicted_label` reflects only the run's threshold.
sections.hint1: Build the evaluation set once (score + label per example).
sections.hint2: CROSS JOIN it with a 6-row list of thresholds (UNION ALL of SELECTs).
sections.hint3: `pred = CASE WHEN score >= threshold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END`, then aggregate per threshold.
sections.solution:
WITH labels AS (
    SELECT x.entity_id, x.observation_date, x.label_value
    FROM (
        SELECT l.entity_id, l.observation_date, l.label_value,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.entity_id, l.observation_date
                                  ORDER BY l.label_available_at DESC, l.label_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM training_labels l
        WHERE l.label_name = 'churned_30d'
    ) x
    JOIN ml_entities e ON e.entity_id = x.entity_id
    WHERE x.rn = 1 AND x.label_value IS NOT NULL AND e.is_test_account = FALSE
),
scored AS (
    SELECT entity_id, pred_date, score
    FROM (
        SELECT p.entity_id, CAST(p.predicted_at AS DATE) AS pred_date, p.score,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.entity_id, CAST(p.predicted_at AS DATE)
                                  ORDER BY p.predicted_at DESC, p.prediction_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM model_predictions p
        WHERE p.model_version_id = 3 AND p.score IS NOT NULL
    ) y
    WHERE rn = 1
),
evalset AS (
    SELECT s.score, l.label_value
    FROM scored s
    JOIN labels l ON l.entity_id = s.entity_id AND l.observation_date = s.pred_date
),
thresholds AS (
    SELECT 0.20 AS threshold UNION ALL SELECT 0.30 UNION ALL SELECT 0.40
    UNION ALL SELECT 0.50 UNION ALL SELECT 0.60 UNION ALL SELECT 0.70
)
SELECT t.threshold,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN e.score >= t.threshold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS flagged_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN e.score >= t.threshold AND e.label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN e.score >= t.threshold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 1)        AS precision_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN e.score >= t.threshold AND e.label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(e.label_value), 0), 1)                                             AS recall_pct,
       ROUND(2.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN e.score >= t.threshold AND e.label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN e.score >= t.threshold THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) + SUM(e.label_value), 0), 3) AS f1
FROM evalset e
CROSS JOIN thresholds t
GROUP BY t.threshold
ORDER BY t.threshold;
sections.explanation:
The CROSS JOIN evaluates every example at every threshold in one pass. Metrics are recomputed from the score, so any threshold can be explored, not just the one the run used.

Choosing the threshold is a **business** decision: with capacity to contact ~25% of accounts, pick the highest-recall threshold whose `flagged_pct` fits. F1 is a reasonable default but it encodes an arbitrary equal weighting of precision and recall.

`score` is DOUBLE PRECISION and the thresholds are DECIMAL literals; `>=` compares them numerically in both engines.
sections.mistakes:
- Re-using `predicted_label` (only valid for one threshold).
- Choosing the F1-maximizing threshold without asking about the cost of false positives versus false negatives.
sections.performance: 6 x evaluation set rows; tiny.
sections.interview: Threshold selection under operational constraints is a realistic MLE interview discussion.

questions.title: Score distribution drift with the Population Stability Index
questions.secondary: fixed-width buckets, shares per run, LN, epsilon for empty buckets

sections.context: Labels for the June run will not arrive until July, so monitoring relies on the score distribution itself. The Population Stability Index (PSI) compares the June 2025 production scores of v3 with May's.
sections.problem: Using v3's valid scores from batches `churn-2025-05-01-a` (reference) and `churn-2025-06-01-a` (current), bucket scores into 10 equal-width bins (`FLOOR(score * 10)`, with 1.0 in the top bin). Return per bucket the share of each month (`may_pct`, `june_pct`, 2 decimals), the PSI contribution `(june − may) x LN(june / may)` (4 decimals, shares as fractions) and the total PSI on every row (4 decimals). Sort by bucket.
sections.expected: Up to 10 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- An empty bucket makes LN undefined; replace zero shares with a small epsilon (0.0001).
- Rule of thumb: PSI < 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate shift, > 0.25 significant shift.
sections.hint1: Count scores per bucket for each batch with conditional aggregation, then divide by each batch's total.
sections.hint2: `LEAST(FLOOR(score * 10), 9)` gives buckets 0–9.
sections.hint3: Total PSI = `SUM(contribution) OVER ()`.
sections.solution:
WITH scores AS (
    SELECT batch_id, LEAST(FLOOR(score * 10), 9) AS bucket
    FROM model_predictions
    WHERE model_version_id = 3
      AND score IS NOT NULL
      AND batch_id IN ('churn-2025-05-01-a', 'churn-2025-06-01-a')
),
counts AS (
    SELECT bucket,
           SUM(CASE WHEN batch_id = 'churn-2025-05-01-a' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_may,
           SUM(CASE WHEN batch_id = 'churn-2025-06-01-a' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_june
    FROM scores
    GROUP BY bucket
),
shares AS (
    SELECT bucket,
           GREATEST(1.0 * n_may  / SUM(n_may)  OVER (), 0.0001) AS p_may,
           GREATEST(1.0 * n_june / SUM(n_june) OVER (), 0.0001) AS p_june
    FROM counts
)
SELECT bucket,
       ROUND(100 * p_may, 2)                                   AS may_pct,
       ROUND(100 * p_june, 2)                                  AS june_pct,
       ROUND((p_june - p_may) * LN(p_june / p_may), 4)          AS psi_contribution,
       ROUND(SUM((p_june - p_may) * LN(p_june / p_may)) OVER (), 4) AS psi_total
FROM shares
ORDER BY bucket;
sections.explanation:
PSI = Σ (actual − expected) · ln(actual / expected) over buckets. It is symmetric in its contribution sign: each term is ≥ 0. It summarizes how much a distribution moved. Score drift without label drift can indicate a changed population (new customer mix), a feature pipeline issue, or a model or config change, so investigate before acting.

Implementation notes:
- Fixed-width bins on [0, 1] make scores comparable across runs. Quantile bins from the reference run are an alternative.
- `GREATEST(share, 0.0001)` avoids `ln(0)` and division by zero.
- `LEAST`, `GREATEST`, `FLOOR` and `LN` exist in both engines.
sections.mistakes:
- Comparing a full run with a partial re-run batch (`-b`), which contains a biased subset of entities.
- Reading a small PSI as "model is fine". It only says the score distribution is stable, not that predictions are accurate.
sections.performance: One scan of two batches.
sections.interview: Drift monitoring without labels is a standard MLOps question; PSI is the expected metric to name and compute.

questions.title: Build the batch-inference input for the next run
questions.secondary: eligibility rules, latest available snapshot at run time, LEFT JOIN for missing features
questions.tables: ml_entities(entity_id, user_id, registered_at, is_test_account); sessions(user_id, started_at); entity_features(entity_id, as_of_ts, ingested_at, sessions_28d, days_since_last_session, open_tickets, avg_session_minutes, seats_used_pct)
questions.columns: entity_id, feature_as_of_ts, sessions_28d, days_since_last_session, open_tickets, avg_session_minutes, seats_used_pct

sections.context: The next monthly scoring run starts on 2025-07-01 at 02:00 UTC. It scores non-test entities that are eligible under the label definition (≥ 2 sessions in the 30 days before 2025-07-01) with the **latest snapshot ingested before the run starts**.
sections.problem: Return the scoring input: `entity_id`, `feature_as_of_ts` and the five features (`avg_session_minutes` and `seats_used_pct` rounded to 2 and 3 decimals). Include eligible entities that have no available snapshot, with NULL features. Sort by `entity_id`.
sections.expected: A few hundred rows, mostly using the 2025-06-30 snapshot; late-arriving rows fall back to 2025-06-16.
sections.edge_cases:
- The 2025-06-30 snapshot is ingested a few hours after midnight; rows ingested after 02:00 are not usable.
- The same eligibility as training (SQL-098) avoids training/serving population mismatch.
sections.hint1: Eligible entities: aggregate sessions per entity in `[2025-06-01, 2025-07-01)` with HAVING `COUNT(*) >= 2`.
sections.hint2: Available snapshots: `ingested_at <= TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 02:00:00'`; rank by `as_of_ts DESC`.
sections.hint3: LEFT JOIN the ranked snapshots with `rn = 1` in the ON clause.
sections.solution:
WITH eligible AS (
    SELECT e.entity_id
    FROM ml_entities e
    JOIN sessions s ON s.user_id = e.user_id
    WHERE e.is_test_account = FALSE
      AND e.registered_at <= TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
      AND s.started_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
      AND s.started_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY e.entity_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
),
available AS (
    SELECT f.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY f.entity_id ORDER BY f.as_of_ts DESC) AS rn
    FROM entity_features f
    WHERE f.ingested_at <= TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 02:00:00'
)
SELECT el.entity_id,
       a.as_of_ts                                    AS feature_as_of_ts,
       a.sessions_28d,
       a.days_since_last_session,
       a.open_tickets,
       CAST(a.avg_session_minutes AS DECIMAL(10,2))  AS avg_session_minutes,
       CAST(a.seats_used_pct AS DECIMAL(10,3))       AS seats_used_pct
FROM eligible el
LEFT JOIN available a ON a.entity_id = el.entity_id AND a.rn = 1
ORDER BY el.entity_id;
sections.explanation:
Batch inference applies the **same population and the same point-in-time rule** as training, only with the run's start time as the cut-off. Defining eligibility with the label rule keeps training and serving populations aligned, and using `ingested_at` reproduces exactly what the scorer will be able to read at 02:00.

Keeping entities without any available snapshot (LEFT JOIN) makes the problem visible: the scorer must decide on a fallback, and the count of such entities is a useful run metric.

`f.*` in a CTE is acceptable for an internal step but the final SELECT lists columns explicitly (SQL-155).
sections.mistakes:
- Joining the 2025-06-30 snapshot by date equality: entities whose row arrived late or is missing would get no features.
- Using a different eligibility rule than training.
sections.performance: The session aggregation uses `sessions(user_id, started_at)`; the window ranks only rows ingested before the cut-off.
sections.interview: Shows that the candidate thinks about serving-time data availability, not only training.

questions.title: Stale features at scoring time and delayed labels
questions.primary: Monitoring stale features and delayed labels
questions.secondary: two grains reported side by side, date-relative thresholds
questions.tables: model_predictions(model_version_id, batch_id, predicted_at, feature_as_of_ts); training_labels(label_id, entity_id, label_name, observation_date, label_value, label_available_at)
questions.columns: run_date, predictions, stale_feature_predictions, unlogged_feature_snapshot, labels, delayed_labels

sections.context: Two health signals per monthly cycle: at scoring time, did predictions use fresh features (snapshot ≤ 14 days old)? After the outcome window, did labels arrive on time (≤ 3 days after the 30-day window closed)?
sections.problem: For each run date (date of the production `-a` batch of churn models v1–v3), return `predictions`, `stale_feature_predictions` (logged `feature_as_of_ts` older than `predicted_at − 14 days`), `unlogged_feature_snapshot` (NULL `feature_as_of_ts`), `labels` (authoritative non-NULL labels with that observation date) and `delayed_labels` (`label_available_at` later than observation date + 33 days). Sort by run date.
sections.expected: 8 rows; the June run has 0 labels.
sections.edge_cases:
- Labels for the latest run are not available yet; LEFT JOIN so the run still appears.
- Stale features and unlogged snapshots are different problems; count them separately.
sections.hint1: Aggregate predictions per run date and labels per observation date separately.
sections.hint2: Join the two aggregates on `run_date = observation_date` with a LEFT JOIN.
sections.hint3: `feature_as_of_ts < predicted_at - INTERVAL '14' DAY` and `label_available_at > observation_date + INTERVAL '33' DAY`.
sections.solution:
WITH runs AS (
    SELECT CAST(predicted_at AS DATE)                                                       AS run_date,
           COUNT(*)                                                                         AS predictions,
           SUM(CASE WHEN feature_as_of_ts < predicted_at - INTERVAL '14' DAY THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS stale_feature_predictions,
           SUM(CASE WHEN feature_as_of_ts IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                        AS unlogged_feature_snapshot
    FROM model_predictions
    WHERE model_version_id IN (1, 2, 3)
      AND batch_id LIKE 'churn-%-a'
    GROUP BY CAST(predicted_at AS DATE)
),
lab AS (
    SELECT observation_date,
           COUNT(*) AS labels,
           SUM(CASE WHEN label_available_at > observation_date + INTERVAL '33' DAY THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delayed_labels
    FROM (
        SELECT l.*,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id, observation_date
                                  ORDER BY label_available_at DESC, label_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM training_labels l
        WHERE label_name = 'churned_30d'
    ) x
    WHERE rn = 1 AND label_value IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY observation_date
)
SELECT r.run_date,
       r.predictions,
       r.stale_feature_predictions,
       r.unlogged_feature_snapshot,
       COALESCE(l.labels, 0)         AS labels,
       COALESCE(l.delayed_labels, 0) AS delayed_labels
FROM runs r
LEFT JOIN lab l ON l.observation_date = r.run_date
ORDER BY r.run_date;
sections.explanation:
Two aggregates at the same grain (one row per monthly cycle) are joined on the date. Each side keeps its own logic:
- **Feature staleness** at scoring time comes from the prediction log (`feature_as_of_ts` vs `predicted_at`). A NULL means the scorer did not log it, which is an observability gap worth tracking on its own.
- **Label delay** compares availability with the earliest possible time (observation + 30 days) plus a 3-day tolerance.

`DATE + INTERVAL` yields a timestamp/datetime in both engines, which compares correctly with `label_available_at`.

Delayed labels shrink the usable training set for the most recent months and delay monitoring; stale features silently degrade predictions. Both belong on an ML health dashboard.
sections.mistakes:
- INNER JOIN, which hides the latest run (no labels yet).
- Counting raw label rows (duplicates) instead of authoritative ones.
sections.performance: Two small aggregations.
sections.interview: MLOps monitoring beyond accuracy (freshness, completeness, delays) is a senior MLE discussion point.

questions.title: Features that changed after the prediction was made
questions.primary: Detecting features updated after prediction time
questions.secondary: availability vs event time, EXISTS for newer late-arriving snapshots
questions.tables: model_predictions(prediction_id, model_version_id, entity_id, batch_id, predicted_at, feature_as_of_ts); entity_features(entity_id, as_of_ts, ingested_at)

sections.context:
Two different problems hide behind "the features changed after the prediction":
1. The prediction log claims a snapshot that was **ingested after** the prediction time, which is impossible in a correct system and points to a logging bug or a re-scored row with an old timestamp.
2. A **newer** snapshot (`as_of_ts <= predicted_at`) existed in event time but was ingested **after** the prediction, so the model legitimately used older features. A re-score would differ.
sections.problem: For churn-model batches (v1–v4), return per `batch_id`: `predictions`, `logged_snapshot_not_yet_ingested` (problem 1) and `newer_snapshot_arrived_later` (problem 2: a snapshot newer than the logged one, with `as_of_ts <= predicted_at` and `ingested_at > predicted_at`). Sort by `batch_id`.
sections.expected: One row per churn batch; problem 1 appears in one batch, problem 2 around late arrivals and the backfill.
sections.edge_cases: - Predictions with NULL `feature_as_of_ts` cannot be checked for problem 1; for problem 2 any late snapshot ≤ predicted_at counts.
sections.hint1: Problem 1: join the logged snapshot and compare its `ingested_at` with `predicted_at`.
sections.hint2: Problem 2: EXISTS a snapshot of the same entity with `as_of_ts > COALESCE(feature_as_of_ts, '1900-01-01')`, `as_of_ts <= predicted_at` and `ingested_at > predicted_at`.
sections.hint3: Aggregate both flags per batch with conditional sums.
sections.solution:
SELECT p.batch_id,
       COUNT(*) AS predictions,
       SUM(CASE WHEN f.ingested_at > p.predicted_at THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS logged_snapshot_not_yet_ingested,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM entity_features n
                             WHERE n.entity_id = p.entity_id
                               AND n.as_of_ts > COALESCE(p.feature_as_of_ts, TIMESTAMP '1900-01-01 00:00:00')
                               AND n.as_of_ts <= p.predicted_at
                               AND n.ingested_at > p.predicted_at)
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS newer_snapshot_arrived_later
FROM model_predictions p
LEFT JOIN entity_features f
       ON f.entity_id = p.entity_id
      AND f.as_of_ts = p.feature_as_of_ts
WHERE p.model_version_id IN (1, 2, 3, 4)
GROUP BY p.batch_id
ORDER BY p.batch_id;
sections.explanation:
Every feature row carries two times: `as_of_ts` (what it describes) and `ingested_at` (when it became readable). Comparing both with the prediction time separates:
- **impossible** situations (logged snapshot not yet ingested), which are integrity bugs that also mean the offline record of "what the model saw" is wrong;
- **expected** late-data situations, where the model correctly used older features. They explain why a later re-score differs and quantify how much late data affects serving.

The LEFT JOIN keeps predictions whose snapshot was not logged. Their comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN and contributes 0 to problem 1.
sections.mistakes:
- Treating problem 2 as leakage: it is the opposite (serving had less information than a later replay).
- Ignoring `ingested_at` and only comparing `as_of_ts` with `predicted_at`.
sections.performance: One correlated EXISTS per prediction (≈ 3,000) on the primary key `(entity_id, as_of_ts)`.
sections.interview: Distinguishing event time from processing time is a key data-engineering concept that MLE interviews probe.

questions.title: ROC AUC in SQL with the rank-sum formula
questions.secondary: Mann-Whitney U, average ranks for ties, per-model partitions
questions.tables: model_predictions(prediction_id, model_version_id, entity_id, predicted_at, score); model_versions(model_version_id, version_label, model_name); training_labels(label_id, entity_id, label_name, observation_date, label_value, label_available_at); ml_entities(entity_id, is_test_account)

sections.context: Thresholds differ between versions, so precision and recall do not compare model quality fairly. ROC AUC is threshold-free: the probability that a random churner receives a higher score than a random non-churner.
sections.problem: Using the same deduplicated (prediction, authoritative label) examples as SQL-107, compute AUC per churn-model version with the rank-sum (Mann–Whitney) formula, giving tied scores their average rank. Return `version_label`, `positives`, `negatives`, `auc` (4 decimals). Sort by version.
sections.expected: 4 rows; AUC increases with newer versions.
sections.edge_cases:
- Ties: each tied score receives the mean of the ranks it spans; otherwise AUC is biased.
- A version with only one class has undefined AUC (NULL).
sections.hint1: Rank all examples of a version by score ascending.
sections.hint2: Average rank = `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY v ORDER BY score) + (COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY v, score) − 1) / 2.0`.
sections.hint3: AUC = (Σ ranks of positives − P(P + 1)/2) / (P · N).
sections.solution:
WITH labels AS (
    SELECT x.entity_id, x.observation_date, x.label_value
    FROM (
        SELECT l.entity_id, l.observation_date, l.label_value,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.entity_id, l.observation_date
                                  ORDER BY l.label_available_at DESC, l.label_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM training_labels l
        WHERE l.label_name = 'churned_30d'
    ) x
    JOIN ml_entities e ON e.entity_id = x.entity_id
    WHERE x.rn = 1 AND x.label_value IS NOT NULL AND e.is_test_account = FALSE
),
preds AS (
    SELECT model_version_id, entity_id, pred_date, score
    FROM (
        SELECT p.model_version_id, p.entity_id, CAST(p.predicted_at AS DATE) AS pred_date, p.score,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.model_version_id, p.entity_id, CAST(p.predicted_at AS DATE)
                                  ORDER BY p.predicted_at DESC, p.prediction_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM model_predictions p
        WHERE p.score IS NOT NULL
    ) y
    WHERE rn = 1
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT v.version_label,
           l.label_value,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY v.version_label ORDER BY p.score)
             + (COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY v.version_label, p.score) - 1) / 2.0 AS avg_rank
    FROM preds p
    JOIN labels l         ON l.entity_id = p.entity_id AND l.observation_date = p.pred_date
    JOIN model_versions v ON v.model_version_id = p.model_version_id
    WHERE v.model_name = 'churn_classifier'
)
SELECT version_label,
       SUM(label_value)                    AS positives,
       COUNT(*) - SUM(label_value)         AS negatives,
       ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN label_value = 1 THEN avg_rank ELSE 0 END)
              - SUM(label_value) * (SUM(label_value) + 1) / 2.0)
             / NULLIF(SUM(label_value) * (COUNT(*) - SUM(label_value)), 0), 4) AS auc
FROM ranked
GROUP BY version_label
ORDER BY version_label;
sections.assert: all(0.5 < num(r[3]) <= 1 for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
The Mann–Whitney U statistic counts, over all (positive, negative) pairs, how often the positive is ranked higher (ties count ½). Dividing by P·N gives exactly the ROC AUC, without building a ROC curve. Using ranks makes it an O(n log n) sort instead of an O(P·N) self-join.

Tie handling: `RANK()` gives tied rows the *lowest* rank of their group; adding (group size − 1)/2 converts it to the average rank.

Comparing versions on AUC removes the threshold confound seen in SQL-107. To compare v3 and v4 strictly, restrict both to the same paired examples (as in SQL-108).
sections.mistakes:
- Using ROW_NUMBER (arbitrary order inside ties), which makes AUC depend on row order.
- Computing AUC over raw, duplicated predictions.
sections.performance: One partitioned sort per version; trivial at this scale and fine for millions of rows in a warehouse.
sections.interview: Computing AUC in SQL is an impressive but practical skill; explaining the probabilistic meaning is the key.

questions.title: Offline test metrics versus production performance
questions.primary: Comparing model versions offline and online
questions.secondary: unpivoting computed metrics, joining to an evaluation table, gap analysis
questions.tables: model_evaluations(model_version_id, eval_split, metric_name, metric_value); model_versions(model_version_id, version_label, model_name); model_predictions(prediction_id, model_version_id, entity_id, predicted_at, predicted_label, score); training_labels(label_id, entity_id, label_name, observation_date, label_value, label_available_at); ml_entities(entity_id, is_test_account)

sections.context: The model registry stores offline test-set metrics computed at training time. Production performance (from predictions and later labels) is often worse. A large gap indicates leakage in offline evaluation, distribution shift, or a training/serving skew.
sections.problem: For churn versions v1–v3 (production models), compute online precision, recall and F1 as in SQL-107 and compare them with `model_evaluations` (`eval_split = 'test'`). Return `version_label`, `metric_name`, `offline_test`, `online` and `gap` = online − offline (all 3 decimals, as fractions). Sort by version, metric.
sections.expected: 9 rows (3 versions x 3 metrics).
sections.edge_cases: - Offline metrics are stored as fractions (0–1); keep the online ones in the same unit.
sections.hint1: Compute TP/FP/FN per version (reuse the SQL-107 CTEs).
sections.hint2: Unpivot to (version, metric_name, online) with UNION ALL.
sections.hint3: Join to `model_evaluations` on version and metric name.
sections.solution:
WITH labels AS (
    SELECT x.entity_id, x.observation_date, x.label_value
    FROM (
        SELECT l.entity_id, l.observation_date, l.label_value,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY l.entity_id, l.observation_date
                                  ORDER BY l.label_available_at DESC, l.label_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM training_labels l
        WHERE l.label_name = 'churned_30d'
    ) x
    JOIN ml_entities e ON e.entity_id = x.entity_id
    WHERE x.rn = 1 AND x.label_value IS NOT NULL AND e.is_test_account = FALSE
),
preds AS (
    SELECT model_version_id, entity_id, pred_date, predicted_label
    FROM (
        SELECT p.model_version_id, p.entity_id, CAST(p.predicted_at AS DATE) AS pred_date, p.predicted_label,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.model_version_id, p.entity_id, CAST(p.predicted_at AS DATE)
                                  ORDER BY p.predicted_at DESC, p.prediction_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM model_predictions p
        WHERE p.score IS NOT NULL AND p.model_version_id IN (1, 2, 3)
    ) y
    WHERE rn = 1
),
cm AS (
    SELECT p.model_version_id,
           SUM(CASE WHEN p.predicted_label = 1 AND l.label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS tp,
           SUM(CASE WHEN p.predicted_label = 1 AND l.label_value = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fp,
           SUM(CASE WHEN p.predicted_label = 0 AND l.label_value = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fn
    FROM preds p
    JOIN labels l ON l.entity_id = p.entity_id AND l.observation_date = p.pred_date
    GROUP BY p.model_version_id
),
online AS (
    SELECT model_version_id, 'precision' AS metric_name, 1.0 * tp / NULLIF(tp + fp, 0) AS online FROM cm
    UNION ALL
    SELECT model_version_id, 'recall', 1.0 * tp / NULLIF(tp + fn, 0) FROM cm
    UNION ALL
    SELECT model_version_id, 'f1', 2.0 * tp / NULLIF(2 * tp + fp + fn, 0) FROM cm
)
SELECT v.version_label,
       o.metric_name,
       ROUND(CAST(ev.metric_value AS DECIMAL(10,4)), 3)            AS offline_test,
       ROUND(o.online, 3)                                          AS online,
       ROUND(o.online - CAST(ev.metric_value AS DECIMAL(10,4)), 3) AS gap
FROM online o
JOIN model_versions v     ON v.model_version_id = o.model_version_id
JOIN model_evaluations ev ON ev.model_version_id = o.model_version_id
                         AND ev.metric_name = o.metric_name
                         AND ev.eval_split = 'test'
ORDER BY v.version_label, o.metric_name;
sections.mistakes:
- Comparing percentages with fractions.
- Comparing online metrics of all runs with offline metrics computed on a test set from a different period without saying so.
sections.performance: Same cost as SQL-107; the final join is tiny.
sections.interview: Shows ownership beyond training: verifying that offline promises hold in production.

questions.title: Daily LLM request volume by feature
questions.secondary: conditional aggregation pivot, date bucketing

sections.context: The AI platform on-call dashboard starts with a simple chart: requests per day and feature for the last two weeks of June 2025.
sections.problem: For each day from 2025-06-17 to 2025-06-30, return the number of requests per feature as columns plus the total. Sort by date.
sections.expected: 14 rows (every day had traffic).
sections.edge_cases: - Weekends have much less traffic. That is normal seasonality, not an incident.
sections.hint1: Group by the request date.
sections.hint2: One `SUM(CASE WHEN feature = '...' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` per feature.
sections.hint3: `COUNT(*)` for the total.
sections.solution:
SELECT CAST(requested_at AS DATE)                                  AS request_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN feature = 'support_bot' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)    AS support_bot,
       SUM(CASE WHEN feature = 'sql_copilot' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)    AS sql_copilot,
       SUM(CASE WHEN feature = 'doc_summary' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)    AS doc_summary,
       COUNT(*)                                                    AS total
FROM llm_requests
WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-17 00:00:00'
  AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CAST(requested_at AS DATE)
ORDER BY request_date;
sections.explanation:
Volume is the first signal of every AI service: it drives cost, rate-limit headroom and capacity. Pivoting features into columns makes a stacked chart trivial. Days without traffic would be missing rows; use a date spine (SQL-053) when that matters.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** a sudden volume spike from one feature (e.g. a client retry loop) is the most common cause of surprise LLM bills.
sections.mistakes: - Grouping by the raw timestamp (one row per request).
sections.performance: `llm_requests(requested_at)` index serves the range.
sections.interview: Warm-up; expect "now add cost per day" (SQL-118).

questions.title: p50 / p95 / p99 latency per model
questions.secondary: nearest-rank percentiles with window functions, PERCENTILE_DISC in PostgreSQL

sections.context: The latency SLO is defined on percentiles: p95 < 6 s for chat features. Means hide the long tail that users actually feel.
sections.problem: For successful, non-cached requests in Q2 2025, return per model the number of requests and the **nearest-rank** p50, p95 and p99 latency (the smallest value such that at least p% of requests are ≤ it). Sort by p95.
sections.expected: 5 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- MySQL has no percentile function; implement nearest-rank with ROW_NUMBER and COUNT.
- Nearest-rank (discrete) percentiles return an observed value; interpolated (continuous) percentiles may not.
sections.hint1: Rank each model's latencies ascending and count them.
sections.hint2: The nearest-rank p-th percentile is the value at position `CEIL(p x n)`.
sections.hint3: `MIN(CASE WHEN rn >= CEIL(0.95 * n) THEN latency_ms END)` returns that value.
sections.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT model_name,
           latency_ms,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY latency_ms) AS rn,
           COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY model_name)                     AS n
    FROM llm_requests
    WHERE status = 'success'
      AND cache_hit = FALSE
      AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
      AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
)
SELECT model_name,
       MAX(n)                                                AS requests,
       MIN(CASE WHEN rn >= CEIL(0.50 * n) THEN latency_ms END) AS p50_ms,
       MIN(CASE WHEN rn >= CEIL(0.95 * n) THEN latency_ms END) AS p95_ms,
       MIN(CASE WHEN rn >= CEIL(0.99 * n) THEN latency_ms END) AS p99_ms
FROM ranked
GROUP BY model_name
ORDER BY p95_ms, model_name;
sections.alternative_pg:
SELECT model_name,
       COUNT(*)                                                    AS requests,
       PERCENTILE_DISC(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms)    AS p50_ms,
       PERCENTILE_DISC(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms)    AS p95_ms,
       PERCENTILE_DISC(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms)    AS p99_ms
FROM llm_requests
WHERE status = 'success'
  AND cache_hit = FALSE
  AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
  AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY model_name
ORDER BY p95_ms, model_name;
sections.alternative_note: `PERCENTILE_DISC(p)` is PostgreSQL's native nearest-rank percentile; it returns exactly the same values as the window-function version. `PERCENTILE_CONT(p)` interpolates and may return values that never occurred.
sections.explanation:
After sorting a model's latencies, the nearest-rank p-th percentile sits at position ⌈p·n⌉. Since rows are sorted ascending, `MIN(latency)` over positions ≥ ⌈p·n⌉ is exactly the value at that position. One window pass gives every percentile.

Excluding cache hits measures the model, not the cache. Excluding failures is a definition choice: timeouts are the worst latency users experience, so an SLO report should also show the timeout rate (SQL-021) next to the percentiles.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** LLM latency is heavy-tailed (long generations, provider hiccups). p95/p99 drive user-perceived quality and timeout settings; the mean is almost irrelevant.
sections.mistakes:
- Reporting AVG latency as "typical".
- `rn = ROUND(0.95 * n)`, which uses a different (inconsistent) definition and can miss on small n.
sections.performance: One sort per model; for big tables, percentile sketches (t-digest) are used in monitoring systems.
sections.interview: Percentiles without a percentile function is a frequent portability question for AI and SRE-flavoured roles.

questions.title: Monthly token cost with time-varying prices
questions.primary: Token cost estimation with a pricing table
questions.secondary: range join on validity periods, cache hits cost nothing, per-dialect month
questions.tables: llm_requests(model_name, requested_at, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_hit); llm_pricing(model_name, effective_from, effective_to, input_usd_per_1k, output_usd_per_1k)

sections.context: Finance needs the LLM bill per model and month for H1 2025. Prices change over time (`atlas-large` got cheaper on 2025-03-01, `nimbus-pro` more expensive on 2025-05-01), so each request must use the price valid on its date. Cache hits are free.
sections.problem: Return per month and model: `requests` and `cost_usd` (2 decimals), with cost = input_tokens/1000 x input price + output_tokens/1000 x output price (NULL output = 0), and 0 for cache hits. Sort by month, model.
sections.expected: One row per (month, model) with traffic.
sections.edge_cases:
- `effective_to` is NULL for current prices and inclusive otherwise.
- A request without a matching price row would silently disappear with an INNER JOIN; validate coverage (should be 100%).
sections.hint1: Join each request to the price row whose validity period contains the request's date.
sections.hint2: `CAST(r.requested_at AS DATE) BETWEEN p.effective_from AND COALESCE(p.effective_to, DATE '9999-12-31')`.
sections.hint3: Cost expression inside SUM with a CASE for cache hits; month truncation per dialect.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT CAST(DATE_TRUNC('month', r.requested_at) AS DATE) AS month_start,
       r.model_name,
       COUNT(*) AS requests,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN r.cache_hit THEN 0
                      ELSE r.input_tokens / 1000.0 * p.input_usd_per_1k
                         + COALESCE(r.output_tokens, 0) / 1000.0 * p.output_usd_per_1k
                 END), 2) AS cost_usd
FROM llm_requests r
JOIN llm_pricing p
  ON p.model_name = r.model_name
 AND CAST(r.requested_at AS DATE) BETWEEN p.effective_from AND COALESCE(p.effective_to, DATE '9999-12-31')
WHERE r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', r.requested_at), r.model_name
ORDER BY month_start, r.model_name;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT CAST(DATE_FORMAT(r.requested_at, '%Y-%m-01') AS DATE) AS month_start,
       r.model_name,
       COUNT(*) AS requests,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN r.cache_hit THEN 0
                      ELSE r.input_tokens / 1000.0 * p.input_usd_per_1k
                         + COALESCE(r.output_tokens, 0) / 1000.0 * p.output_usd_per_1k
                 END), 2) AS cost_usd
FROM llm_requests r
JOIN llm_pricing p
  ON p.model_name = r.model_name
 AND CAST(r.requested_at AS DATE) BETWEEN p.effective_from AND COALESCE(p.effective_to, DATE '9999-12-31')
WHERE r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CAST(DATE_FORMAT(r.requested_at, '%Y-%m-01') AS DATE), r.model_name
ORDER BY month_start, r.model_name;
sections.explanation:
Prices are **slowly changing** reference data. The range join picks, for each request, the price row whose `[effective_from, effective_to]` contains the request date. Because periods never overlap and leave no gaps (documented), each request matches exactly one row. Here BETWEEN is correct: the columns are DATEs with an inclusive end.

Coverage check (do it once): `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM llm_requests r WHERE NOT EXISTS (<matching price>)` should be 0. Otherwise the INNER JOIN under-reports cost.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** using today's price for history misstates past spend and makes cost-per-feature trends meaningless after every price change.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining on `model_name` only, which multiplies each request by the number of price periods.
- Charging cache hits.
- Integer division `input_tokens / 1000` in PostgreSQL, which truncates small requests to 0.
sections.performance: The pricing table is tiny; the join is effectively a lookup per request.
sections.interview: Point-in-time joins appear in AI cost analysis too. Mentioning the coverage check is a plus.

questions.title: Most expensive prompt versions
questions.secondary: cost expression, LEFT JOIN for ad-hoc prompts, unit economics
questions.tables: llm_requests(prompt_version_id, model_name, requested_at, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_hit, status); llm_pricing(model_name, effective_from, effective_to, input_usd_per_1k, output_usd_per_1k); prompts(prompt_version_id, prompt_name, version)

sections.context: Prompt engineers want to know which prompt versions drive spend in Q2 2025, including requests sent without a registered prompt ("ad-hoc").
sections.problem: Per prompt version (label like `'support_answer v4'`, or `'ad-hoc'` when `prompt_version_id` is NULL), return `requests`, `total_cost_usd` (2 decimals), `cost_per_request_usd` and `cost_per_success_usd` (4 decimals). Sort by total cost descending.
sections.expected: One row per prompt version used in Q2 2025, plus `ad-hoc`.
sections.edge_cases: - Failed requests still cost input tokens; cost per *success* captures that waste.
sections.hint1: Reuse the cost expression and price range join from SQL-118.
sections.hint2: LEFT JOIN `prompts`; build the label with CASE + CONCAT.
sections.hint3: `cost_per_success = total_cost / NULLIF(successful requests, 0)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN pr.prompt_version_id IS NULL THEN 'ad-hoc'
            ELSE CONCAT(pr.prompt_name, ' v', pr.version) END                 AS prompt,
       COUNT(*)                                                               AS requests,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN r.cache_hit THEN 0
                      ELSE r.input_tokens / 1000.0 * p.input_usd_per_1k
                         + COALESCE(r.output_tokens, 0) / 1000.0 * p.output_usd_per_1k END), 2) AS total_cost_usd,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN r.cache_hit THEN 0
                      ELSE r.input_tokens / 1000.0 * p.input_usd_per_1k
                         + COALESCE(r.output_tokens, 0) / 1000.0 * p.output_usd_per_1k END) / COUNT(*), 4) AS cost_per_request_usd,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN r.cache_hit THEN 0
                      ELSE r.input_tokens / 1000.0 * p.input_usd_per_1k
                         + COALESCE(r.output_tokens, 0) / 1000.0 * p.output_usd_per_1k END)
             / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 4) AS cost_per_success_usd
FROM llm_requests r
JOIN llm_pricing p
  ON p.model_name = r.model_name
 AND CAST(r.requested_at AS DATE) BETWEEN p.effective_from AND COALESCE(p.effective_to, DATE '9999-12-31')
LEFT JOIN prompts pr ON pr.prompt_version_id = r.prompt_version_id
WHERE r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
  AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CASE WHEN pr.prompt_version_id IS NULL THEN 'ad-hoc'
              ELSE CONCAT(pr.prompt_name, ' v', pr.version) END
ORDER BY total_cost_usd DESC, prompt;
sections.explanation:
Grouping by a derived label (CASE + CONCAT) keeps ad-hoc requests visible instead of losing them in an INNER JOIN. Three cost views answer different questions: total spend (budget), cost per request (efficiency of the prompt/model choice), and cost per success (efficiency including failures and retries).

Both engines accept CONCAT with an integer argument (`version`) and convert it to text.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** prompt versions change token counts a lot (longer instructions, more retrieved context). Tracking cost per version catches expensive regressions before they reach the monthly bill.
sections.mistakes:
- INNER JOIN to prompts, which hides ad-hoc traffic (often the most expensive: unbounded prompts).
- Comparing prompt versions that used different models without noting it.
sections.performance: Same scan as SQL-118 plus a primary-key lookup.
sections.interview: Unit economics of AI features (cost per successful answer) is a strong AI-engineering talking point.

questions.title: Detect a failure-rate spike against a trailing baseline
questions.secondary: daily rates, trailing window excluding the current day, alert rule
questions.columns: request_date, requests, failures, failure_rate_pct, baseline_pct, alert

sections.context: On-call wants an alert when a model's daily failure rate exceeds 3x its trailing 7-day average (with at least 10 requests that day). Evaluate the rule on `nimbus-pro` from its launch in production (2025-03-10) to 2025-04-10.
sections.problem: Per active day, return `requests`, `failures` (non-success), `failure_rate_pct` (1 decimal), `baseline_pct` (average daily failure rate over the previous 7 active days, excluding today; 1 decimal) and `alert` (1/0). Sort by date.
sections.expected: One row per active day; the 2025-03-18 incident triggers the alert.
sections.edge_cases:
- The baseline must exclude the current day, otherwise the spike dilutes its own baseline.
- The first day has no baseline (NULL): no alert.
sections.hint1: Aggregate daily counts first.
sections.hint2: `AVG(rate) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)`.
sections.hint3: `CASE WHEN requests >= 10 AND rate > 3 * baseline THEN 1 ELSE 0 END`.
sections.solution:
WITH daily AS (
    SELECT CAST(requested_at AS DATE)                                         AS request_date,
           COUNT(*)                                                           AS requests,
           SUM(CASE WHEN status <> 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)               AS failures,
           100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status <> 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS rate
    FROM llm_requests
    WHERE model_name = 'nimbus-pro'
      AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-03-10 00:00:00'
      AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-04-11 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY CAST(requested_at AS DATE)
),
with_base AS (
    SELECT request_date, requests, failures, rate,
           AVG(rate) OVER (ORDER BY request_date ROWS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS baseline
    FROM daily
)
SELECT request_date,
       requests,
       failures,
       ROUND(rate, 1)     AS failure_rate_pct,
       ROUND(baseline, 1) AS baseline_pct,
       CASE WHEN requests >= 10 AND rate > 3 * baseline THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS alert
FROM with_base
ORDER BY request_date;
sections.explanation:
A trailing baseline that **excludes** the current row (`7 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING`) compares today with recent normal behaviour. The minimum-volume rule suppresses alerts on quiet days where one failure is already a high rate.

Limitations worth stating: a baseline of 0% makes "3x" meaningless (any failure alerts, and `rate > 0` is true). Production systems add an absolute floor (e.g. rate > 5%) and use statistical tests or SLO burn rates.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** provider incidents are frequent; detecting them per model quickly enables automatic fallback to another model.
sections.mistakes:
- Including today in the baseline.
- Averaging per-request instead of per-day rates without saying so (both are valid but different).
sections.performance: One small aggregation; the window runs over ≤ 32 rows.
sections.interview: Anomaly detection with window frames on operational metrics is common in AI platform interviews.

questions.title: Requests with abnormal input token counts
questions.secondary: robust baseline (median per feature), ratio threshold, cost impact
questions.columns: request_id, feature, model_name, input_tokens, feature_median, ratio_to_median

sections.context: Some users paste entire log files or schemas into the AI features (it happens in all three). These requests are slow, expensive and often fail. Flag requests whose input exceeds 10x the **median** input size of their feature (the median is robust to the outliers themselves).
