sections.problem: Return `request_id`, `feature`, `model_name`, `input_tokens`, `feature_median` (median input tokens of that feature over all requests, averaging the two middle values for even counts) and `ratio_to_median` (1 decimal) for flagged requests. Sort by ratio descending, then `request_id`.
sections.expected: A short list (about 10 requests).
sections.edge_cases: - A mean-based threshold would be pulled up by the outliers it should detect.
sections.hint1: Compute the median per feature with the portable ROW_NUMBER/COUNT method (SQL-089).
sections.hint2: Join each request to its feature's median.
sections.hint3: Filter `input_tokens > 10 * feature_median`.
sections.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT feature, input_tokens,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY feature ORDER BY input_tokens) AS rn,
           COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY feature)                       AS n
    FROM llm_requests
),
medians AS (
    SELECT feature,
           AVG(CASE WHEN rn IN (FLOOR((n + 1) / 2.0), FLOOR((n + 2) / 2.0)) THEN input_tokens END) AS feature_median
    FROM ranked
    GROUP BY feature
)
SELECT r.request_id,
       r.feature,
       r.model_name,
       r.input_tokens,
       ROUND(m.feature_median, 1)                       AS feature_median,
       ROUND(r.input_tokens / m.feature_median, 1)      AS ratio_to_median
FROM llm_requests r
JOIN medians m ON m.feature = r.feature
WHERE r.input_tokens > 10 * m.feature_median
ORDER BY ratio_to_median DESC, r.request_id;
sections.explanation:
A robust baseline (median, or MAD-based thresholds) keeps the detector stable when outliers are present. The mean and standard deviation are inflated by the very events you want to find. The median is computed once per feature and joined back to individual requests.

Follow-ups for a real system: cap input size per feature (truncate or summarize long context), route oversized requests to a long-context model, and alert on the share of oversized requests.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** a handful of 100k-token requests can cost more than thousands of normal ones and exhaust rate limits for everyone.
sections.mistakes:
- Mean + 3σ thresholds dominated by the outliers.
- A global median across features (doc summaries are naturally much longer than copilot prompts).
sections.performance: One partitioned sort for medians plus a join; fine for millions of rows in a warehouse.
sections.interview: Shows robust-statistics thinking applied to AI operations.

questions.title: Users experiencing repeated failures
questions.secondary: failure rate per user, most common failure status (mode with ROW_NUMBER)
questions.columns: user_id, org_id, requests, failures, failure_rate_pct, most_common_failure

sections.context: Support wants to proactively contact users who hit errors repeatedly in Q2 2025, together with the type of failure they see most.
sections.problem: For users (non-NULL `user_id`) with at least 3 non-success requests in Q2 2025, return `user_id`, `org_id`, `requests`, `failures`, `failure_rate_pct` (1 decimal) and `most_common_failure` (the most frequent non-success status; ties broken alphabetically). Sort by failures descending, then `user_id`.
sections.expected: A handful of users, mostly from organizations that hit rate limits.
sections.edge_cases:
- `org_id` is constant per user here (a user belongs to one org), so it can be grouped with the user.
- The mode needs a deterministic tie-breaker.
sections.hint1: CTE 1: per-user totals. CTE 2: per-user, per-failure-status counts.
sections.hint2: Rank statuses per user: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY cnt DESC, status)`.
sections.hint3: Join totals with the rank-1 status and apply the failure threshold.
sections.solution:
WITH q2 AS (
    SELECT user_id, org_id, status
    FROM llm_requests
    WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL
      AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
      AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
),
totals AS (
    SELECT user_id, org_id,
           COUNT(*)                                            AS requests,
           SUM(CASE WHEN status <> 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failures
    FROM q2
    GROUP BY user_id, org_id
),
modes AS (
    SELECT user_id, status,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, status) AS rn
    FROM q2
    WHERE status <> 'success'
    GROUP BY user_id, status
)
SELECT t.user_id,
       t.org_id,
       t.requests,
       t.failures,
       ROUND(100.0 * t.failures / t.requests, 1) AS failure_rate_pct,
       m.status                                  AS most_common_failure
FROM totals t
JOIN modes m ON m.user_id = t.user_id AND m.rn = 1
WHERE t.failures >= 3
ORDER BY t.failures DESC, t.user_id;
sections.explanation:
The **mode** (most frequent value) has no portable aggregate. ROW_NUMBER over grouped counts implements it, and the window can rank the GROUP BY result directly (`ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC`). Joining totals with the rank-1 status yields one row per user.

Most users never see a failure, so a small group with several failures stands out. Look at the mode: rate limiting points to quotas and client backoff, provider errors and timeouts to model or prompt-size issues.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** failure experience is unevenly distributed. Global error rates of 2% can hide a customer who sees 30% failures.
sections.mistakes:
- Using `MAX(status)` as "most common" (alphabetically last, not most frequent).
- Mixing NULL-user (system) traffic into per-user statistics.
sections.performance: Two small aggregations over one quarter.
sections.interview: Per-entity error analysis and the mode-with-ROW_NUMBER trick are both commonly tested.

questions.title: Missing trace IDs and incomplete request metadata
questions.primary: Finding requests with missing trace IDs or incomplete metadata
questions.secondary: JSON key existence per dialect, daily data-quality rates

sections.context: Observability depends on every request carrying a `trace_id` and metadata with a `region`. A deploy in early April 2025 broke the tracing middleware for a few days.
sections.problem: For each day in April 2025, return `requests`, `missing_trace_pct`, `missing_metadata_pct` (NULL `request_metadata`) and `missing_region_pct` (metadata present but without a `region` key), all 1 decimal. Return only days where any of the three percentages exceeds 10%. Sort by date.
sections.expected: The tracing regression of 2025-04-07 to 2025-04-09 (40-50% missing trace IDs), plus a few low-volume days where a couple of bad requests already exceed 10%. That second group is a reason to add a minimum-volume rule to the alert.
sections.edge_cases:
- JSON key tests differ by engine: PostgreSQL `jsonb ? 'region'`, MySQL `JSON_CONTAINS_PATH(doc, 'one', '$.region')`.
- A NULL metadata document is a different defect from a document without the key; count them separately.
sections.hint1: Compute all three counts per day with conditional aggregation.
sections.hint2: PostgreSQL: `request_metadata IS NOT NULL AND NOT (request_metadata ? 'region')`.
sections.hint3: Filter days in HAVING with the three percentage expressions.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT CAST(requested_at AS DATE) AS request_date,
       COUNT(*) AS requests,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN trace_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS missing_trace_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN request_metadata IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS missing_metadata_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN request_metadata IS NOT NULL AND NOT (request_metadata ? 'region')
                              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS missing_region_pct
FROM llm_requests
WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
  AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-05-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CAST(requested_at AS DATE)
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN trace_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0.10 * COUNT(*)
    OR SUM(CASE WHEN request_metadata IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0.10 * COUNT(*)
    OR SUM(CASE WHEN request_metadata IS NOT NULL AND NOT (request_metadata ? 'region') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0.10 * COUNT(*)
ORDER BY request_date;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT CAST(requested_at AS DATE) AS request_date,
       COUNT(*) AS requests,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN trace_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS missing_trace_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN request_metadata IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS missing_metadata_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN request_metadata IS NOT NULL
                               AND NOT JSON_CONTAINS_PATH(request_metadata, 'one', '$.region')
                              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS missing_region_pct
FROM llm_requests
WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
  AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-05-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY CAST(requested_at AS DATE)
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN trace_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0.10 * COUNT(*)
    OR SUM(CASE WHEN request_metadata IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0.10 * COUNT(*)
    OR SUM(CASE WHEN request_metadata IS NOT NULL
                 AND NOT JSON_CONTAINS_PATH(request_metadata, 'one', '$.region') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0.10 * COUNT(*)
ORDER BY request_date;
sections.dialect_note: Key existence: PostgreSQL's `jsonb ? 'key'` operator (top-level keys), and MySQL's `JSON_CONTAINS_PATH(doc, 'one', '$.key')`. A portable approximation is to test whether the extracted value is NULL. That works here but cannot distinguish a missing key from an explicit JSON `null` value. Note that `?` conflicts with placeholder syntax in some drivers (JDBC, psycopg with parameters), where `jsonb_exists(doc, 'key')` is the escape hatch.
sections.explanation:
Each completeness defect gets its own rate so that the cause can be found: NULL `trace_id` (middleware bug), NULL metadata (client did not send it), missing key (old client SDK). HAVING keeps only problem days, using `> 0.10 * COUNT(*)` to avoid repeating the percentage arithmetic.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** without trace IDs you cannot connect an LLM call to the user request, the retrieved chunks and the feedback. Incident analysis and evaluation datasets both depend on that join.
sections.mistakes:
- Treating NULL metadata and missing keys as one problem.
- Using `->>` key extraction syntax from one engine in the other (`'region'` vs `'$.region'`).
sections.performance: One scan over April; JSON checks are per-row CPU.
sections.interview: Shows practical JSON handling and observability awareness.

questions.title: Chunks of the latest published document versions
questions.primary: Retrieving chunks belonging to the latest document version
questions.secondary: latest version per key with ROW_NUMBER, excluding drafts and deleted docs
questions.tables: documents(document_id, doc_key, version_number, status, is_deleted, source_type); document_chunks(chunk_id, document_id, token_count, embedding_model)

sections.context: The retriever must only search chunks of each document's **latest published** version. Drafts must never be served, and deleted documents not at all. Summarize the servable index per source type.
sections.problem: For each non-deleted `doc_key`, pick the published version with the highest `version_number`. Return per `source_type`: `documents`, `documents_with_chunks` (latest version has at least one embedded chunk), `embedded_chunks` and `avg_tokens_per_chunk` (1 decimal). Sort by source type.
sections.expected: 5 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- The newest version can be a draft; the latest *published* version is then an older one.
- Published versions that were never indexed have no chunks; LEFT JOIN keeps them in `documents`.
sections.hint1: Rank versions per `doc_key` among published, non-deleted rows.
sections.hint2: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY doc_key ORDER BY version_number DESC)`.
sections.hint3: LEFT JOIN embedded chunks (`embedding_model IS NOT NULL`) to the rank-1 versions.
sections.solution:
WITH latest AS (
    SELECT document_id, doc_key, source_type
    FROM (
        SELECT document_id, doc_key, source_type,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY doc_key ORDER BY version_number DESC) AS rn
        FROM documents
        WHERE status = 'published'
          AND is_deleted = FALSE
    ) x
    WHERE rn = 1
)
SELECT l.source_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT l.document_id)                      AS documents,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.document_id)                      AS documents_with_chunks,
       COUNT(c.chunk_id)                                  AS embedded_chunks,
       ROUND(AVG(c.token_count), 1)                       AS avg_tokens_per_chunk
FROM latest l
LEFT JOIN document_chunks c
       ON c.document_id = l.document_id
      AND c.embedding_model IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY l.source_type
ORDER BY l.source_type;
sections.explanation:
"Latest version" must be defined with the business filter applied **before** ranking: rank among published, non-deleted rows. Ranking all versions and filtering `status = 'published'` afterwards would drop documents whose newest version is a draft.

Counting `DISTINCT c.document_id` after the LEFT JOIN counts documents that have chunks; NULLs from unmatched rows are ignored.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** serving superseded or draft content causes confidently wrong answers. A "servable set" query like this is what an index-cleanup or retriever filter should implement (e.g. as a metadata filter in the vector DB).
sections.mistakes:
- `MAX(version_number)` per `doc_key` without the status filter (picks drafts).
- Filtering after ranking.
sections.performance: One window sort over documents (~550 rows); `document_chunks(document_id, chunk_index)` unique index supports the join.
sections.interview: Versioned-document handling is a core RAG data-engineering question.

questions.title: What is in the index that should not be?
questions.primary: Finding stale or superseded document versions in the index
questions.secondary: CASE classification with precedence, distinct counts per class
questions.tables: document_chunks(chunk_id, document_id, embedding_model); documents(document_id, status, is_deleted)

sections.context: The index-cleanup job is unreliable. Classify every chunk in `document_chunks` by whether it should be servable.
sections.problem: Classify each chunk with this precedence: `'deleted_document'` (version `is_deleted`), `'unpublished_draft'` (status draft), `'superseded_version'` (status archived), `'embedding_failed'` (`embedding_model IS NULL`), else `'servable'`. Return per class the distinct `documents` and the number of `chunks`. Sort by class.
sections.expected: 5 rows.
sections.edge_cases: - The order of CASE branches defines precedence: a deleted draft counts as deleted.
sections.hint1: Join chunks to their document version.
sections.hint2: One searched CASE with the branches in the given order.
sections.hint3: Group by the CASE expression.
sections.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN d.is_deleted = TRUE        THEN 'deleted_document'
            WHEN d.status = 'draft'         THEN 'unpublished_draft'
            WHEN d.status = 'archived'      THEN 'superseded_version'
            WHEN c.embedding_model IS NULL  THEN 'embedding_failed'
            ELSE 'servable' END              AS chunk_status,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.document_id)         AS documents,
       COUNT(*)                              AS chunks
FROM document_chunks c
JOIN documents d ON d.document_id = c.document_id
GROUP BY CASE WHEN d.is_deleted = TRUE        THEN 'deleted_document'
              WHEN d.status = 'draft'         THEN 'unpublished_draft'
              WHEN d.status = 'archived'      THEN 'superseded_version'
              WHEN c.embedding_model IS NULL  THEN 'embedding_failed'
              ELSE 'servable' END
ORDER BY chunk_status;
sections.explanation:
A single classification CASE turns several data-quality rules into one report, and the branch order resolves overlaps explicitly. Grouping by the same expression is required in PostgreSQL. MySQL would also accept `GROUP BY chunk_status` (alias), and PostgreSQL accepts output-column names in GROUP BY too, but repeating the expression is the most portable form.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** superseded and draft chunks are the root cause of "the bot quoted the old refund policy". Deleted-document chunks can be a compliance problem (content that must no longer be served).
sections.mistakes:
- Checking only `status`, which misses deleted documents whose status is still 'published'.
- Counting documents with `COUNT(*)`.
sections.performance: Join over ~3,000 chunks; trivial.
sections.interview: Turning ambiguous "index hygiene" into explicit, prioritized rules is a good engineering signal.

questions.title: Documents not re-indexed after their last update
questions.secondary: NULL-aware timestamp comparison, issue labels
questions.tables: documents(document_id, doc_key, version_number, status, is_deleted, updated_at, last_indexed_at)
questions.columns: document_id, doc_key, version_number, updated_at, last_indexed_at, issue

sections.context: The indexer sometimes misses edits. A published document version whose `updated_at` is later than its `last_indexed_at`, or which was never indexed, serves stale or no content.
sections.problem: List published, non-deleted versions that were never indexed (`'never_indexed'`) or were edited after their last indexing (`'stale_index'`). Return `document_id`, `doc_key`, `version_number`, `updated_at`, `last_indexed_at`, `issue`. Sort by `issue`, then `updated_at` descending, then `document_id`.
sections.expected: A few dozen versions.
sections.edge_cases: - `last_indexed_at < updated_at` is UNKNOWN when `last_indexed_at` is NULL; handle NULL explicitly.
sections.hint1: Two conditions joined with OR, one of them an IS NULL test.
sections.hint2: Label them with CASE, testing IS NULL first.
sections.hint3: `WHERE status = 'published' AND is_deleted = FALSE AND (last_indexed_at IS NULL OR last_indexed_at < updated_at)`.
sections.solution:
SELECT document_id,
       doc_key,
       version_number,
       updated_at,
       last_indexed_at,
       CASE WHEN last_indexed_at IS NULL THEN 'never_indexed' ELSE 'stale_index' END AS issue
FROM documents
WHERE status = 'published'
  AND is_deleted = FALSE
  AND (last_indexed_at IS NULL OR last_indexed_at < updated_at)
ORDER BY issue, updated_at DESC, document_id;
sections.explanation:
Comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN, so "never indexed" needs its own `IS NULL` branch. Without it, those documents would be silently excluded, and they are the most severe case.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** this list is the work queue of a re-indexing job. Ordering by most recent update puts the freshest edits first, which are usually the ones users are asking about.
sections.mistakes:
- `WHERE last_indexed_at < updated_at` alone.
- Including drafts and archived versions, which should not be (re-)indexed at all.
sections.performance: Small table scan; an index on `status` helps when most documents are archived.
sections.interview: Simple, but it is exactly the kind of query behind RAG freshness monitors.

questions.title: Answers grounded in content that was already superseded
questions.primary: Detecting retrieval of superseded document versions at request time
questions.secondary: EXISTS with a time-relative condition, monthly rates, documented assumptions
questions.tables: llm_requests(request_id, feature, requested_at); llm_request_chunks(request_id, chunk_id); document_chunks(chunk_id, document_id); documents(document_id, doc_key, version_number, status, created_at)

sections.context: A chunk is "superseded at request time" if, when the request was made, a **newer non-draft version** of the same `doc_key` already existed (created before the request). Because status history is not stored, assume a version that is now `published` or `archived` was published from its `created_at` on.
sections.problem: For support-bot requests in H1 2025 that retrieved chunks, return per month: `rag_requests`, `requests_with_superseded_chunk` and `pct` (1 decimal). Sort by month.
sections.expected: 6 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- Compare with the request time, not with today: a version superseded later was fine when retrieved.
- Count requests, not chunks: one bad chunk is enough to taint an answer.
sections.hint1: For each retrieved chunk, look up its document version (`doc_key`, `version_number`).
sections.hint2: EXISTS a version of the same `doc_key` with a higher version number, status not draft, and `created_at <= requested_at`.
sections.hint3: Aggregate per request (MAX of a 0/1 flag), then per month.
sections.solution_pg:
WITH per_request AS (
    SELECT r.request_id,
           r.requested_at,
           MAX(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM documents newer
                                 WHERE newer.doc_key = d.doc_key
                                   AND newer.version_number > d.version_number
                                   AND newer.status <> 'draft'
                                   AND newer.created_at <= r.requested_at)
                    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_superseded
    FROM llm_requests r
    JOIN llm_request_chunks rc ON rc.request_id = r.request_id
    JOIN document_chunks c     ON c.chunk_id = rc.chunk_id
    JOIN documents d           ON d.document_id = c.document_id
    WHERE r.feature = 'support_bot'
      AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
      AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY r.request_id, r.requested_at
)
SELECT CAST(DATE_TRUNC('month', requested_at) AS DATE) AS month_start,
       COUNT(*)                                         AS rag_requests,
       SUM(has_superseded)                              AS requests_with_superseded_chunk,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(has_superseded) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct
FROM per_request
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', requested_at)
ORDER BY month_start;
sections.solution_mysql:
WITH per_request AS (
    SELECT r.request_id,
           r.requested_at,
           MAX(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM documents newer
                                 WHERE newer.doc_key = d.doc_key
                                   AND newer.version_number > d.version_number
                                   AND newer.status <> 'draft'
                                   AND newer.created_at <= r.requested_at)
                    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_superseded
    FROM llm_requests r
    JOIN llm_request_chunks rc ON rc.request_id = r.request_id
    JOIN document_chunks c     ON c.chunk_id = rc.chunk_id
    JOIN documents d           ON d.document_id = c.document_id
    WHERE r.feature = 'support_bot'
      AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
      AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY r.request_id, r.requested_at
)
SELECT CAST(DATE_FORMAT(requested_at, '%Y-%m-01') AS DATE) AS month_start,
       COUNT(*)                                             AS rag_requests,
       SUM(has_superseded)                                  AS requests_with_superseded_chunk,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(has_superseded) / COUNT(*), 1)     AS pct
FROM per_request
GROUP BY CAST(DATE_FORMAT(requested_at, '%Y-%m-01') AS DATE)
ORDER BY month_start;
sections.explanation:
The check is **time-relative**: each retrieved chunk's version is compared with the versions that existed when that request ran. The correlated EXISTS references both the chunk's document (`d`) and the request time (`r.requested_at`). The MAX over a request's chunks yields one flag per request, which is then rolled up to months.

The assumption about status history is written into the problem. Without a status-history table, "not draft now" approximates "was published then". In production, store document state transitions (valid_from/valid_to) so the question can be answered exactly.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** the share of answers grounded in superseded content is a direct, measurable proxy for "outdated answer" complaints (compare with `reason_tag = 'outdated'` feedback).
sections.mistakes:
- Comparing with current status only (`status = 'archived'`), which flags chunks that were current at request time.
- Counting chunk rows instead of requests.
sections.performance: One EXISTS probe per retrieved chunk (~10k) on `documents(doc_key, version_number)` unique index.
sections.interview: Time-aware correctness in RAG data is an advanced but increasingly common AI-engineering question.

questions.title: Duplicate chunks: within documents, across versions, across documents
questions.secondary: content-hash grouping at three scopes, UNION ALL report

sections.context: Duplicate chunks waste index space and crowd out diverse results (the top-5 can contain the same paragraph twice). Duplicates come from three sources with different fixes.
sections.problem: Using `content_hash`, report three scopes: `'within_version'` (same hash ≥ 2 times in one document version), `'across_versions_same_doc'` (same hash in ≥ 2 versions of one `doc_key`), `'across_documents'` (same hash in ≥ 2 different `doc_key`s). Return `duplicate_scope`, `duplicate_hashes` and `chunks_involved`. Sort by scope.
sections.expected: 3 rows.
sections.edge_cases: - A boilerplate footer appears in many documents: one hash, many chunks.
sections.hint1: Each scope is a GROUP BY on a different key with a HAVING condition.
sections.hint2: Across versions: group by `(doc_key, content_hash)` having `COUNT(DISTINCT document_id) > 1`.
sections.hint3: Across documents: group by `content_hash` having `COUNT(DISTINCT doc_key) > 1`.
sections.solution:
WITH c AS (
    SELECT ch.chunk_id, ch.document_id, ch.content_hash, d.doc_key
    FROM document_chunks ch
    JOIN documents d ON d.document_id = ch.document_id
),
within_version AS (
    SELECT document_id, content_hash, COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM c GROUP BY document_id, content_hash HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
),
across_versions AS (
    SELECT doc_key, content_hash, COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM c GROUP BY doc_key, content_hash HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT document_id) > 1
),
across_docs AS (
    SELECT content_hash, COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM c GROUP BY content_hash HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT doc_key) > 1
)
SELECT 'across_documents' AS duplicate_scope, COUNT(*) AS duplicate_hashes, SUM(n) AS chunks_involved FROM across_docs
UNION ALL
SELECT 'across_versions_same_doc', COUNT(*), SUM(n) FROM across_versions
UNION ALL
SELECT 'within_version', COUNT(*), SUM(n) FROM within_version
ORDER BY duplicate_scope;
sections.mistakes:
- Grouping by `chunk_text` (slow, and sensitive to whitespace) instead of the hash.
- Deleting duplicates across versions while old versions are still being served.
sections.performance: `document_chunks(content_hash)` is indexed; all three aggregations scan the chunk table.
sections.interview: Shows that the candidate understands *why* duplicates exist before removing them.

questions.title: Retrieval hit rate at K and MRR per configuration
questions.secondary: first relevant rank per query, MRR, NULL judgments as not relevant
questions.tables: retrieval_evaluations(config_id, query_id, rank_position, is_relevant); retrieval_configs(config_id, config_name, top_k)
questions.columns: config_name, queries, hit_at_1_pct, hit_at_3_pct, hit_at_5_pct, mrr_at_5

sections.context: The offline evaluation set has 200 golden questions. For each configuration, the retrieved chunks were judged for relevance. Compare configurations on the same cut-off (k ≤ 5), since config 3 returns 10 results.
sections.problem: Per configuration, compute for k = 1, 3, 5 the share of queries with at least one relevant result in the top k (1 decimal), and MRR@5: the mean of 1 / (rank of the first relevant result), 0 if none in the top 5 (4 decimals). Treat unjudged results (`is_relevant IS NULL`) as not relevant. Sort by config name.
sections.expected: 3 rows; the reranking config should be best.
sections.edge_cases:
- Every query must be in the denominator, including those with no relevant result.
- `top_k` differs between configs; evaluating hit@10 would favour config 3 unfairly.
sections.hint1: Reduce to one row per (config, query) with the rank of the first relevant result.
sections.hint2: `MIN(CASE WHEN is_relevant = TRUE THEN rank_position END)`; NULL when none.
sections.hint3: hit@k = share of queries with `first_rank <= k`; MRR@5 = `AVG(CASE WHEN first_rank <= 5 THEN 1.0 / first_rank ELSE 0 END)`.
sections.solution:
WITH first_hit AS (
    SELECT config_id,
           query_id,
           MIN(CASE WHEN is_relevant = TRUE THEN rank_position END) AS first_rank
    FROM retrieval_evaluations
    GROUP BY config_id, query_id
)
SELECT c.config_name,
       COUNT(*)                                                                     AS queries,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN f.first_rank <= 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS hit_at_1_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN f.first_rank <= 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS hit_at_3_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN f.first_rank <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS hit_at_5_pct,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN f.first_rank <= 5 THEN 1.0 / f.first_rank ELSE 0 END), 4)   AS mrr_at_5
FROM first_hit f
JOIN retrieval_configs c ON c.config_id = f.config_id
GROUP BY c.config_name
ORDER BY c.config_name;
sections.assert: len(rows) == 3 and all(r[1] == '200' for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
**Definitions** (state them in every report):
- Hit@k (a.k.a. success@k): fraction of queries with ≥ 1 relevant result in the top k.
- MRR@k: mean over queries of 1/rank of the first relevant result within k, else 0.

The `first_hit` CTE reduces each query's ranked list to a single number. `first_rank <= k` is UNKNOWN for queries without a relevant result (NULL) and falls into ELSE 0, so they stay in the denominator. `is_relevant = TRUE` treats NULL judgments as not relevant, which is a conservative choice that should be stated.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** retrieval quality caps answer quality. If the right chunk is not in the context, the LLM cannot answer correctly. Hit@k with k = the number of chunks you actually put into the prompt is the most decision-relevant number.
sections.mistakes:
- Averaging over queries that have a relevant result only (inflates the metric).
- Comparing hit@10 of one config with hit@5 of another.
sections.performance: 4,000 rows; trivial.
sections.interview: Expect to define hit rate, MRR, and (as a follow-up) nDCG and recall@k.

questions.title: Retrieval quality by query type
questions.secondary: pivot configurations into columns, per-segment evaluation
questions.tables: retrieval_evaluations(config_id, query_id, rank_position, is_relevant); eval_queries(query_id, query_type)

sections.context: An aggregate improvement can hide a regression on one kind of question. Break hit@5 down by query type with the configurations side by side.
sections.problem: Return per `query_type`: number of queries and hit@5 (1 decimal) for configs 1, 2 and 3 as columns. Sort by query type.
sections.expected: One row per query type.
sections.edge_cases: - Each query appears once per configuration; the query count is per type, not per (type, config).
sections.hint1: Compute a 0/1 hit@5 flag per (config, query).
sections.hint2: Join query types and pivot with `AVG(CASE WHEN config_id = 1 THEN hit END)`.
sections.hint3: `COUNT(DISTINCT query_id)` for the number of queries.
sections.solution:
WITH hits AS (
    SELECT config_id,
           query_id,
           MAX(CASE WHEN is_relevant = TRUE AND rank_position <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS hit5
    FROM retrieval_evaluations
    GROUP BY config_id, query_id
)
SELECT q.query_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT h.query_id)                                            AS queries,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(CASE WHEN h.config_id = 1 THEN h.hit5 END), 1)       AS cfg1_hit5_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(CASE WHEN h.config_id = 2 THEN h.hit5 END), 1)       AS cfg2_hit5_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(CASE WHEN h.config_id = 3 THEN h.hit5 END), 1)       AS cfg3_hit5_pct
FROM hits h
JOIN eval_queries q ON q.query_id = h.query_id
GROUP BY q.query_type
ORDER BY q.query_type;
sections.explanation:
`AVG(CASE WHEN config_id = 1 THEN hit5 END)` averages the 0/1 flags of config 1 only (other rows yield NULL and are ignored), which gives a per-config hit rate in a single pass. This conditional-AVG pivot is shorter than three separate queries.

Small query types (a few dozen queries) have wide confidence intervals; treat differences of a few points as noise unless confirmed with paired tests.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** policy questions or troubleshooting queries often need different retrieval strategies (keyword vs semantic). Per-type evaluation guides routing and hybrid search tuning.
sections.mistakes:
- `COUNT(*)` as queries (counts each query three times).
- Averaging `is_relevant` over all ranks (that is precision@k, a different metric).
sections.performance: Small aggregation over 4,000 rows.
sections.interview: Shows evaluation rigour: slicing metrics to find hidden regressions.

questions.title: Answer acceptance rate from final user feedback
questions.primary: Calculating answer acceptance rates from feedback
questions.secondary: latest feedback per request, coverage vs acceptance, LEFT JOIN
questions.tables: llm_requests(request_id, feature, model_name, status, requested_at); ai_feedback(feedback_id, request_id, feedback_type, created_at)
questions.columns: feature, model_name, answers, with_feedback, feedback_coverage_pct, acceptance_pct, flagged

sections.context: Users can click thumbs up/down (and change their mind) or flag an answer. Product reports two numbers: how many answers receive feedback at all (coverage), and how many of those are finally accepted (thumbs up).
sections.problem: For successful requests in Q2 2025, return per `feature` and `model_name`: `answers`, `with_feedback`, `feedback_coverage_pct`, `acceptance_pct` (final feedback = thumbs_up among requests with feedback) and `flagged` (final feedback = flag). Percentages with 1 decimal. Keep groups with at least 50 answers. Sort by feature, model.
sections.expected: A few (feature, model) rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- A request can have several feedback rows; only the latest counts (`created_at`, then `feedback_id`).
- Acceptance is computed over requests **with** feedback; state the denominator.
sections.hint1: Reduce feedback to one final row per request with ROW_NUMBER.
sections.hint2: LEFT JOIN the final feedback to successful requests.
sections.hint3: `acceptance = SUM(thumbs_up) / NULLIF(COUNT(final feedback), 0)`.
sections.solution:
WITH final_fb AS (
    SELECT request_id, feedback_type
    FROM (
        SELECT request_id, feedback_type,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY request_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, feedback_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM ai_feedback
    ) x
    WHERE rn = 1
)
SELECT r.feature,
       r.model_name,
       COUNT(*)                                                                      AS answers,
       COUNT(f.request_id)                                                           AS with_feedback,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(f.request_id) / COUNT(*), 1)                              AS feedback_coverage_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN f.feedback_type = 'thumbs_up' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(COUNT(f.request_id), 0), 1)                                    AS acceptance_pct,
       SUM(CASE WHEN f.feedback_type = 'flag' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                     AS flagged
FROM llm_requests r
LEFT JOIN final_fb f ON f.request_id = r.request_id
WHERE r.status = 'success'
  AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
  AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY r.feature, r.model_name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50
ORDER BY r.feature, r.model_name;
sections.explanation:
Feedback is an event log, but the metric is per answer, so feedback must be reduced to one final verdict per request before joining. Joining raw feedback would count a changed-mind request twice (once up, once down).

Two denominators, two metrics: coverage (feedback / answers) tells you how representative acceptance is; acceptance (thumbs up / feedback) is the quality signal. Feedback is voluntary and biased toward strong reactions, so pair it with sampled human or LLM-judge evaluation.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** acceptance by model and feature is the main online quality metric for LLM features, and the outcome metric for prompt and model experiments.
sections.mistakes:
- Using all feedback rows.
- Computing acceptance over all answers (treating no feedback as rejection).
sections.performance: `ai_feedback(request_id)` index supports the join; the window sorts ~1,500 feedback rows.
sections.interview: Expect to discuss feedback bias and how to complement it (LLM-as-judge, human review samples).

questions.title: Compare prompt versions during their rollout overlap
questions.primary: Comparing prompt versions using evaluation outcomes
questions.secondary: fair comparison window from metadata, joins to prompts and feedback
questions.tables: prompts(prompt_version_id, prompt_name, version, created_at); llm_requests(request_id, prompt_version_id, status, output_tokens, requested_at); ai_feedback(feedback_id, request_id, feedback_type, created_at)
questions.columns: prompt_version, requests, success_pct, avg_output_tokens, feedback_requests, thumbs_up_pct

sections.context: New prompt versions are rolled out 50/50 against the previous version for 14 days. Comparing versions over their whole lifetimes would mix different months, models and traffic; the rollout window is the fair comparison.
sections.problem: For the latest `support_answer` version, define its rollout window as `[created_at, created_at + 14 days)`. For requests in that window served by the latest or the previous version, return per version: `requests`, `success_pct`, `avg_output_tokens` (successful requests, 1 decimal), `feedback_requests` (requests with final feedback) and `thumbs_up_pct` (1 decimal). Look the versions up from `prompts`, without hard-coded IDs. Sort by version.
sections.expected: 2 rows (the previous and the latest version).
sections.edge_cases: - The two arms must share the same time window; any other window confounds the prompt effect with time.
sections.hint1: Find the latest version and its predecessor from `prompts` (ROW_NUMBER by version DESC).
sections.hint2: Filter requests to the latest version's rollout window and the two prompt IDs.
sections.hint3: Join the final feedback per request (SQL-131) and aggregate per version.
sections.solution:
WITH versions AS (
    SELECT prompt_version_id, version, created_at,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY version DESC) AS recency
    FROM prompts
    WHERE prompt_name = 'support_answer'
),
win AS (
    SELECT created_at AS win_start, created_at + INTERVAL '14' DAY AS win_end
    FROM versions WHERE recency = 1
),
final_fb AS (
    SELECT request_id, feedback_type
    FROM (
        SELECT request_id, feedback_type,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY request_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, feedback_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM ai_feedback
    ) x
    WHERE rn = 1
)
SELECT CONCAT('support_answer v', v.version)                                         AS prompt_version,
       COUNT(*)                                                                      AS requests,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS success_pct,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN r.status = 'success' THEN r.output_tokens END), 1)         AS avg_output_tokens,
       COUNT(f.request_id)                                                           AS feedback_requests,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN f.feedback_type = 'thumbs_up' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(COUNT(f.request_id), 0), 1)                                    AS thumbs_up_pct
FROM llm_requests r
JOIN versions v ON v.prompt_version_id = r.prompt_version_id AND v.recency <= 2
CROSS JOIN win
LEFT JOIN final_fb f ON f.request_id = r.request_id
WHERE r.requested_at >= win.win_start
  AND r.requested_at <  win.win_end
GROUP BY v.version
ORDER BY prompt_version;
sections.explanation:
The comparison window is derived from the prompt registry itself (`created_at` of the latest version), so the query stays valid when the next version ships. Restricting both versions to the same 14-day rollout window makes the comparison an approximate A/B test: same period, same models and same traffic mix, with the prompt as the main difference.

Small feedback counts make thumbs-up differences noisy. Apply a two-proportion test (SQL-084/SQL-135) before declaring a winner, and look at cost (`avg_output_tokens`) as well as quality.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** prompt changes are deployments. Comparing them under controlled conditions is how prompt engineering becomes engineering.
sections.mistakes:
- Comparing lifetime averages of each version (different months, models and features).
- Hard-coding prompt IDs that differ between environments.
sections.performance: Small; requests are filtered by time first, and prompt lookups are primary-key joins.
sections.interview: Shows experimental thinking applied to LLM operations.

questions.title: Week-over-week cost regressions per model
questions.secondary: per-dialect week truncation, cost per successful request, LAG per model, alert threshold
questions.tables: llm_requests(model_name, requested_at, status, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_hit); llm_pricing(model_name, effective_from, effective_to, input_usd_per_1k, output_usd_per_1k)
questions.columns: week_start, model_name, successful_requests, cost_usd, cost_per_success, prev_cost_per_success, change_pct

sections.context: FinOps reviews weekly cost per **successful** request per model and wants alerts when it rises by more than 20% week-over-week (weeks start on Monday). Price changes, longer prompts and higher failure rates all show up in this metric.
sections.problem: For H1 2025, compute per ISO week and model: successful requests, total cost (all requests), cost per success (4 decimals), the previous week's value and the change in percent (1 decimal). Return only rows with `change_pct > 20` and at least 20 successful requests in both weeks. Sort by week, model.
sections.expected: About a dozen flagged (week, model) rows. Two stories stand out. The nimbus-pro incident week (2025-03-17) is flagged because failed calls still consume input tokens. The week of 2025-04-14 is flagged because the new top-10 retrieval config (from 2025-04-15) roughly doubled the context sent per request. The nimbus-pro price increase in May (+17%) stays below the 20% threshold. Cheap models (orbit-8b, atlas-mini) produce noisy percentage changes on tiny absolute costs; real alert rules add an absolute floor.
sections.edge_cases:
- Week truncation differs by engine. PostgreSQL `DATE_TRUNC('week', ...)` starts on Monday; MySQL needs `DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL WEEKDAY(d) DAY)`.
- Partial weeks at the start and end of the range produce noisy values.
sections.hint1: Aggregate cost and successes per (week, model) with the price range join.
sections.hint2: `LAG(cost_per_success) OVER (PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY week_start)` and the previous week's success count.
sections.hint3: Filter in an outer query on the change and on both weeks' volume.
sections.solution_pg:
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT CAST(DATE_TRUNC('week', r.requested_at) AS DATE) AS week_start,
           r.model_name,
           SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS successful_requests,
           SUM(CASE WHEN r.cache_hit THEN 0
                    ELSE r.input_tokens / 1000.0 * p.input_usd_per_1k
                       + COALESCE(r.output_tokens, 0) / 1000.0 * p.output_usd_per_1k END) AS cost_usd
    FROM llm_requests r
    JOIN llm_pricing p
      ON p.model_name = r.model_name
     AND CAST(r.requested_at AS DATE) BETWEEN p.effective_from AND COALESCE(p.effective_to, DATE '9999-12-31')
    WHERE r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-06 00:00:00'
      AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('week', r.requested_at), r.model_name
),
with_prev AS (
    SELECT week_start, model_name, successful_requests, cost_usd,
           cost_usd / NULLIF(successful_requests, 0) AS cps,
           LAG(cost_usd / NULLIF(successful_requests, 0)) OVER (PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY week_start) AS prev_cps,
           LAG(successful_requests) OVER (PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY week_start) AS prev_success
    FROM weekly
)
SELECT week_start, model_name, successful_requests,
       ROUND(cost_usd, 2)                        AS cost_usd,
       ROUND(cps, 4)                             AS cost_per_success,
       ROUND(prev_cps, 4)                        AS prev_cost_per_success,
       ROUND(100.0 * (cps / prev_cps - 1), 1)    AS change_pct
FROM with_prev
WHERE successful_requests >= 20
  AND prev_success >= 20
  AND cps > 1.2 * prev_cps
ORDER BY week_start, model_name;
sections.solution_mysql:
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT DATE_SUB(CAST(r.requested_at AS DATE), INTERVAL WEEKDAY(r.requested_at) DAY) AS week_start,
           r.model_name,
           SUM(CASE WHEN r.status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS successful_requests,
           SUM(CASE WHEN r.cache_hit THEN 0
                    ELSE r.input_tokens / 1000.0 * p.input_usd_per_1k
                       + COALESCE(r.output_tokens, 0) / 1000.0 * p.output_usd_per_1k END) AS cost_usd
    FROM llm_requests r
    JOIN llm_pricing p
      ON p.model_name = r.model_name
     AND CAST(r.requested_at AS DATE) BETWEEN p.effective_from AND COALESCE(p.effective_to, DATE '9999-12-31')
    WHERE r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-06 00:00:00'
      AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY DATE_SUB(CAST(r.requested_at AS DATE), INTERVAL WEEKDAY(r.requested_at) DAY), r.model_name
),
with_prev AS (
    SELECT week_start, model_name, successful_requests, cost_usd,
           cost_usd / NULLIF(successful_requests, 0) AS cps,
           LAG(cost_usd / NULLIF(successful_requests, 0)) OVER (PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY week_start) AS prev_cps,
           LAG(successful_requests) OVER (PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY week_start) AS prev_success
    FROM weekly
)
SELECT week_start, model_name, successful_requests,
       ROUND(cost_usd, 2)                        AS cost_usd,
       ROUND(cps, 4)                             AS cost_per_success,
       ROUND(prev_cps, 4)                        AS prev_cost_per_success,
       ROUND(100.0 * (cps / prev_cps - 1), 1)    AS change_pct
FROM with_prev
WHERE successful_requests >= 20
  AND prev_success >= 20
  AND cps > 1.2 * prev_cps
ORDER BY week_start, model_name;
sections.dialect_note: PostgreSQL `DATE_TRUNC('week', ts)` follows ISO weeks (Monday start). MySQL has no week truncation; `DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL WEEKDAY(d) DAY)` moves a date back to its Monday (`WEEKDAY`: Monday = 0). Avoid MySQL `WEEK()`/`YEARWEEK()` for this purpose: their week numbering depends on a mode argument and `default_week_format`.
sections.assert: any(r[0] == '2025-04-14' and r[1] == 'nimbus-pro' for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
1. Weekly aggregation with point-in-time prices (SQL-118).
2. Cost per **success** penalizes both price increases and failures (failed calls still cost input tokens).
3. LAG per model compares each week with the previous one; the volume guard avoids alerts on tiny weeks. The date range starts and ends on full weeks (Monday 2025-01-06 to Sunday 2025-06-29).

The DECIMAL arithmetic matches in both engines because all price columns are DECIMAL and token counts are integers divided by `1000.0`.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** LLM cost regressions are rarely caused by one event. A provider price change, a longer prompt, a retrieval config returning more chunks, or a failure spike all move this single metric, so it is the right first alarm.
sections.mistakes:
- Using MySQL `WEEK()` without a mode (weeks start on Sunday by default).
- Comparing total cost week over week, which is dominated by traffic growth.
sections.performance: One aggregation over H1 requests; the window runs over ~25 weeks x models.
sections.interview: Advanced FinOps-for-AI scenario combining point-in-time joins, period-over-period windows and alert design.

questions.title: Build a RAG ingestion manifest from document metadata
questions.primary: Preparing metadata records for a RAG ingestion pipeline
questions.secondary: JSON extraction per dialect, COALESCE defaults, estimated chunk counts
questions.tables: documents(document_id, doc_key, version_number, status, is_deleted, language, access_level, word_count, metadata, updated_at, last_indexed_at)
questions.columns: document_id, doc_key, version_number, language, access_level, product_area, tags, word_count, estimated_chunks, reason

sections.context: The ingestion pipeline (chunk → embed → upsert into the vector DB) consumes a manifest. Each record carries the metadata the retriever will filter on (language, access level, product area, tags).
sections.problem: For published, non-deleted versions that need (re)indexing (never indexed or edited after indexing), return the manifest: `document_id`, `doc_key`, `version_number`, `language` (`'unknown'` if NULL), `access_level`, `product_area` (from `metadata`, `'unknown'` if missing), `tags` (the JSON array as text, NULL if missing), `word_count`, `estimated_chunks` (= ceiling of word_count / 90) and `reason`. Sort by `document_id`.
sections.expected: One row per document version needing ingestion.
sections.edge_cases:
- `metadata` can be NULL: every extracted field must fall back to a default.
- JSON path syntax differs: PostgreSQL `metadata->>'product_area'`, MySQL `metadata->>'$.product_area'`.
sections.hint1: Filter like SQL-126.
sections.hint2: Extract text with `->>` (both engines support it, with different path syntax).
sections.hint3: `CEIL(word_count / 90.0)` for the estimate.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT document_id,
       doc_key,
       version_number,
       COALESCE(language, 'unknown')                         AS language,
       access_level,
       COALESCE(metadata->>'product_area', 'unknown')        AS product_area,
       metadata->>'tags'                                     AS tags,
       word_count,
       CEIL(word_count / 90.0)                               AS estimated_chunks,
       CASE WHEN last_indexed_at IS NULL THEN 'never_indexed' ELSE 'stale_index' END AS reason
FROM documents
WHERE status = 'published'
  AND is_deleted = FALSE
  AND (last_indexed_at IS NULL OR last_indexed_at < updated_at)
ORDER BY document_id;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT document_id,
       doc_key,
       version_number,
       COALESCE(language, 'unknown')                         AS language,
       access_level,
       COALESCE(metadata->>'$.product_area', 'unknown')      AS product_area,
       metadata->>'$.tags'                                   AS tags,
       word_count,
       CEIL(word_count / 90.0)                               AS estimated_chunks,
       CASE WHEN last_indexed_at IS NULL THEN 'never_indexed' ELSE 'stale_index' END AS reason
FROM documents
WHERE status = 'published'
  AND is_deleted = FALSE
  AND (last_indexed_at IS NULL OR last_indexed_at < updated_at)
ORDER BY document_id;
sections.dialect_note: Both engines have a `->>` operator that returns text, but the right-hand side differs: a key name in PostgreSQL (`'product_area'`) and a JSON path in MySQL (`'$.product_area'`). For an array, `->>` returns its JSON text (`["a", "b"]`) in both. PostgreSQL's `jsonb_array_elements_text` (or MySQL's `JSON_TABLE`, SQL-168) would unnest the tags into rows instead.
sections.explanation:
A manifest is a projection of the document table into the exact shape the ingestion job needs. Defaults (COALESCE) are applied in SQL so the pipeline never receives NULL filter attributes: a vector-DB filter on `language = 'en'` would silently skip documents with a NULL language.

`CEIL(word_count / 90.0)` mirrors the chunker's sizing (≈ 90 words per chunk) and lets the pipeline estimate embedding cost before running.

**Why it matters for AI apps:** metadata quality decides whether access control and filtered retrieval work. An `internal` document without its access level is a data-leak risk.
sections.mistakes:
- Passing NULL metadata straight through.
- Using MySQL path syntax in PostgreSQL or vice versa.
sections.performance: Same filter as SQL-126; JSON extraction is per-row CPU.
sections.interview: Practical JSON + data-contract question for AI data pipelines.

questions.title: Did citations improve answer acceptance? (AI experiment readout)
questions.secondary: exposure filter, final feedback per request, two-proportion z-test
questions.tables: experiments(experiment_id, experiment_name); experiment_assignments(experiment_id, user_id, variant, assigned_at); llm_requests(request_id, user_id, feature, status, requested_at); ai_feedback(feedback_id, request_id, feedback_type, created_at)
questions.columns: variant, users, answers, rated_answers, thumbs_up, thumbs_up_pct, z_vs_control

sections.context: `rag_answer_citations` shows source citations under support-bot answers for the treatment group. The pre-registered metric is the thumbs-up rate of rated support-bot answers given **after** the user's assignment.
sections.problem: Per variant, return `users` (assigned), `answers` (successful support-bot requests of assigned users after their `assigned_at`), `rated_answers` (with final feedback), `thumbs_up`, `thumbs_up_pct` (1 decimal) and `z_vs_control` (pooled two-proportion z over rated answers, 2 decimals; NULL for control). Sort by variant.
sections.expected: 2 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- Answers before assignment are not exposed to the treatment.
- The unit of analysis is the rated answer, but answers from the same user are correlated, so the naive z overstates significance. Say so.
sections.hint1: Join assignments to the user's support-bot requests with `requested_at >= assigned_at`.
sections.hint2: Attach the final feedback per request, then aggregate per variant.
sections.hint3: Attach control's counts with a one-row CTE and compute z like SQL-084.
sections.solution:
WITH exp AS (
    SELECT a.user_id, a.variant, a.assigned_at
    FROM experiment_assignments a
    JOIN experiments x ON x.experiment_id = a.experiment_id
    WHERE x.experiment_name = 'rag_answer_citations'
),
final_fb AS (
    SELECT request_id, feedback_type
    FROM (
        SELECT request_id, feedback_type,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY request_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, feedback_id DESC) AS rn
        FROM ai_feedback
    ) x
    WHERE rn = 1
),
answers AS (
    SELECT e.variant, r.request_id, f.feedback_type
    FROM exp e
    JOIN llm_requests r ON r.user_id = e.user_id
                       AND r.feature = 'support_bot'
                       AND r.status = 'success'
                       AND r.requested_at >= e.assigned_at
    LEFT JOIN final_fb f ON f.request_id = r.request_id
),
users_per_variant AS (
    SELECT variant, COUNT(*) AS users
    FROM exp
    GROUP BY variant
),
answer_stats AS (
    SELECT variant,
           COUNT(*)                                               AS answers,
           COUNT(feedback_type)                                   AS rated,
           SUM(CASE WHEN feedback_type = 'thumbs_up' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS ups
    FROM answers
    GROUP BY variant
),
agg AS (
    SELECT u.variant, u.users,
           COALESCE(s.answers, 0) AS answers,
           COALESCE(s.rated, 0)   AS rated,
           COALESCE(s.ups, 0)     AS ups
    FROM users_per_variant u
    LEFT JOIN answer_stats s ON s.variant = u.variant
),
ctrl AS (
    SELECT rated AS n_c, ups AS x_c FROM agg WHERE variant = 'control'
)
SELECT g.variant,
       g.users,
       g.answers,
       g.rated AS rated_answers,
       g.ups   AS thumbs_up,
       ROUND(100.0 * g.ups / NULLIF(g.rated, 0), 1) AS thumbs_up_pct,
       CASE WHEN g.variant <> 'control' THEN
            ROUND((1.0 * g.ups / g.rated - 1.0 * c.x_c / c.n_c)
                  / SQRT((1.0 * (g.ups + c.x_c) / (g.rated + c.n_c))
                         * (1 - 1.0 * (g.ups + c.x_c) / (g.rated + c.n_c))
                         * (1.0 / g.rated + 1.0 / c.n_c)), 2) END AS z_vs_control
FROM agg g
CROSS JOIN ctrl c
ORDER BY g.variant;
sections.explanation:
1. **Exposure**: only answers given after the user's assignment can have been affected.
2. **Outcome**: the final feedback verdict per answer (SQL-131).
3. **Readout**: thumbs-up rate among rated answers per variant, and a pooled z statistic versus control.

User counts and answer counts live at different grains (assigned user vs answer), so they are aggregated in two separate CTEs and joined per variant. Joining answers to users before counting users would require `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` everywhere. `COUNT(feedback_type)` counts answers with a final verdict, because unrated answers carry NULL from the LEFT JOIN.

Statistical caveats that a strong readout states:
- **Unit mismatch**: randomization was by *user*, the metric is per *answer*. Heavy users contribute many correlated answers, so the naive z is too optimistic. Use a user-level metric, cluster-robust standard errors or the delta method.
- Feedback is voluntary; check that the feedback *rate* did not differ between arms (it could itself be affected by citations).

**Why it matters for AI apps:** UI changes around LLM answers (citations, confidence hints) are tested like any product change, but the per-answer metrics make the unit-of-analysis trap very common.
sections.mistakes:
- Counting answers before assignment.
- Using raw feedback rows (changed minds double count).
sections.performance: Small; the join from assignments to requests uses `llm_requests(user_id)`.
sections.interview: Advanced: combining experiment design knowledge with LLM feedback data and identifying the unit-of-analysis problem.

questions.title: UNION versus UNION ALL for a contact list
questions.secondary: duplicate elimination, normalization before set operations
questions.tables: users(user_id, email, role, status); support_tickets(user_id, priority, created_at)

sections.context: Customer success e-mails two groups about a new escalation process: active admins, and every user who opened an urgent ticket in H1 2025. Each person should receive one e-mail.
sections.problem: Build both lists as normalized e-mails (`LOWER(TRIM(email))`). Return one row with `union_all_rows` (rows from UNION ALL of the two lists) and `union_rows` (rows from UNION).
sections.expected: One row; `union_rows` is smaller.
sections.edge_cases:
- A person can appear in both lists and several times in the ticket list (several urgent tickets).
- **Normalize before UNION.** MySQL's case-insensitive collation would treat `Anna@x.com` and `anna@x.com` as duplicates, but PostgreSQL would not, so the raw UNION gives different counts on the two engines.
sections.hint1: UNION ALL concatenates the results; UNION also removes duplicate rows.
sections.hint2: Count each variant in a derived table.
sections.hint3: `SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (... UNION ALL ...) a) AS union_all_rows, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (... UNION ...) b) AS union_rows`.
sections.solution:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
       SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email FROM users WHERE role = 'admin' AND status = 'active'
       UNION ALL
       SELECT LOWER(TRIM(u.email)) FROM support_tickets t JOIN users u ON u.user_id = t.user_id
       WHERE t.priority = 'urgent'
         AND t.created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
         AND t.created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
   ) a) AS union_all_rows,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
       SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email FROM users WHERE role = 'admin' AND status = 'active'
       UNION
       SELECT LOWER(TRIM(u.email)) FROM support_tickets t JOIN users u ON u.user_id = t.user_id
       WHERE t.priority = 'urgent'
         AND t.created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
         AND t.created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
   ) b) AS union_rows;
sections.explanation:
- `UNION ALL` keeps every row, so it is cheap: no sort or hash.
- `UNION` removes duplicate rows across **and within** both inputs, which costs a sort or hash step.

Use UNION when you need a set, and UNION ALL when duplicates are meaningful or impossible. Duplicate detection depends on the column collation. Normalizing explicitly (`LOWER(TRIM(...))`) makes the result identical on PostgreSQL and MySQL.

Column names come from the first SELECT; later SELECTs only need compatible types and the same number of columns.
sections.mistakes:
- Using UNION "to be safe" in pipelines where duplicates matter (e.g. event logs).
- Relying on engine collation for deduplication.
sections.performance: UNION adds a deduplication step over all rows; UNION ALL streams.
sections.interview: Classic question; mentioning cost and collation shows depth.

questions.title: Users who use AI features and buy (INTERSECT)
questions.secondary: MySQL version support, EXISTS alternative, segment rollup
questions.tables: llm_requests(user_id, status, requested_at); orders(user_id, status, order_ts); users(user_id, org_id); organizations(org_id, segment)

sections.context: Product marketing wants to know how many users in each segment both used an AI feature successfully and completed a purchase in Q2 2025.
sections.problem: Compute the set of users with a successful LLM request in Q2 2025, INTERSECT the set with a completed order in Q2 2025, and count the result per customer segment. Return `segment`, `ai_buyers`, sorted by segment.
sections.expected: 3 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- **INTERSECT and EXCEPT require MySQL 8.0.31 or later.** On older MySQL versions use EXISTS (see the alternative).
- `llm_requests.user_id` can be NULL (system calls); NULL never matches a real user, but exclude it explicitly.
sections.hint1: Both inputs of INTERSECT must return the same columns (here just `user_id`).
sections.hint2: Wrap the INTERSECT in a derived table and join it to users and organizations.
sections.hint3: INTERSECT returns distinct rows, so each user is counted once.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.segment,
       COUNT(*) AS ai_buyers
FROM (
    SELECT user_id FROM llm_requests
    WHERE status = 'success' AND user_id IS NOT NULL
      AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
      AND requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    INTERSECT
    SELECT user_id FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
      AND order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
      AND order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
) both_sets
JOIN users u         ON u.user_id = both_sets.user_id
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id
GROUP BY o.segment
ORDER BY o.segment;
sections.alternative:
SELECT o.segment,
       COUNT(*) AS ai_buyers
FROM users u
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM llm_requests r
              WHERE r.user_id = u.user_id AND r.status = 'success'
                AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                AND r.requested_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders x
              WHERE x.user_id = u.user_id AND x.status = 'completed'
                AND x.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                AND x.order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
GROUP BY o.segment
ORDER BY o.segment;
sections.alternative_note: Two EXISTS semi-joins give the same set, work on every MySQL 8.0 version, and make it easy to add more columns. INTERSECT is more declarative when you only compare keys.
sections.explanation:
`A INTERSECT B` returns the distinct rows present in both inputs. It expresses "users in both groups" directly and removes duplicates automatically, because a user with ten requests still appears once.

Set operations compare whole rows, so they need matching column lists. When you need columns from only one side, join afterwards (as here) or use EXISTS.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining requests to orders on `user_id` and counting rows, which multiplies requests by orders.
- Using INTERSECT on MySQL 8.0.30 or older (syntax error).
sections.performance: Both forms read each table once; EXISTS can stop early per user.
sections.interview: Shows command of set operators and their portability limits.

questions.title: Paying but inactive customers (EXCEPT)
questions.secondary: set difference of keys, join back for attributes, churn-risk list
questions.tables: subscriptions(org_id, ended_at, mrr); users(user_id, org_id); sessions(user_id, started_at); organizations(org_id, org_name, segment)

sections.context: An organization that pays (open subscription) but has nobody using the product is a churn risk. Customer success wants that list.
sections.problem: Compute organizations with an open subscription EXCEPT organizations with at least one session in the 30 days before 2025-07-01. Return `org_id`, `org_name`, `segment` and `open_mrr` (sum of open subscriptions' MRR). Sort by `open_mrr` descending, then `org_id`.
sections.expected: A list of organizations.
sections.edge_cases: - EXCEPT (MySQL 8.0.31+) returns distinct rows of the first input that are not in the second.
sections.hint1: First input: `SELECT org_id FROM subscriptions WHERE ended_at IS NULL`.
sections.hint2: Second input: org IDs of users with sessions in the window (join sessions → users).
sections.hint3: Join the difference back to organizations and the open subscriptions for the attributes.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.org_id,
       o.org_name,
       o.segment,
       SUM(s.mrr) AS open_mrr
FROM (
    SELECT org_id FROM subscriptions WHERE ended_at IS NULL
    EXCEPT
    SELECT u.org_id
    FROM sessions se
    JOIN users u ON u.user_id = se.user_id
    WHERE se.started_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00' - INTERVAL '30' DAY
      AND se.started_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
) inactive
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = inactive.org_id
JOIN subscriptions s ON s.org_id = inactive.org_id AND s.ended_at IS NULL
GROUP BY o.org_id, o.org_name, o.segment
ORDER BY open_mrr DESC, o.org_id;
sections.alternative:
SELECT o.org_id,
       o.org_name,
       o.segment,
       SUM(s.mrr) AS open_mrr
FROM organizations o
JOIN subscriptions s ON s.org_id = o.org_id AND s.ended_at IS NULL
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM sessions se
                  JOIN users u ON u.user_id = se.user_id
                  WHERE u.org_id = o.org_id
                    AND se.started_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00' - INTERVAL '30' DAY
                    AND se.started_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
GROUP BY o.org_id, o.org_name, o.segment
ORDER BY open_mrr DESC, o.org_id;
sections.alternative_note: `NOT EXISTS` is the anti-join equivalent of EXCEPT on keys. It works on all MySQL 8.0 versions and is NULL-safe. EXCEPT also treats NULLs as equal, unlike NOT IN.
sections.explanation:
`A EXCEPT B` keeps distinct rows of A that do not appear in B, a set difference. On a single key column it is equivalent to an anti-join. Unlike NOT IN, EXCEPT compares NULLs as "not distinct", so a NULL in B does not wipe out the result.

The difference contains only keys; joining back to organizations and subscriptions adds the attributes and MRR. Organizations with two open subscriptions (the billing bug) sum both, matching what they are actually billed.
sections.mistakes:
- `org_id NOT IN (subquery)` where the subquery could return NULL.
- Using `ended_at > '2025-07-01'` for "open"; open periods have NULL `ended_at`.
sections.performance: EXCEPT deduplicates both inputs (hash or sort); the NOT EXISTS version probes `users(org_id)` and `sessions(user_id, started_at)`.
sections.interview: Set-difference questions often come with "how else could you write it?".

questions.title: Reconcile order headers with order lines (symmetric difference)
questions.secondary: (A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (B EXCEPT A), labelling the side
questions.tables: orders(order_id, order_total); order_items(order_id, quantity, unit_price, discount_amount)

sections.context: The finance warehouse has two sources for an order's amount: the header (`orders.order_total`) and the sum of its lines. A reconciliation lists every (order, amount) pair present in one source but not in the other.
sections.problem: Return the symmetric difference of the two sets of `(order_id, amount)`: rows only in the header set labelled `'header_only'`, and rows only in the line set labelled `'lines_only'`. Sort by `order_id`, then `side`.
sections.expected: Two rows per mismatching order (about 2% of orders).
sections.edge_cases:
- Set operators compare values, not formatting: `10.0` and `10.00` are equal DECIMALs.
- An order without lines would appear only on the header side.
sections.hint1: Build both sets with the same two columns.
sections.hint2: `(headers EXCEPT lines)` gives header-only rows; swap for the other side.
sections.hint3: Label each side with a constant column and UNION ALL them.
sections.solution:
SELECT 'header_only' AS side, order_id, amount
FROM (
    SELECT order_id, order_total AS amount FROM orders
    EXCEPT
    SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price - discount_amount) FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
) h
UNION ALL
SELECT 'lines_only', order_id, amount
FROM (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price - discount_amount) AS amount FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
    EXCEPT
    SELECT order_id, order_total FROM orders
) l
ORDER BY order_id, side;
sections.explanation:
A symmetric difference is the standard "diff" between two datasets: everything that is not in both. Because the comparison covers the whole row `(order_id, amount)`, an order with a wrong total shows up twice, once with each amount, which makes the mismatch obvious.

This pattern is how pipeline outputs are regression-tested: run the old and the new version and diff the outputs. An empty result means identical datasets.
sections.mistakes:
- Comparing only `order_id`, which misses value differences.
- Using UNION instead of UNION ALL for the final step (harmless here, but it hides duplicate diffs in other cases).
sections.performance: Each EXCEPT needs a hash or sort of both inputs; fine for thousands of rows.
sections.interview: "How would you verify that a refactored pipeline produces the same output?" A symmetric diff is the expected answer.

questions.title: Orders billed to an organization other than the buyer's
questions.secondary: self-referencing hierarchy, CASE classification
questions.tables: orders(order_id, user_id, org_id, order_ts); users(user_id, org_id); organizations(org_id, parent_org_id)

sections.context: `orders.org_id` is copied from the buyer's organization at checkout. A few orders disagree with the user's current organization. Some are legitimate (billed to the parent company), others are bugs.
sections.problem: List orders whose `org_id` differs from the purchasing user's `org_id`, with `relationship`: `'billed_to_parent'` when the order's org is the parent of the user's org, `'billed_to_subsidiary'` when it is a child, else `'unrelated'`. Sort by `order_id`.
sections.expected: About ten orders.
sections.edge_cases: - `parent_org_id` is NULL for top-level organizations; comparisons with NULL fall through to `'unrelated'`.
sections.hint1: Join orders to users and compare the two `org_id`s.
sections.hint2: Join both organizations to read their parents.
sections.hint3: CASE on `uo.parent_org_id = o.org_id` and `oo.parent_org_id = u.org_id`.
sections.solution:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.order_ts,
       o.org_id AS order_org_id,
       u.org_id AS user_org_id,
       CASE WHEN uo.parent_org_id = o.org_id THEN 'billed_to_parent'
            WHEN oo.parent_org_id = u.org_id THEN 'billed_to_subsidiary'
            ELSE 'unrelated' END AS relationship
FROM orders o
JOIN users u          ON u.user_id = o.user_id
JOIN organizations uo ON uo.org_id = u.org_id
JOIN organizations oo ON oo.org_id = o.org_id
WHERE o.org_id <> u.org_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
sections.explanation:
Denormalized copies (like `orders.org_id`) speed up queries but can drift from their source. The check compares the copy with the source, and the hierarchy explains part of the difference. The two joins to `organizations` (aliases `uo` and `oo`) are a self-referencing lookup: each organization's parent is read from the same table.

`unrelated` rows are data bugs to fix at the source. Parent billing may be a valid business process that should be documented, for example as a separate `billing_org_id` column.
sections.mistakes:
- Treating every mismatch as an error.
- Comparing with `!=`. It works in both engines, but `<>` is the SQL standard operator.
sections.performance: Primary-key joins only.
sections.interview: Shows judgment: distinguishing legitimate business cases from data bugs.

questions.title: A data-quality scorecard in one query
questions.primary: Data-quality checks combined with UNION ALL
questions.secondary: anti-joins, self-joins on intervals, duplicate detection, pass/fail status
questions.tables: users(email); orders(order_id, user_id, org_id, status, order_total); order_items(order_id, quantity, unit_price, discount_amount); payments(order_id); subscriptions(subscription_id, org_id, started_at, ended_at); events(user_id, session_id, event_name, event_ts); support_tickets(first_response_at, resolved_at)

sections.context: Before the nightly ML training job, a data-quality gate runs a fixed set of checks. Each check returns the number of failing rows; any non-zero count is a FAIL.
sections.problem:
Return one row per check with `check_name`, `failing_rows` and `status` (`'PASS'`/`'FAIL'`):
1. `email_whitespace`: users whose e-mail has leading/trailing spaces
2. `duplicate_person_accounts`: accounts beyond the first per normalized e-mail
3. `order_total_mismatch`: orders whose total differs from their lines by more than 0.005
4. `completed_without_payment`
5. `order_org_mismatch`: orders whose `org_id` differs from the user's
6. `overlapping_subscriptions`: pairs of overlapping periods of the same org
7. `duplicate_client_events`: extra copies of (user, session, name, timestamp)
8. `response_after_resolution`: tickets with `first_response_at > resolved_at`
Sort by `check_name`.
sections.expected: 8 rows; most checks fail on this deliberately imperfect dataset, and some pass.
sections.edge_cases:
- Each check must return exactly one number, even when nothing fails (COUNT returns 0).
- Overlap between open periods: treat `ended_at IS NULL` as "far future".
sections.hint1: Write each check as a `SELECT 'name' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS failing_rows FROM ...`.
sections.hint2: Stack them with UNION ALL inside a derived table.
sections.hint3: Add `CASE WHEN failing_rows = 0 THEN 'PASS' ELSE 'FAIL' END` in the outer query.
sections.solution:
SELECT check_name,
       failing_rows,
       CASE WHEN failing_rows = 0 THEN 'PASS' ELSE 'FAIL' END AS status
FROM (
    SELECT 'email_whitespace' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS failing_rows
    FROM users WHERE email <> TRIM(email)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'duplicate_person_accounts', COALESCE(SUM(n - 1), 0)
    FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM users GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) d
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'order_total_mismatch', COUNT(*)
    FROM orders o
    JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price - discount_amount) AS s
          FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE ABS(o.order_total - i.s) > 0.005
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'completed_without_payment', COUNT(*)
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.order_id = o.order_id)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'order_org_mismatch', COUNT(*)
    FROM orders o JOIN users u ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.org_id <> u.org_id
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'overlapping_subscriptions', COUNT(*)
    FROM subscriptions a
    JOIN subscriptions b
      ON b.org_id = a.org_id
     AND a.subscription_id < b.subscription_id
     AND a.started_at < COALESCE(b.ended_at, TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31 00:00:00')
     AND b.started_at < COALESCE(a.ended_at, TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31 00:00:00')
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'duplicate_client_events', COALESCE(SUM(n - 1), 0)
    FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM events
          WHERE session_id IS NOT NULL
          GROUP BY user_id, session_id, event_name, event_ts
          HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) e
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'response_after_resolution', COUNT(*)
    FROM support_tickets
    WHERE first_response_at > resolved_at
) checks
ORDER BY check_name;
sections.assert:
len(rows) == 8
any(r[2] == 'PASS' for r in rows) and any(r[2] == 'FAIL' for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
Each branch is an independent check reduced to a single count; UNION ALL stacks them into a report with a fixed schema `(check_name, failing_rows)`. The outer query turns counts into a status. New checks are added by appending a branch.

Notable techniques:
- **Interval overlap**: two periods overlap iff `a.start < b.end AND b.start < a.end`. Open periods use a far-future sentinel via COALESCE. `a.subscription_id < b.subscription_id` counts each pair once.
- **Duplicates beyond the first**: `SUM(n − 1)` over groups with `n > 1`; COALESCE turns "no duplicate groups" into 0.
- `email <> TRIM(email)` is reliable in both engines because the default MySQL 8 collation is NO PAD; case problems need a binary comparison (SQL-009).

Data-quality gates like this belong *before* training. A failing gate should block the training job or at least be recorded with the model version.
sections.mistakes:
- Checks that return no row instead of 0 (e.g. grouped queries without an outer aggregate), which silently drop out of the report.
- The interval test `a.start BETWEEN b.start AND b.end`, which misses periods that fully contain the other.
sections.performance: Eight independent scans; acceptable for a nightly gate. At scale, run checks in parallel or on partitions.
sections.interview: Data-quality tests are central to MLE and analytics-engineering roles; a clean, extensible pattern is what interviewers want to see.

questions.title: Person-level clusters of duplicate accounts
questions.secondary: canonical ID per cluster, string aggregation per dialect (STRING_AGG vs GROUP_CONCAT)

sections.context: Pairs of duplicates (SQL-044) are not enough for a merge job: it needs **clusters**, one row per real person with all their account IDs, a canonical ID (the oldest account) and merged activity.
sections.problem: For every normalized e-mail with more than one account, return `canonical_user_id` (smallest user ID), `normalized_email`, `accounts`, `account_ids` (comma-separated, ascending) and `completed_orders` across all accounts. Sort by `canonical_user_id`.
sections.expected: About two dozen clusters.
sections.edge_cases:
- String aggregation is engine-specific: PostgreSQL `STRING_AGG(text, sep ORDER BY ...)`, MySQL `GROUP_CONCAT(expr ORDER BY ... SEPARATOR sep)`.
- Joining orders before aggregating account IDs would repeat IDs (fan-out); aggregate orders per user first.
sections.hint1: Group users by `LOWER(TRIM(email))` with `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
sections.hint2: LEFT JOIN a per-user completed-order count so accounts without orders still appear.
sections.hint3: PostgreSQL: `STRING_AGG(CAST(u.user_id AS TEXT), ',' ORDER BY u.user_id)`; MySQL: `GROUP_CONCAT(u.user_id ORDER BY u.user_id SEPARATOR ',')`.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT MIN(u.user_id)                                              AS canonical_user_id,
       LOWER(TRIM(u.email))                                        AS normalized_email,
