       COUNT(*)                                                    AS accounts,
       STRING_AGG(CAST(u.user_id AS TEXT), ',' ORDER BY u.user_id) AS account_ids,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.n), 0)                                       AS completed_orders
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY user_id) o
       ON o.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(u.email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY canonical_user_id;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT MIN(u.user_id)                                              AS canonical_user_id,
       LOWER(TRIM(u.email))                                        AS normalized_email,
       COUNT(*)                                                    AS accounts,
       GROUP_CONCAT(u.user_id ORDER BY u.user_id SEPARATOR ',')    AS account_ids,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.n), 0)                                       AS completed_orders
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY user_id) o
       ON o.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(u.email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY canonical_user_id;
sections.dialect_note: `STRING_AGG(expr, delimiter ORDER BY ...)` is the SQL-standard-style aggregate in PostgreSQL; its argument must be text. MySQL's `GROUP_CONCAT(expr ORDER BY ... SEPARATOR ...)` converts automatically, but **truncates silently at `group_concat_max_len` (default 1024 bytes)**. Raise it (`SET SESSION group_concat_max_len = 100000`) for long lists. In MySQL's default collation, grouping by `LOWER(TRIM(email))` behaves the same as in PostgreSQL because the expression is already normalized.
sections.explanation:
Grouping by the normalized key forms clusters; HAVING keeps real duplicates. The canonical ID (MIN) is deterministic and stable: the oldest account survives a merge. Orders are pre-aggregated per user so that the LEFT JOIN is one-to-one and cannot duplicate account IDs in the string.

A merge job would use this table to repoint foreign keys (orders, tickets, events) from duplicate accounts to the canonical one. ML pipelines use the same mapping so that one person is never in train and test at the same time.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining raw orders, which repeats account IDs in `account_ids` and inflates counts.
- Forgetting `group_concat_max_len` on large clusters.
sections.performance: Grouping by an expression requires computing it per row; a generated normalized column with an index helps (SQL-163).
sections.interview: Entity resolution is common in DS/MLE interviews; the dialect-specific string aggregation is a frequent portability question.

questions.title: Validate the evaluation set against the document corpus
questions.primary: Referential integrity without a foreign key
questions.secondary: soft references, servability rules, status summary
questions.tables: eval_queries(query_id, gold_doc_key); documents(document_id, doc_key, status, is_deleted); document_chunks(document_id, embedding_model)

sections.context: `eval_queries.gold_doc_key` refers to `documents.doc_key`, but there is no foreign key because `doc_key` is not unique (one row per version). Before trusting retrieval metrics, check that every golden question can actually be answered from the servable index.
sections.problem: Classify every evaluation query as `'unknown_doc_key'` (no document with that key), `'no_servable_chunks'` (the key exists but no published, non-deleted version has embedded chunks) or `'ok'`. Return `status`, `queries`, sorted by status.
sections.expected: 1-3 rows; most queries are `ok`.
sections.edge_cases: - A gold document whose only indexed version is archived cannot be retrieved correctly, so the query measures nothing.
sections.hint1: Two EXISTS tests per query, from strictest to loosest.
sections.hint2: Servable: EXISTS a chunk with `embedding_model IS NOT NULL` whose document has the key, `status = 'published'` and `is_deleted = FALSE`.
sections.hint3: CASE WHEN NOT EXISTS (key) THEN ... WHEN NOT EXISTS (servable) THEN ... ELSE 'ok' END, then group.
sections.solution:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS queries
FROM (
    SELECT q.query_id,
           CASE WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM documents d WHERE d.doc_key = q.gold_doc_key)
                     THEN 'unknown_doc_key'
                WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                                 FROM documents d
                                 JOIN document_chunks c ON c.document_id = d.document_id
                                 WHERE d.doc_key = q.gold_doc_key
                                   AND d.status = 'published'
                                   AND d.is_deleted = FALSE
                                   AND c.embedding_model IS NOT NULL)
                     THEN 'no_servable_chunks'
                ELSE 'ok' END AS status
    FROM eval_queries q
) s
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;
sections.explanation:
Foreign keys enforce references between unique keys. When the reference is to a non-unique attribute (here a version family), integrity has to be checked by queries. The CASE evaluates the conditions in order, so each query gets the most specific problem.

Golden sets decay as documents are deleted or re-structured. Evaluation pipelines should run this check first and exclude (or fix) unanswerable questions, otherwise retrieval metrics silently drop for reasons unrelated to the retriever.
sections.mistakes:
- Joining eval queries to documents with an INNER JOIN, which hides unknown keys.
- Considering any version servable, including archived and draft ones.
sections.performance: Two indexed EXISTS probes per query (`documents(doc_key, version_number)` unique index, `document_chunks(document_id, ...)`).
sections.interview: Shows that the candidate validates evaluation data, not just models.

questions.title: Create a feature registry table with constraints
questions.secondary: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, NOT NULL, DEFAULT, multi-row INSERT

sections.context: The ML platform documents every feature in a registry table. The table must reject bad metadata at write time instead of relying on code reviews. All workbook DDL exercises create `sb_` sandbox tables, so the main dataset stays untouched.
sections.problem: Create `sb_feature_registry` with: `feature_name` (primary key), `entity_type` (only `'user'` or `'org'`), `value_type` (only `'int'`, `'float'`, `'bool'`), `owner_team` (required), `first_model_version_id` (optional, must reference `model_versions`) and `is_active` (required, default TRUE). Insert the seven `entity_features` features, then return per `entity_type` the number of features and of active features.
sections.expected: 2 rows (org, user).
sections.edge_cases:
- **MySQL ignores inline `REFERENCES` clauses on a column definition**; only table-level `FOREIGN KEY` constraints are enforced. Declare foreign keys at table level for portability.
- MySQL enforces CHECK constraints only from 8.0.16; earlier versions parse and ignore them.
sections.hint1: List columns with types and NOT NULL first, then add named table-level constraints.
sections.hint2: `CONSTRAINT ck_... CHECK (entity_type IN ('user', 'org'))`, `CONSTRAINT fk_... FOREIGN KEY (...) REFERENCES model_versions (model_version_id)`.
sections.hint3: Omit `is_active` in the INSERT column list to use the default.
sections.solution:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sb_feature_registry;
CREATE TABLE sb_feature_registry (
    feature_name            VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    entity_type             VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    value_type              VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    owner_team              VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    first_model_version_id  INT,
    is_active               BOOLEAN     NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    CONSTRAINT pk_sb_feature_registry PRIMARY KEY (feature_name),
    CONSTRAINT ck_sb_fr_entity_type   CHECK (entity_type IN ('user', 'org')),
    CONSTRAINT ck_sb_fr_value_type    CHECK (value_type IN ('int', 'float', 'bool')),
    CONSTRAINT fk_sb_fr_model_version FOREIGN KEY (first_model_version_id)
        REFERENCES model_versions (model_version_id)
);
INSERT INTO sb_feature_registry (feature_name, entity_type, value_type, owner_team, first_model_version_id) VALUES
    ('sessions_7d',             'user', 'int',   'growth-data',  1),
    ('sessions_28d',            'user', 'int',   'growth-data',  1),
    ('events_28d',              'user', 'int',   'growth-data',  2),
    ('days_since_last_session', 'user', 'int',   'growth-data',  1),
    ('avg_session_minutes',     'user', 'float', 'growth-data',  3),
    ('open_tickets',            'org',  'int',   'support-data', 2),
    ('seats_used_pct',          'org',  'float', 'billing-data', 3);
sections.verify:
SELECT entity_type,
       COUNT(*)                                       AS features,
       SUM(CASE WHEN is_active THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)     AS active_features
FROM sb_feature_registry
GROUP BY entity_type
ORDER BY entity_type;
sections.explanation:
Constraints move data-quality rules into the database, where they cannot be bypassed:
- **PRIMARY KEY**: unique and not NULL; one row per feature.
- **CHECK**: restricts values. An INSERT with `entity_type = 'account'` fails with a constraint violation.
- **FOREIGN KEY**: a referenced model version must exist. Inserting `first_model_version_id = 99` fails.
- **NOT NULL / DEFAULT**: required columns and sensible defaults.

Naming constraints (`CONSTRAINT ck_...`) produces readable error messages and lets you drop or alter them later. In MySQL, CHECK and FOREIGN KEY names must be unique within the schema, hence the `sb_fr` prefix.

To see a violation, try `INSERT INTO sb_feature_registry (feature_name, entity_type, value_type, owner_team) VALUES ('x', 'account', 'int', 't');`. Both engines reject it.
sections.mistakes:
- `first_model_version_id INT REFERENCES model_versions(model_version_id)` inline: enforced by PostgreSQL, silently ignored by MySQL.
- Encoding allowed values only in application code.
sections.performance: Constraints add a small cost on writes (index lookups for FKs and unique keys) and protect every read.
sections.interview: DDL questions test whether a candidate designs for data quality, not just storage.

questions.title: Materialize a monthly revenue summary with INSERT ... SELECT
questions.secondary: summary tables, per-dialect month truncation, idempotent reloads

sections.context: Dashboards query a small summary table instead of scanning orders every time. The job recreates the summary from the source each night.
sections.problem: Create `sb_monthly_revenue(month_start DATE PRIMARY KEY, completed_orders INT, revenue DECIMAL(14,2))` and fill it with INSERT ... SELECT for 2024-01 to 2025-06 from completed orders. Verify with one row: number of months, total revenue, first and last month.
sections.expected: One row: 18 months.
sections.edge_cases: - Re-running the job must not create duplicates: drop/recreate (as here), TRUNCATE first, or use an upsert (SQL-149).
sections.hint1: CREATE TABLE first, then `INSERT INTO sb_monthly_revenue (cols) SELECT ...`.
sections.hint2: Reuse the monthly aggregation from SQL-020.
sections.hint3: The column order of the SELECT must match the INSERT column list.
sections.verify:
SELECT COUNT(*)          AS months,
       SUM(revenue)      AS total_revenue,
       MIN(month_start)  AS first_month,
       MAX(month_start)  AS last_month
FROM sb_monthly_revenue;
sections.explanation:
`INSERT ... SELECT` writes a query result into an existing table in one statement, with no round trip through the application. Declaring the table first (instead of `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT`) fixes the column types, the primary key and NOT NULL rules explicitly. CTAS copies whatever types the expressions happen to produce, and no constraints.

The primary key on `month_start` turns accidental double loads into errors instead of silently duplicated revenue.
sections.mistakes:
- Relying on positional column order without a column list (`INSERT INTO t SELECT ...`): fragile when the table changes.
- Appending each night without clearing old rows.
sections.performance: The summary has 18 rows; dashboards reading it no longer scan orders.
sections.interview: Expect follow-ups on incremental loads (only recompute recent months) and on upserts.

questions.title: Deactivate users of deleted organizations (UPDATE with a join)
questions.secondary: multi-table UPDATE syntax per dialect, sandbox copy with CREATE TABLE AS

sections.context: SQL-048 found active users in organizations that left. A clean-up job sets them to `'inactive'`. Practise on a sandbox copy of `users`.
sections.problem: Create `sb_users` as a copy of `users(user_id, org_id, status)`. Update users with status `'active'` whose organization is soft-deleted to `'inactive'` using a join-style UPDATE. Verify with the count of users per (organization deleted?, status).
sections.expected: After the update no row has `org_deleted = true` and status `active`.
sections.edge_cases:
- **Multi-table UPDATE syntax differs:** PostgreSQL `UPDATE t SET ... FROM other WHERE ...`; MySQL `UPDATE t JOIN other ON ... SET ...`.
- A portable alternative is `WHERE org_id IN (SELECT org_id FROM organizations WHERE is_deleted = TRUE)`.
sections.hint1: `CREATE TABLE sb_users AS SELECT user_id, org_id, status FROM users`.
sections.hint2: PostgreSQL: `UPDATE sb_users u SET status = 'inactive' FROM organizations o WHERE o.org_id = u.org_id AND ...`.
sections.hint3: MySQL: `UPDATE sb_users u JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id SET u.status = 'inactive' WHERE ...`.
sections.verify:
SELECT o.is_deleted AS org_deleted,
       u.status,
       COUNT(*)     AS users
FROM sb_users u
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id
GROUP BY o.is_deleted, u.status
ORDER BY org_deleted, u.status;
sections.dialect_note: PostgreSQL extends UPDATE with a `FROM` list (the target must not be repeated there). MySQL supports multi-table UPDATE with JOIN syntax and can even update several tables in one statement. Neither syntax works on the other engine. The subquery form `WHERE org_id IN (SELECT ...)` is portable when you only need the other table for filtering.
sections.assert: not any(r[0] in ('t', '1', 'true') and r[1] == 'active' for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
An UPDATE that depends on another table filters target rows through a join. Before running it on real data:
1. Run the same join as a SELECT to see which rows will change.
2. Wrap the change in a transaction (SQL-148) so it can be rolled back.
3. Keep the WHERE clause narrow (`u.status = 'active'`) so the statement is idempotent: running it twice changes nothing the second time.

CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) is the quickest way to get a disposable copy for practice. It copies data but not constraints or indexes.
sections.mistakes:
- Forgetting the WHERE clause (every user becomes inactive).
- Using a correlated subquery in SET that returns NULL for unmatched rows.
sections.performance: Updates on large tables lock rows and write WAL/binlog. Batch big updates by key range.
sections.interview: Knowing both UPDATE-join syntaxes and the safe-update workflow is expected for analytics engineers.

questions.title: Delete duplicate events but keep one copy
questions.secondary: window function in a derived table, MySQL error 1093, sandbox copy

sections.context: SQL-064 counted duplicate client events. Now remove them physically from a sandbox copy of June's events, keeping the copy with the smallest `event_id`.
sections.problem: Create `sb_events` from June 2025 events, delete every duplicate except the first per `(user_id, session_id, event_name, event_ts)`, and verify with the remaining row count and the number of duplicate groups left (must be 0).
sections.expected: One row with `duplicate_groups = 0`.
sections.edge_cases:
- **MySQL error 1093** ("You can't specify target table for update in FROM clause") occurs when a DELETE's subquery reads the same table directly. Wrapping the window function in a derived table forces materialization and avoids it.
- `session_id` is NULL for server events; PARTITION BY groups NULLs together, which is correct here.
sections.hint1: Identify rows to delete with `ROW_NUMBER() ... > 1`.
sections.hint2: `DELETE FROM sb_events WHERE event_id IN (SELECT event_id FROM (<ranked rows>) d WHERE d.rn > 1)`.
sections.hint3: The inner derived table is what makes the statement legal in MySQL.
sections.solution:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sb_events;
CREATE TABLE sb_events AS
SELECT event_id, user_id, session_id, event_name, event_ts
FROM events
WHERE event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-01 00:00:00'
  AND event_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00';
DELETE FROM sb_events
WHERE event_id IN (
    SELECT event_id
    FROM (
        SELECT event_id,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, session_id, event_name, event_ts
                                  ORDER BY event_id) AS rn
        FROM sb_events
    ) ranked
    WHERE ranked.rn > 1
);
sections.verify:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sb_events) AS rows_left,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT 1 AS x FROM sb_events
                              GROUP BY user_id, session_id, event_name, event_ts
                              HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) d) AS duplicate_groups;
sections.explanation:
Deleting duplicates is a two-step idea: rank the copies within each duplicate key, then delete every rank above 1. Expressing the "rows to delete" as a set of primary keys (`event_id IN (...)`) works in both engines. PostgreSQL also offers `DELETE ... USING` (join syntax), and MySQL offers multi-table `DELETE e FROM sb_events e JOIN (...) d ON ...`.

The verification query proves the post-condition (no duplicate groups) instead of just trusting the DELETE.

In production, prefer preventing duplicates (a unique constraint on the natural key, or idempotent ingestion with upserts) over periodic clean-up.
sections.mistakes:
- `DELETE ... WHERE event_id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(event_id) ... GROUP BY ...)`. It works, but it is easy to get wrong, and NOT IN has NULL pitfalls.
- Deleting from the real `events` table while practising.
sections.performance: Large deletes generate a lot of undo/redo; batch them, or rebuild the table with `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` of the survivors and swap.
sections.interview: "Delete duplicates keeping one" is asked constantly; mentioning MySQL's 1093 restriction shows hands-on experience.

questions.title: Credit transfers with transactions and savepoints
questions.secondary: SAVEPOINT, atomicity, DDL behaviour per engine

sections.context: Organizations hold prepaid AI credits. Moving credits between organizations must be atomic: debit and credit happen together or not at all.
sections.problem:
In a sandbox table `sb_credit_balances(org_id, credits >= 0)` with balances 12 → 500, 49 → 100, 94 → 0:
1. Transfer 200 credits from 12 to 49 and COMMIT.
2. Start a transfer of 50 from 49, credit the wrong recipient (12), roll back to a savepoint taken after the debit, credit 94 instead, COMMIT.
3. Start a transfer of 300 from 12 to 94, then abandon it with ROLLBACK.
Return the final balances, sorted by `org_id`.
sections.expected: 3 rows: 12 → 300, 49 → 250, 94 → 50 (the total of 600 is conserved).
sections.edge_cases:
- `START TRANSACTION` works in both engines (`BEGIN` also works in both, but means something else inside MySQL stored programs).
- **DDL inside a transaction:** PostgreSQL DDL is transactional (it can be rolled back); MySQL commits implicitly before and after most DDL statements.
sections.hint1: Group each transfer's statements between `START TRANSACTION` and `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`.
sections.hint2: `SAVEPOINT after_debit` marks a point to which `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_debit` can return without abandoning the whole transaction.
sections.hint3: Verify that the total balance is unchanged at the end.
sections.explanation:
A transaction groups statements into one atomic unit:
- **COMMIT** makes all changes durable and visible to others.
- **ROLLBACK** discards every change since `START TRANSACTION`.
- **SAVEPOINT / ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT** undoes only the work after the savepoint, which is useful for retrying one step of a longer transaction.

The CHECK constraint is the last line of defence: a transfer that would make a balance negative fails, and the application must then roll back the whole transaction. Otherwise a debit without its matching credit could be committed.

Concurrency (two transfers at once) needs row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) or serializable isolation. That is beyond this exercise, but a classic follow-up question.
sections.mistakes:
- Running the debit and the credit as two auto-committed statements (a crash in between loses credits).
- Assuming `ROLLBACK` undoes a `CREATE TABLE` in MySQL.
sections.performance: Short transactions hold locks briefly; never wait for user input inside a transaction.
sections.interview: ACID basics and savepoints are standard backend/data-engineering questions; the DDL difference is a good bonus.

questions.title: Idempotent daily usage loads with an upsert
questions.secondary: ON CONFLICT vs ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, composite primary key, re-runnable jobs

sections.context: A job aggregates LLM usage per organization and day into `sb_daily_usage`. Because late events arrive, the job re-processes the last two days on every run. Rows must be updated, not duplicated.
sections.problem: Create `sb_daily_usage(org_id, usage_date, requests, tokens)` with primary key `(org_id, usage_date)`. Load 2025-06-28 and 2025-06-29, then run the next job for 2025-06-29 and 2025-06-30 as an **upsert**. Verify with per-day totals.
sections.expected: 3 rows (06-28, 06-29, 06-30), each day loaded once.
sections.edge_cases:
- PostgreSQL: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (org_id, usage_date) DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col`.
- MySQL: `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE col = <alias>.col`. With INSERT ... SELECT, reference the derived table's alias. The older `VALUES(col)` function is deprecated since 8.0.20.
sections.hint1: The composite primary key defines what counts as "the same row".
sections.hint2: In PostgreSQL, `EXCLUDED` holds the row proposed for insertion.
sections.hint3: In MySQL, wrap the SELECT in a derived table (`... FROM (SELECT ...) AS new`) and use `new.requests` in the UPDATE list.
sections.solution_pg:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sb_daily_usage;
CREATE TABLE sb_daily_usage (
    org_id      INT    NOT NULL,
    usage_date  DATE   NOT NULL,
    requests    INT    NOT NULL,
    tokens      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_sb_daily_usage PRIMARY KEY (org_id, usage_date)
);
INSERT INTO sb_daily_usage (org_id, usage_date, requests, tokens)
SELECT org_id, CAST(requested_at AS DATE), COUNT(*), SUM(input_tokens + COALESCE(output_tokens, 0))
FROM llm_requests
WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-28 00:00:00' AND requested_at < TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 00:00:00'
GROUP BY org_id, CAST(requested_at AS DATE);
INSERT INTO sb_daily_usage (org_id, usage_date, requests, tokens)
SELECT org_id, CAST(requested_at AS DATE), COUNT(*), SUM(input_tokens + COALESCE(output_tokens, 0))
FROM llm_requests
WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-29 00:00:00' AND requested_at < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY org_id, CAST(requested_at AS DATE)
ON CONFLICT (org_id, usage_date)
DO UPDATE SET requests = EXCLUDED.requests,
              tokens   = EXCLUDED.tokens;
sections.solution_mysql:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sb_daily_usage;
CREATE TABLE sb_daily_usage (
    org_id      INT    NOT NULL,
    usage_date  DATE   NOT NULL,
    requests    INT    NOT NULL,
    tokens      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_sb_daily_usage PRIMARY KEY (org_id, usage_date)
);
INSERT INTO sb_daily_usage (org_id, usage_date, requests, tokens)
SELECT org_id, CAST(requested_at AS DATE), COUNT(*), SUM(input_tokens + COALESCE(output_tokens, 0))
FROM llm_requests
WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-28 00:00:00' AND requested_at < TIMESTAMP '2025-06-30 00:00:00'
GROUP BY org_id, CAST(requested_at AS DATE);
INSERT INTO sb_daily_usage (org_id, usage_date, requests, tokens)
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT org_id, CAST(requested_at AS DATE) AS usage_date, COUNT(*) AS requests,
           SUM(input_tokens + COALESCE(output_tokens, 0)) AS tokens
    FROM llm_requests
    WHERE requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-06-29 00:00:00' AND requested_at < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY org_id, CAST(requested_at AS DATE)
) AS new
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE requests = new.requests,
                        tokens   = new.tokens;
sections.verify:
SELECT usage_date,
       COUNT(*)       AS orgs,
       SUM(requests)  AS requests,
       SUM(tokens)    AS tokens
FROM sb_daily_usage
GROUP BY usage_date
ORDER BY usage_date;
sections.dialect_note:
| | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|---|---|---|
| syntax | `ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET c = EXCLUDED.c` | `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE c = alias.c` |
| conflict target | explicit unique constraint/columns | any unique key (ambiguous with several unique keys) |
| do nothing | `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` | `INSERT IGNORE` (also hides other errors!) |
| SQL standard | `MERGE` (PostgreSQL 15+, SQL-169) | not available |
sections.explanation:
An **upsert** inserts new keys and updates existing ones atomically, which makes the load **idempotent**: re-running the same job leaves the table in the same state. That is essential for pipelines that retry or re-process late data.

The 2025-06-29 rows from the first load are overwritten by the second job's fresh aggregates (same values here, because the data is static); 2025-06-30 rows are inserted.
sections.mistakes:
- DELETE + INSERT without a transaction (readers see a gap).
- `INSERT IGNORE` in MySQL, which silently skips *all* errors on conflicting rows, including data errors.
sections.performance: Each conflicting row costs an index lookup plus an update; batch upserts by date to keep transactions small.
sections.interview: Upserts and idempotency are core data-engineering topics; knowing both dialects is expected for MLE/DE roles.

questions.title: A view for servable RAG chunks
questions.secondary: encapsulating business rules, CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW, querying a view
questions.tables: document_chunks(chunk_id, document_id, token_count, embedding_model); documents(document_id, doc_key, source_type, status, is_deleted)

sections.context: Several teams (retrieval, evaluation, analytics) need "the chunks the bot may serve". Encode the rule once in a view instead of copying the WHERE clause everywhere.
sections.problem: Create the view `sb_v_servable_chunks` (published, non-deleted document versions; embedded chunks only) exposing `chunk_id`, `document_id`, `doc_key`, `source_type`, `token_count`. Then query it: per `source_type`, distinct documents, chunks and total tokens.
sections.expected: 5 rows.
sections.edge_cases: - A view stores the query, not the data; it always reflects current table contents.
sections.hint1: `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW name AS SELECT ...`.
sections.hint2: Reuse the servability rule from SQL-125.
sections.hint3: Query the view like a table.
sections.solution:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW sb_v_servable_chunks AS
SELECT c.chunk_id,
       c.document_id,
       d.doc_key,
       d.source_type,
       c.token_count
FROM document_chunks c
JOIN documents d ON d.document_id = c.document_id
WHERE d.status = 'published'
  AND d.is_deleted = FALSE
  AND c.embedding_model IS NOT NULL;
sections.verify:
SELECT source_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT doc_key) AS documents,
       COUNT(*)                AS chunks,
       SUM(token_count)        AS tokens
FROM sb_v_servable_chunks
GROUP BY source_type
ORDER BY source_type;
sections.explanation:
A view is a named, stored query. Benefits: one definition of a business rule, simpler downstream SQL, and a stable interface while the underlying tables change. Permissions can also be granted on the view without exposing the base tables.

Both engines inline simple views into the calling query, so filtering a view costs about the same as filtering the base query. Materialized views (PostgreSQL `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`; MySQL has none) store results and must be refreshed.
sections.mistakes:
- Stacking views on views until no one understands the final query.
- `SELECT *` in a view definition: in PostgreSQL the column list is frozen at creation time, and MySQL expands `*` immediately too, so later table changes are not reflected.
sections.performance: Same as the underlying query; views are not a caching mechanism.
sections.interview: Views as "single source of truth" for metric definitions are a common analytics-engineering topic.

questions.title: Reuse an intermediate result with a temporary table
questions.secondary: session scope, MySQL "can't reopen table" limitation, CTE alternative
questions.tables: sessions(user_id, started_at); users(user_id, org_id); organizations(org_id, segment); orders(user_id, status, order_ts)

sections.context: An analysis session repeatedly uses "users active in Q2 2025". Computing it once into a temporary table keeps later queries short.
sections.problem: Create the temporary table `tmp_q2_active` with the distinct users who started a session in Q2 2025, then return per segment the active users, those with a completed order in Q2 2025 (`buyers`), and `buyer_pct` (1 decimal). Sort by segment.
sections.expected: 3 rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- Temporary tables live only in the current session (connection) and disappear when it ends.
- **MySQL cannot reference the same TEMPORARY table twice in one statement** (error 1137 "Can't reopen table"), e.g. in a self-join or in both an outer query and a subquery. Use a CTE or a regular table for that.
sections.hint1: `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_q2_active AS SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM sessions WHERE ...`.
sections.hint2: Join it to users and organizations; test purchases with EXISTS.
sections.hint3: Reference `tmp_q2_active` only once in the final statement.
sections.solution:
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_q2_active AS
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM sessions
WHERE started_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
  AND started_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00';
SELECT o.segment,
       COUNT(*) AS active_users,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders x
                             WHERE x.user_id = t.user_id
                               AND x.status = 'completed'
                               AND x.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                               AND x.order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS buyers,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders x
                                           WHERE x.user_id = t.user_id
                                             AND x.status = 'completed'
                                             AND x.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
                                             AND x.order_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00')
                              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS buyer_pct
FROM tmp_q2_active t
JOIN users u         ON u.user_id = t.user_id
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id
GROUP BY o.segment
ORDER BY o.segment;
sections.explanation:
`CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE ... AS SELECT` materializes an intermediate result for the rest of the session. Compared with a CTE:
- a temp table is computed once and can be indexed and reused by many statements;
- a CTE lives only inside one statement but has no "reopen" limitation in MySQL.

Temporary tables shadow permanent tables with the same name, and they are private to the session, so two analysts can use `tmp_q2_active` simultaneously without conflict.
sections.mistakes:
- Self-joining a temp table in MySQL (error 1137).
- Using temp tables in connection-pooled applications and assuming they persist between requests.
sections.performance: Materializing a small set (≈ 800 user IDs) once can be cheaper than recomputing a heavy subquery in many statements; add an index on large temp tables.
sections.interview: Shows practical knowledge of session-scoped objects and engine limitations.

questions.title: Normalize a flat ticket import into dimension and fact tables
questions.secondary: surrogate keys with ROW_NUMBER, natural keys, FK-linked tables, reconstruction check
questions.tables: support_tickets(ticket_id, org_id, category, priority, created_at); organizations(org_id, org_name, country_code, segment)

sections.context: A partner sends support tickets as a flat file: every row repeats the organization's name, country and segment. Repeated attributes waste space and drift apart when one copy is updated (an update anomaly). Normalize the import into an organization dimension and a ticket fact table.
sections.problem:
1. Build the flat import `sb_ticket_import` from Q2-2025 tickets (ticket ID, source org ID, org name, country, segment, category, priority, created date).
2. Create `sb_dim_org` (surrogate `org_key`, unique `source_org_id`, attributes) and `sb_fact_ticket` (ticket attributes + `org_key` FK).
3. Load both with INSERT ... SELECT.
Verify with the row counts and the number of import rows that cannot be reconstructed by joining fact and dimension (must be 0).
sections.expected: One row; `dim_rows` much smaller than `fact_rows`, and `unreconstructable_rows = 0`.
sections.edge_cases: - `org_name` is not unique in this dataset; using it as the natural key would merge two companies. Keep the source system's ID as the natural key.
sections.hint1: Distinct organizations from the import → dimension rows; `ROW_NUMBER()` creates surrogate keys.
sections.hint2: The fact load joins the import to the dimension on `source_org_id` to look up `org_key`.
sections.hint3: Reconstruction check: import rows with NOT EXISTS a matching fact⋈dimension row.
sections.solution:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sb_fact_ticket;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sb_dim_org;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sb_ticket_import;
CREATE TABLE sb_ticket_import AS
SELECT t.ticket_id,
       t.org_id                   AS source_org_id,
       o.org_name,
       o.country_code,
       o.segment,
       t.category,
       t.priority,
       CAST(t.created_at AS DATE) AS created_date
FROM support_tickets t
JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = t.org_id
WHERE t.created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00'
  AND t.created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00';
CREATE TABLE sb_dim_org (
    org_key        INT          NOT NULL,
    source_org_id  INT          NOT NULL,
    org_name       VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
    country_code   CHAR(2)      NOT NULL,
    segment        VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_sb_dim_org PRIMARY KEY (org_key),
    CONSTRAINT uq_sb_dim_org_source UNIQUE (source_org_id)
);
INSERT INTO sb_dim_org (org_key, source_org_id, org_name, country_code, segment)
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY source_org_id), source_org_id, org_name, country_code, segment
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT source_org_id, org_name, country_code, segment FROM sb_ticket_import) d;
CREATE TABLE sb_fact_ticket (
    ticket_id     INT         NOT NULL,
    org_key       INT         NOT NULL,
    category      VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    priority      VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    created_date  DATE        NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_sb_fact_ticket PRIMARY KEY (ticket_id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_sb_fact_ticket_org FOREIGN KEY (org_key) REFERENCES sb_dim_org (org_key)
);
INSERT INTO sb_fact_ticket (ticket_id, org_key, category, priority, created_date)
SELECT i.ticket_id, d.org_key, i.category, i.priority, i.created_date
FROM sb_ticket_import i
JOIN sb_dim_org d ON d.source_org_id = i.source_org_id;
sections.verify:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sb_ticket_import) AS import_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sb_dim_org)       AS dim_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sb_fact_ticket)   AS fact_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sb_ticket_import i
         WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                           FROM sb_fact_ticket f
                           JOIN sb_dim_org d ON d.org_key = f.org_key
                           WHERE f.ticket_id = i.ticket_id
                             AND d.org_name = i.org_name
                             AND d.country_code = i.country_code
                             AND d.segment = i.segment
                             AND f.category = i.category
                             AND f.priority = i.priority
                             AND f.created_date = i.created_date)) AS unreconstructable_rows;
sections.explanation:
**Normalization** stores each fact once:
- 1NF: atomic columns, no repeating groups;
- 2NF/3NF: non-key attributes depend on the whole key and only on the key. Organization attributes depend on the organization, not on the ticket, so they move to their own table.

The surrogate key (`org_key`) decouples the warehouse from the source system, while the unique natural key (`source_org_id`) prevents duplicate dimension rows on reloads. Choosing `org_name` as the natural key would be a real bug here: two different companies share a name.

The **reconstruction check** proves the decomposition is lossless: joining fact and dimension reproduces every import row. Analytical warehouses often denormalize again for speed (star schema); the point is to do it deliberately.
sections.mistakes:
- Natural keys that are not actually unique (names).
- Loading facts before dimensions (FK violations), or dropping tables in the wrong order (drop facts first).
sections.performance: The FK on `org_key` costs a lookup per inserted fact; bulk loads sometimes disable checks temporarily, which then requires re-validation.
sections.interview: Normalization questions are common for data engineering; showing a lossless-join check is a strong answer.

questions.title: Create, inspect and drop indexes
questions.secondary: composite and unique indexes, redundant prefix indexes, catalog queries per dialect

sections.context: On a sandbox copy of the request log, the platform team adds indexes for the two most common access paths (model + time range, and trace lookups) and removes an index made redundant by the composite one.
sections.problem: Create `sb_requests` from `llm_requests (request_id, model_name, requested_at, trace_id)`. Create a single-column index on `model_name`, a composite index on `(model_name, requested_at)` and a unique index on `trace_id`. Then drop the single-column index and list the remaining indexes with their columns from the system catalog.
sections.expected: 3 rows: the composite index (2 columns) and the unique trace index.
sections.edge_cases:
- `DROP INDEX` syntax differs: PostgreSQL `DROP INDEX name;` (index names are schema-wide), MySQL `DROP INDEX name ON table;` (names are per table).
- Unique indexes allow several NULLs in both engines (NULLs are not equal to each other); PostgreSQL 15+ offers `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` to change that.
sections.hint1: `CREATE INDEX name ON table (col1, col2);`, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ...`.
sections.hint2: The single-column index on `model_name` is a prefix of the composite index, so the composite one can serve its queries too.
sections.hint3: Catalog: PostgreSQL `pg_index` + `pg_attribute`; MySQL `information_schema.statistics`.
sections.dialect_note: PostgreSQL has no `information_schema` view for indexes; use `pg_indexes` (definition text) or `pg_index` joined to `pg_attribute` (columns), as here. MySQL exposes them in `information_schema.statistics` (one row per index column, `seq_in_index` = position). Also note: MySQL automatically creates an index for every foreign key if none exists; PostgreSQL does not.
sections.explanation:
- A **composite index** on `(model_name, requested_at)` serves `WHERE model_name = ?`, `WHERE model_name = ? AND requested_at BETWEEN ...` and ordered scans by time within a model. It makes a separate index on `model_name` alone **redundant**, since that index only costs write time and storage.
- A **unique index** both speeds up lookups and enforces uniqueness (trace IDs must not repeat).
- Dropping and creating indexes are schema changes: on big tables, use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (PostgreSQL) or online DDL (`ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` in MySQL) to avoid blocking writes.
sections.mistakes:
- Creating one index per column "just in case" (write amplification, worse plans).
- Copying PostgreSQL's `DROP INDEX name` to MySQL (syntax error without `ON table`).
sections.performance: Every index speeds up some reads and slows every write; review index usage (`pg_stat_user_indexes`, MySQL `sys.schema_unused_indexes`) periodically.
sections.interview: Expect "which indexes would you create for these queries, and which would you drop?".

questions.title: Read your first execution plan: index versus full scan
questions.secondary: sequential/table scan vs index lookup, statistics with ANALYZE

sections.context: Incident responders look up LLM requests by `trace_id` and by `error_code`. On a sandbox copy of the request log, `trace_id` gets an index and `error_code` does not. One plan can show both access paths if you EXPLAIN a UNION ALL of the two lookups.
sections.problem: Create `sb_req_perf` from `llm_requests`, index `trace_id`, refresh statistics, and EXPLAIN a query that counts rows for one trace ID and, separately (UNION ALL), for one error code. Identify which branch uses the index.
sections.expected: A plan whose trace branch uses the index (PostgreSQL "Index Only Scan"/"Index Scan"/"Bitmap Index Scan", MySQL "Index lookup"/"Covering index lookup") and whose error-code branch scans the whole table ("Seq Scan" / "Table scan").
sections.edge_cases:
- On very small tables the planner may prefer a full scan even when an index exists, because reading a few pages sequentially is cheaper.
- Plans depend on statistics: always ANALYZE after bulk loads.
sections.hint1: `EXPLAIN` shows the plan without running the query.
sections.hint2: PostgreSQL: `EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) ...` for compact output. MySQL: `EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE ...`.
sections.hint3: Statistics: PostgreSQL `ANALYZE sb_req_perf;`, MySQL `ANALYZE TABLE sb_req_perf;`.
sections.assert: any('Index' in r[0] for r in rows) and any('Seq Scan' in r[0] for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
An execution plan is a tree of operators; read it from the innermost (most indented) nodes upwards:
- **Seq Scan** (PostgreSQL) / **Table scan** (MySQL) reads every row and applies the filter.
- **Index Scan / Index Only Scan / Bitmap Index Scan** (PostgreSQL) / **Index lookup** (MySQL) navigates the B-tree to the matching keys.

For an equality lookup that returns a handful of rows out of thousands, the index wins by orders of magnitude on big tables. EXPLAIN shows the *chosen* plan and estimated costs. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (SQL-159) also runs the query and shows actual row counts and time.

The UNION ALL trick puts two access paths into one plan for comparison; in practice you would EXPLAIN each query separately.
sections.mistakes:
- Reading costs as milliseconds (they are planner units).
- Concluding "the index is not used, so it is useless" from one plan on a tiny table.
sections.performance: The trace index turns an O(n) scan into an O(log n) lookup; the cost is extra storage and slower inserts.
sections.interview: Expect to be handed a plan and asked "what is slow here and why?".

questions.title: SELECT * versus a covering index
questions.secondary: covering (index-only) scans, heap/table lookups, VACUUM and the visibility map

sections.context: A latency dashboard needs only `requested_at` and `latency_ms` for one model and month. The first version used `SELECT *`.
sections.problem: On `sb_req_perf`, create an index on `(model_name, requested_at, latency_ms)`, refresh statistics (and in PostgreSQL the visibility map with VACUUM), then EXPLAIN the column-specific query and the `SELECT *` version together (UNION ALL of two counts over derived tables). Which branch is answered from the index alone?
sections.expected: The column-specific branch is an index-only/covering scan; the `SELECT *` branch must also read the table rows.
sections.edge_cases:
- PostgreSQL can only skip the table (heap) for pages marked all-visible; run `VACUUM ANALYZE` after bulk loads.
- MySQL InnoDB secondary indexes contain the primary key, and covering scans show "Covering index range scan".
sections.hint1: An index *covers* a query when every column the query reads is in the index.
sections.hint2: `CREATE INDEX ... ON sb_req_perf (model_name, requested_at, latency_ms)`.
sections.hint3: Wrap each variant in `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (<variant>) x` so they can be combined with UNION ALL.
sections.assert: any('Index Only Scan' in r[0] for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
When all needed columns are in the index, the engine answers from the index alone: an **index-only scan** (PostgreSQL) or **covering index** (MySQL). That avoids one random table lookup per row. `SELECT *` (here: needing `input_tokens` too, which is not in the index) forces those lookups.

Note that a bare `COUNT(*)` over `SELECT *` could be optimized away, because the optimizer prunes unused columns of a derived table. The extra predicate on `input_tokens` makes the wide branch genuinely need table columns, which mirrors what happens when an application really fetches all columns.

Beyond performance, explicit column lists protect consumers from schema changes and reduce network transfer, which matters a lot for wide tables with JSON or TEXT columns.
sections.mistakes:
- Adding every column to an index to make it "covering": huge indexes, slow writes.
- Expecting index-only scans in PostgreSQL right after a bulk load without VACUUM.
sections.performance: Covering indexes are a precise tool for hot, narrow queries such as dashboards and lookups.
sections.interview: "Why is SELECT * bad?" A good answer covers I/O, covering indexes, network and schema coupling.

questions.title: Sargable versus non-sargable date filters
questions.secondary: functions on indexed columns, equivalent range rewrite, EXPLAIN comparison

sections.context: A daily report filters events with `CAST(event_ts AS DATE) = DATE '2025-06-15'`. An index on `event_ts` exists but the query still scans the whole table.
sections.problem: On `sb_events_perf` (a copy of `events` with an index on `event_ts`), EXPLAIN the function-wrapped filter and the equivalent half-open range together (UNION ALL of two counts). Explain the difference.
sections.expected: The range branch is an index range scan over about 70 index entries. The CAST branch reads everything: PostgreSQL does a Seq Scan of the table, and MySQL a full *covering index scan* that reads all ~33,000 index entries and evaluates the CAST on each. Compare the estimated rows of the two branches.
sections.edge_cases:
- Both predicates select exactly the same rows; only their index-friendliness differs.
- An expression index on `CAST(event_ts AS DATE)` (PostgreSQL) or a functional index (MySQL 8.0.13+) would make the first form indexable too.
sections.hint1: An index on `event_ts` stores `event_ts` values in order, not `CAST(event_ts AS DATE)` values.
sections.hint2: Rewrite the date equality as `event_ts >= DATE AND event_ts < DATE + 1 day`.
sections.hint3: EXPLAIN a UNION ALL of both counts to compare access paths.
sections.assert: any('Seq Scan' in r[0] for r in rows) and any('Index' in r[0] for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
A predicate is **sargable** (Search ARGument ABLE) when the engine can turn it into an index range: `column op constant`. Wrapping the column in a function (`CAST`, `DATE()`, `LOWER()`, arithmetic like `event_ts + INTERVAL ...`) hides the indexed value, so every row must be computed and tested.

Rewrite rules:
- `CAST(ts AS DATE) = d` → `ts >= d AND ts < d + 1 day`
- `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM ts) = 2025` → `ts >= '2025-01-01' AND ts < '2026-01-01'`
- `col + 10 > 100` → `col > 90`

When the function form is unavoidable (e.g. case-insensitive lookups), index the expression itself.

Note the MySQL plan: it still "uses" the index for the CAST branch, but as a **full index scan** (the index is narrower than the table), not a range. "Uses an index" in a plan is not the same as "uses the index efficiently". Look for range or lookup access and the row estimates.
sections.mistakes:
- Assuming the optimizer rewrites function predicates automatically. It does not in general.
- Using `BETWEEN d AND d + 1` (inclusive end, see SQL-005).
sections.performance: On 35k rows the difference is small in absolute time; on hundreds of millions of rows it decides between milliseconds and minutes.
sections.interview: One of the most common SQL performance questions; candidates should rewrite the predicate without being prompted.

questions.title: Composite index column order
questions.secondary: leftmost-prefix rule, equality before range, skip scans

sections.context: The request log has a composite index on `(model_name, requested_at)`. Two dashboard queries: (A) one model in June, (B) all models in June. Only one of them can use the index as a simple range.
sections.problem: On `sb_req_perf` with an index on `(model_name, requested_at)`, EXPLAIN query A (`model_name = 'nimbus-pro'` and June) and query B (June only) together as UNION ALL of two counts. Explain why A gets an index range scan and B does not.
sections.expected: A: an index range scan on (model, time). B cannot use a simple range. On the engines used to validate this workbook (PostgreSQL 18, MySQL 8.4) the planner chooses a **skip scan**, jumping through each of the 5 model sections. On PostgreSQL 16/17 you will see a full scan instead.
sections.edge_cases:
- B-tree composite indexes are sorted by the first column, then by the second within each first-column value.
- PostgreSQL 18 and MySQL 8.0.13+ can sometimes "skip scan" a leading column with few distinct values; older versions cannot.
sections.hint1: Think of a phone book sorted by (last name, first name): can you quickly find everyone named "Maria"?
sections.hint2: Equality on the leading column + range on the next column is the ideal pattern.
sections.hint3: For B, an index on `(requested_at)` or `(requested_at, model_name)` would be needed.
sections.assert: any('model_name' in r[0] and 'requested_at' in r[0] for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
A composite B-tree index is sorted lexicographically: by `model_name`, and within each model by `requested_at`. Query A pins the first column with equality and ranges over the second, a single contiguous slice of the index. Query B constrains only the second column, so matching entries are scattered across every model's section. The engine must either scan everything or jump between model sections. That jumping is a *skip scan* (PostgreSQL 18 "Index Only Scan" with an Index Cond on `requested_at` only; MySQL "Covering index skip scan"). It is cheap here only because `model_name` has 5 distinct values. With thousands of distinct leading values it degrades to scanning everything.

Design rules:
1. Put equality-filtered columns first, then the range column.
2. Order by selectivity only among equality columns.
3. One index can serve several queries via its leftmost prefixes: `(a, b, c)` serves filters on `a`, `a+b` and `a+b+c`.
sections.mistakes:
- Creating `(requested_at, model_name)` for query A. It works, but it scans all models for the date range before filtering by model.
- Assuming that the order of columns in the WHERE clause matters. It does not; the index column order does.
sections.performance: Index column order is one of the highest-impact physical design decisions for time-series and log tables.
sections.interview: "Which composite index would you create for these three queries?" is a frequent system-design-meets-SQL question.

Index Cond: ((model_name = 'nimbus-pro'::text) AND (requested_at >= '2025-06-01 00:00:00'::timestamp without time zone) AND (requested_at < '2025-07-01 00:00:00'::timestamp without time zone))

questions.title: When an index is not useful (selectivity)
questions.primary: Selectivity and when an index is not useful
questions.secondary: low-cardinality columns, value-dependent plans, statistics

sections.context: Someone added an index on `llm_requests.status` "to speed up status filters". About 92% of requests are `'success'`, and less than 1% are `'content_filtered'`.
sections.problem: On `sb_req_perf` with an index on `status`, EXPLAIN a count of `'success'` rows and a count of `'content_filtered'` rows together (UNION ALL). Explain why the same index is used for one value and ignored for the other.
sections.expected: `content_filtered` → index; `success` → full scan.
sections.edge_cases: - The planner needs value-level statistics (PostgreSQL most-common-values lists; MySQL index dives or histograms) to tell the two cases apart.
sections.hint1: Selectivity = fraction of rows a predicate returns.
sections.hint2: Reading 92% of a table through an index means one random access per row, which is slower than one sequential pass.
sections.hint3: Compare the plans of the two branches.
sections.assert: any('Seq Scan' in r[0] for r in rows) and any('Index' in r[0] for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
Indexes help when a predicate is **selective** (returns a small fraction of rows). For `'success'`, the planner estimates ~92% of rows and chooses a sequential scan. For `'content_filtered'` it estimates a few dozen rows and uses the index. Same column, same index, different values, different plans.

`COUNT(latency_ms)` (rather than `COUNT(*)`) needs a column that is not in the index, which prevents a trivial index-only count and makes the comparison fair.

Practical guidance:
- Low-cardinality columns rarely deserve a standalone index. A **partial index** (PostgreSQL: `CREATE INDEX ... WHERE status <> 'success'`) indexes only the rare, interesting rows.
- Combine a low-cardinality column with a selective one in a composite index if queries filter on both.
sections.mistakes:
- "Index every column used in WHERE."
- Forcing index use with hints without measuring.
sections.performance: An unused index still costs storage and write time on every insert.
sections.interview: Shows understanding of cost-based optimization rather than rule-of-thumb indexing.

questions.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE: correlated subquery versus window function
questions.secondary: recognizing expensive correlated subqueries, loops/executions, deterministic output options

sections.context: SQL-047 used a correlated subquery to find each organization's latest ticket; SQL-061 showed the ROW_NUMBER pattern. Measure both with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
sections.problem: EXPLAIN ANALYZE a UNION ALL of (a) the count of tickets that are their organization's latest via a correlated scalar subquery and (b) the same count via ROW_NUMBER. Find in the plan how often the correlated subquery is executed.
sections.expected: The correlated branch shows a subplan executed once per ticket (loops ≈ number of tickets); the window branch shows one sort plus one pass.
sections.edge_cases:
- PostgreSQL: use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)` for stable, readable output.
- MySQL 8.0.18+: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (tree format with actual times and loops).
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE **executes** the query; never run it on a destructive statement outside a transaction you roll back.
sections.hint1: Look for "SubPlan" (PostgreSQL) or "Select #n (subquery in condition; dependent)" (MySQL) and its `loops` value.
sections.hint2: Both branches return the same number (one latest ticket per organization).
sections.hint3: Compare the work: n index probes versus one sort.
sections.solution_pg:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM support_tickets t
WHERE t.ticket_id = (SELECT t2.ticket_id FROM support_tickets t2
                     WHERE t2.org_id = t.org_id
                     ORDER BY t2.created_at DESC, t2.ticket_id DESC
                     LIMIT 1)
UNION ALL
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM (SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY org_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, ticket_id DESC) AS rn
      FROM support_tickets) r
WHERE rn = 1;
sections.solution_mysql:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM support_tickets t
WHERE t.ticket_id = (SELECT t2.ticket_id FROM support_tickets t2
                     WHERE t2.org_id = t.org_id
                     ORDER BY t2.created_at DESC, t2.ticket_id DESC
                     LIMIT 1)
UNION ALL
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM (SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY org_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, ticket_id DESC) AS rn
      FROM support_tickets) r
WHERE rn = 1;
sections.assert: any('SubPlan' in r[0] for r in rows) and any('loops=' in r[0] for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and annotates each node with actual rows and loops. The correlated subquery is a **SubPlan** that runs once per outer row (`loops` ≈ 1,400 here). Each run is a cheap index probe thanks to `support_tickets(org_id, created_at)`, but the cost grows linearly with the outer table and much worse without the index. The window version sorts once and scans once.

Reading tips:
- `rows=` actual vs estimated: large differences point to stale statistics or correlated predicates.
- `loops=`: total work = per-loop rows × loops.
- In PostgreSQL, TIMING OFF and SUMMARY OFF remove noise from the output; for real tuning, keep timings on.

Optimizers can sometimes decorrelate subqueries into joins, but a scalar subquery with ORDER BY ... LIMIT usually stays correlated in both engines.
sections.mistakes:
- Comparing two plans by total cost only; check the loops of the inner nodes.
- Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on DELETE/UPDATE without a transaction.
sections.performance: Correlated subqueries are fine with a supporting index on small inputs, and dangerous on large ones; window functions scale more predictably.
sections.interview: Reading `loops` in an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan is a concrete skill senior interviewers probe.

questions.title: Let the index provide the order (avoiding a sort)
questions.secondary: ORDER BY ... LIMIT with a matching composite index, top-N sort

sections.context: The customer console shows an organization's 20 most recent LLM requests, and sometimes its 20 slowest. With an index on `(org_id, requested_at)`, only one of the two can skip sorting.
sections.problem: On `sb_req_perf` with an index on `(org_id, requested_at)`, EXPLAIN a UNION ALL of two parenthesized queries for organization 195: latest 20 by `requested_at DESC`, and slowest 20 by `latency_ms DESC`. Which branch needs a Sort node?
sections.expected: The `requested_at` branch reads the index backwards with no sort; the `latency_ms` branch sorts.
sections.edge_cases: - A top-N with LIMIT uses a bounded "top-N heapsort" (PostgreSQL) instead of sorting everything, but it still reads all of the organization's rows.
sections.hint1: An index stores entries sorted by its columns.
sections.hint2: Equality on `org_id` + order by `requested_at` = a contiguous, already-sorted index slice.
sections.hint3: Use `(SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 20) UNION ALL (SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 20)`.
sections.assert: any('Sort' in r[0] for r in rows) and any('Backward' in r[0] for r in rows)
sections.explanation:
Sorting is often the most expensive part of a query after I/O: it needs memory (work_mem / sort_buffer_size) and spills to disk when that is exceeded. When an index already delivers rows in the requested order, the engine just reads the first N entries ("Index Scan Backward" in PostgreSQL, "Index lookup ... (reverse)" in MySQL) and stops. That is the cheapest possible top-N.

The `latency_ms` branch cannot use the index order, so it reads all of the organization's rows and sorts them. Add `(org_id, latency_ms)` only if that query is frequent; each index has write costs.
sections.mistakes: - Adding `ORDER BY` columns in a different direction mix (`a ASC, b DESC`) than the index supports. MySQL 8 and PostgreSQL support descending index columns for that case.
sections.performance: Index-ordered top-N queries stay fast regardless of table size; sort-based ones grow with the number of matching rows.
sections.interview: "How would you make this paginated feed fast?" Matching index order plus keyset pagination (SQL-012) is the answer.

questions.title: Compute once: repeated subqueries versus a single derived table
questions.secondary: duplicated subplans in EXPLAIN, CTE/derived-table rewrite, join order intuition
questions.tables: organizations(org_id, segment, is_deleted); llm_requests(org_id, status, requested_at)

sections.context: SQL-035 (first version) repeated the same EXISTS subquery twice, once for the count and once for the percentage. Does the engine compute it twice?
sections.problem: EXPLAIN the repeated-EXISTS version of the AI adoption query and identify the duplicated subplan. Then write the single-pass version (the set of adopting organizations computed once and LEFT JOINed) and compare its plan.
sections.expected: The repeated version contains two identical subplans (hashed or per-row); the rewritten version scans `llm_requests` once.
sections.edge_cases: - Some optimizers can merge identical expressions, but you cannot rely on it; the plan tells you.
sections.hint1: Look for two "SubPlan n" nodes (PostgreSQL) or two "Select #n (subquery ...; dependent)" nodes (MySQL).
sections.hint2: Compute the adopting organizations once in a derived table with DISTINCT.
sections.hint3: The solution EXPLAINs the repeated version; EXPLAIN the rewrite yourself and compare.
sections.solution_pg:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT o.segment,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM llm_requests r
                             WHERE r.org_id = o.org_id AND r.status = 'success'
                               AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00')
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS adopting_orgs,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM llm_requests r
                                           WHERE r.org_id = o.org_id AND r.status = 'success'
                                             AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00')
                              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS adoption_pct
FROM organizations o
WHERE o.is_deleted = FALSE
GROUP BY o.segment;
sections.solution_mysql:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE
SELECT o.segment,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM llm_requests r
                             WHERE r.org_id = o.org_id AND r.status = 'success'
                               AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00')
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS adopting_orgs,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM llm_requests r
                                           WHERE r.org_id = o.org_id AND r.status = 'success'
                                             AND r.requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00')
                              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS adoption_pct
FROM organizations o
WHERE o.is_deleted = FALSE
GROUP BY o.segment;
sections.alternative_note: The single-pass rewrite: adopting organizations are computed once in a DISTINCT derived table and LEFT JOINed. Its plan contains one aggregation over `llm_requests` and no per-organization subplans.
sections.alternative_pg:
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT o.segment,
       COUNT(a.org_id)                              AS adopting_orgs,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(a.org_id) / COUNT(*), 1) AS adoption_pct
FROM organizations o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT org_id FROM llm_requests
           WHERE status = 'success' AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00') a
       ON a.org_id = o.org_id
WHERE o.is_deleted = FALSE
GROUP BY o.segment;
sections.alternative_mysql:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE
SELECT o.segment,
       COUNT(a.org_id)                              AS adopting_orgs,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(a.org_id) / COUNT(*), 1) AS adoption_pct
FROM organizations o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT org_id FROM llm_requests
           WHERE status = 'success' AND requested_at >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00') a
       ON a.org_id = o.org_id
WHERE o.is_deleted = FALSE
GROUP BY o.segment;
sections.assert: sum(1 for r in rows if r[0].strip().startswith('SubPlan')) >= 2
sections.explanation:
SQL is declarative, but repeated subexpressions are often *executed* repeatedly. In the plan, each EXISTS shows up as its own subplan, so the request table is probed twice per organization. (PostgreSQL may "hash" an uncorrelated version, but a correlated EXISTS stays per row.)

Rewrite: compute the set of adopting organizations once (a DISTINCT derived table or CTE) and LEFT JOIN it. The plan then contains a single aggregation over `llm_requests` and a hash join to `organizations`. The rewritten query (shown as the alternative solution) is the version to keep.

**Join order intuition:** the optimizer, not the textual order of the joins, decides the join order and the join algorithm. Your job is to give it a simple, set-based query with good statistics and indexes, and then check the plan. Rewrites that reduce rows early (filtering, pre-aggregation, semi-joins) usually help most.
sections.mistakes:
- Copy-pasting a subquery into several SELECT expressions.
- Believing a CTE is always computed once: inlined CTEs can be expanded at every reference (PostgreSQL 12+ inlines single-reference CTEs; `MATERIALIZED` forces one evaluation).
sections.performance: Halving the number of probes halves the subquery cost; on large fact tables the difference is substantial.
sections.interview: Reading a plan to spot duplicated work is a practical optimization skill.

questions.title: Query event properties stored as JSONB
questions.secondary: ->> extraction, @> containment, GIN index concept, MySQL equivalent

sections.context: Event properties are semi-structured: `view_pricing` carries a `referrer`, `ai_assist_used` a `feature`. Product analysts want breakdowns without a schema change.
sections.problem: For Q2 2025, return per `event_name` and property value: `view_pricing` events by `properties->>'referrer'`, and `ai_assist_used` events by `properties->>'feature'`. Additionally count `ai_assist_used` events whose properties **contain** `{"feature": "sql_copilot"}` with the `@>` operator, labelled `'sql_copilot (@>)'`. Sort by event name, then events descending, then value.
sections.expected: A handful of rows; the `@>` count equals the `sql_copilot` row of the extraction branch.
sections.edge_cases:
- `->` returns JSONB, `->>` returns text. Compare text with text.
- Missing keys yield NULL, not an error.
sections.hint1: `properties->>'referrer'` extracts a text value.
sections.hint2: `properties @> '{"feature": "sql_copilot"}'` tests containment and can use a GIN index.
sections.hint3: Combine the three breakdowns with UNION ALL.
sections.solution:
SELECT event_name, properties->>'referrer' AS property_value, COUNT(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'view_pricing'
  AND event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00' AND event_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY event_name, properties->>'referrer'
UNION ALL
SELECT event_name, properties->>'feature', COUNT(*)
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'ai_assist_used'
  AND event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00' AND event_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY event_name, properties->>'feature'
UNION ALL
SELECT event_name, 'sql_copilot (@>)', COUNT(*)
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'ai_assist_used'
  AND properties @> '{"feature": "sql_copilot"}'
  AND event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00' AND event_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY event_name, events DESC, property_value;
sections.equivalent_mysql:
SELECT event_name, properties->>'$.referrer' AS property_value, COUNT(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'view_pricing'
  AND event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00' AND event_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY event_name, properties->>'$.referrer'
UNION ALL
SELECT event_name, properties->>'$.feature', COUNT(*)
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'ai_assist_used'
  AND event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00' AND event_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY event_name, properties->>'$.feature'
UNION ALL
SELECT event_name, 'sql_copilot (@>)', COUNT(*)
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'ai_assist_used'
  AND JSON_CONTAINS(properties, '{"feature": "sql_copilot"}')
  AND event_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-04-01 00:00:00' AND event_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-07-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY event_name, events DESC, property_value;
sections.dialect_note: PostgreSQL stores JSON as `JSONB` (binary, keys de-duplicated and sorted) with operators `->`, `->>`, `#>>`, `@>` (containment), `?` (key exists) and GIN indexes (`CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN (properties)` or `jsonb_path_ops`). MySQL's `JSON` type uses path expressions (`'$.key'`) with `->`/`->>` shortcuts and `JSON_CONTAINS` instead of `@>`. MySQL cannot index a JSON column directly; it indexes a generated column or uses a functional index (and multi-valued indexes for arrays). The MySQL equivalent above returns the same rows.
sections.explanation:
JSONB keeps flexible attributes queryable: `->>` extracts values for grouping, and `@>` asks "does this document contain this sub-document?". Containment is what GIN indexes accelerate, so filters written as `@>` scale to large event tables, while `properties->>'feature' = 'sql_copilot'` needs an expression index.

The last branch double-checks the extraction branch: both count the same `sql_copilot` events.

Semi-structured columns are convenient but weakly typed. Promote frequently used keys to real columns (or generated columns, SQL-163) once they stabilize.
sections.mistakes:
- Comparing `properties->'feature'` (JSONB) with a text literal.
- Putting every attribute into JSON and losing constraints and types.
sections.performance: A GIN index on `properties` serves `@>` and `?` predicates; without it, both are full scans.
sections.interview: JSONB operators and indexing strategy are common PostgreSQL interview topics.

questions.title: Generated column for a normalized e-mail key
questions.secondary: STORED generated columns, indexing a derived value, duplicate lookup

sections.context: SQL-009, SQL-044 and SQL-142 normalize e-mails with `LOWER(TRIM(email))` on the fly, which prevents index use. A generated column computes the value once per row and can be indexed.
sections.problem: Create `sb_user_emails(user_id PK, email, email_norm)` where `email_norm` is a **stored generated column** `LOWER(TRIM(email))`, index it, load all users, and return the normalized e-mails that belong to more than one account with the account count. Sort by `email_norm`.
sections.expected: About two dozen rows, matching the duplicate clusters of SQL-142.
sections.edge_cases:
- You cannot insert into a generated column; omit it from the INSERT column list.
- MySQL also supports `VIRTUAL` generated columns (computed on read, still indexable); PostgreSQL supports `STORED` (and from PostgreSQL 18 also `VIRTUAL`).
sections.hint1: `email_norm VARCHAR(255) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (LOWER(TRIM(email))) STORED`.
sections.hint2: `CREATE INDEX ... ON sb_user_emails (email_norm)`.
sections.hint3: `GROUP BY email_norm HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
sections.verify:
SELECT email_norm, COUNT(*) AS accounts
FROM sb_user_emails
GROUP BY email_norm
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY email_norm;
sections.explanation:
A generated column is defined by an expression over other columns of the same row. `STORED` computes it on write and keeps it on disk, so it can be indexed and read like a normal column. The same DDL (`GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED`) works in PostgreSQL and MySQL. It is a rare case of fully portable advanced DDL.

The index on `email_norm` turns duplicate lookups ("does this normalized e-mail exist?") into index lookups, and could be made `UNIQUE` once the existing duplicates are merged. That is the database-level fix for the duplicate-account problem.
sections.mistakes:
- Trying to `UPDATE sb_user_emails SET email_norm = ...` (error: generated columns are read-only).
- Using non-deterministic functions (e.g. `NOW()`) in a generated column (rejected).
sections.performance: Stored generated columns cost a little on write and save repeated computation and full scans on read.
sections.interview: Shows knowledge of modern DDL features that bridge data quality and performance.

questions.title: Sign-ups per local calendar day (time zones)
questions.secondary: AT TIME ZONE semantics, DST, local-day bucketing, MySQL time zone tables

sections.context: Timestamps are stored in UTC. The Americas sales team asks: "How many users of our Americas-based customers signed up on each *local* day in March 2025 (the month of the US DST change)?" Each organization has its own IANA time zone (`organizations.timezone`), and bucketing by UTC date moves evening sign-ups into the next day.
sections.problem: For organizations whose `timezone` starts with `'America/'`, convert each sign-up to the organization's **own** zone and count sign-ups per local calendar date from 2025-03-01 to 2025-03-31. Next to it, show how many of the same users' sign-ups fall on that date when bucketed by **UTC** date. Sort by local date.
sections.expected: One row per local date with sign-ups; the two counts differ on some days.
sections.edge_cases:
- `ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'` turns a naive UTC timestamp into an absolute instant (timestamptz); applying `AT TIME ZONE o.timezone` to that converts it to the organization's wall-clock time. The zone can come from a column. US zones switch to DST on 2025-03-09 (offsets change by one hour), and Sao Paulo has no DST.
- MySQL: `CONVERT_TZ(ts, 'UTC', 'America/New_York')` works only when the time zone tables are loaded, otherwise it **silently returns NULL**.
sections.hint1: Convert first, then truncate to a date.
sections.hint2: `CAST((u.signup_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE o.timezone AS DATE)`.
sections.hint3: Count UTC-date sign-ups for the same date with a correlated subquery or conditional aggregation over both bucketings.
sections.solution:
WITH americas_users AS (
    SELECT u.user_id,
           u.signup_at,
           CAST((u.signup_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE o.timezone AS DATE) AS local_date
    FROM users u
    JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id
    WHERE o.timezone LIKE 'America/%'
)
SELECT l.local_signup_date,
       l.signups,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM americas_users n2
         WHERE CAST(n2.signup_at AS DATE) = l.local_signup_date) AS utc_date_signups
FROM (
    SELECT local_date AS local_signup_date, COUNT(*) AS signups
    FROM americas_users
    WHERE local_date >= DATE '2025-03-01' AND local_date < DATE '2025-04-01'
    GROUP BY local_date
) l
ORDER BY l.local_signup_date;
sections.equivalent_mysql:
WITH americas_users AS (
    SELECT u.user_id,
           u.signup_at,
           CAST(CONVERT_TZ(u.signup_at, 'UTC', o.timezone) AS DATE) AS local_date
    FROM users u
    JOIN organizations o ON o.org_id = u.org_id
    WHERE o.timezone LIKE 'America/%'
)
SELECT l.local_signup_date,
       l.signups,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM americas_users n2
         WHERE CAST(n2.signup_at AS DATE) = l.local_signup_date) AS utc_date_signups
FROM (
    SELECT local_date AS local_signup_date, COUNT(*) AS signups
    FROM americas_users
    WHERE local_date >= DATE '2025-03-01' AND local_date < DATE '2025-04-01'
    GROUP BY local_date
) l
ORDER BY l.local_signup_date;
sections.assert: any(r[1] != r[2] for r in rows)
sections.dialect_note:
**PostgreSQL** ships the IANA time zone database, so `AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'` (or a zone taken from a column) always works. Mind the double application: on a `timestamp without time zone`, `AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'` *interprets* it as UTC and returns `timestamptz`; on a `timestamptz`, `AT TIME ZONE zone` *renders* local wall-clock time.

**MySQL** needs its time zone tables populated (`mysql_tzinfo_to_sql /usr/share/zoneinfo | mysql -u root mysql` on Linux/macOS, or the downloadable package on Windows). Without them, `CONVERT_TZ` with named zones returns NULL and every row falls out of the date filter **without an error**. Fixed offsets (`'+00:00'`, `'-05:00'`) always work but ignore DST. The MySQL equivalent was validated with loaded time zone tables.
sections.explanation:
Business days are local. "Sign-ups on 2025-03-14" for a Chicago customer means midnight-to-midnight Chicago time, which is 05:00 or 06:00 UTC depending on DST. Converting each timestamp to its organization's zone **before** truncating to a date gives the correct buckets. Truncating the UTC timestamp attributes evening sign-ups to the next day, which is why the two count columns differ on several days.

Practical rules: store timestamps in UTC (as this dataset does), store each entity's IANA zone name, convert at query time, and never hard-code offsets for zones with DST.
sections.mistakes:
- `signup_at - INTERVAL '5' HOUR` as "New York time" (wrong for half the year).
- Converting the filter boundaries instead of the data, and getting DST transition days wrong.
sections.performance: Converting each row prevents index use on `signup_at`; for large tables, filter a padded UTC range first (local range ± 14 hours), then apply the exact local filter.
sections.interview: Time zone bugs are among the most common production analytics errors; explaining DST and the double `AT TIME ZONE` is a strong signal.

questions.title: Extract numeric limits from document text (regular expressions)
questions.secondary: regex match and capture per dialect, casting extracted text, case sensitivity

sections.context: The support bot often answers questions about limits ("How many X per workspace?"). The content team wants an inventory of the numeric limits mentioned in the knowledge-base chunks, to check that they are consistent.
sections.problem: Find chunks whose text contains `limit is <number>` and extract the first such number. Return per `limit_value` (integer) the number of chunks and of distinct document versions. Sort by `limit_value`.
sections.edge_cases:
- PostgreSQL `~` is case-sensitive (`~*` is case-insensitive); MySQL's `REGEXP_LIKE` follows the column collation, so it is **case-insensitive** by default unless you pass the `'c'` match type.
- Only the first occurrence per chunk is extracted.
sections.hint1: Filter chunks with a regex match, then extract the digits.
sections.hint2: PostgreSQL: `SUBSTRING(chunk_text FROM 'limit is ([0-9]+)')` returns the capture group.
sections.hint3: MySQL: `REGEXP_SUBSTR(chunk_text, 'limit is [0-9]+')`, then strip the non-digits with `REGEXP_REPLACE(..., '[^0-9]', '')` and CAST.
sections.solution_pg:
SELECT CAST(SUBSTRING(chunk_text FROM 'limit is ([0-9]+)') AS INT) AS limit_value,
       COUNT(*)                                                    AS chunks,
       COUNT(DISTINCT document_id)                                 AS documents
FROM document_chunks
WHERE chunk_text ~ 'limit is [0-9]+'
GROUP BY CAST(SUBSTRING(chunk_text FROM 'limit is ([0-9]+)') AS INT)
ORDER BY limit_value;
sections.solution_mysql:
SELECT CAST(REGEXP_REPLACE(REGEXP_SUBSTR(chunk_text, 'limit is [0-9]+', 1, 1, 'c'), '[^0-9]', '') AS UNSIGNED) AS limit_value,
       COUNT(*)                                                                                             AS chunks,
       COUNT(DISTINCT document_id)                                                                          AS documents
FROM document_chunks
WHERE REGEXP_LIKE(chunk_text, 'limit is [0-9]+', 'c')
GROUP BY CAST(REGEXP_REPLACE(REGEXP_SUBSTR(chunk_text, 'limit is [0-9]+', 1, 1, 'c'), '[^0-9]', '') AS UNSIGNED)
ORDER BY limit_value;
sections.dialect_note:
| task | PostgreSQL | MySQL 8 |
|---|---|---|
| match | `s ~ 'pat'`, `s ~* 'pat'` (case-insensitive) | `REGEXP_LIKE(s, 'pat', 'c')`, `s REGEXP 'pat'` |
